docs.title: Zeta-80 a Z80 ROMless SBC
docs.text: Repository: github.com/gloveboxes/Z80ROMlessSBC

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The project breadboard runs the specified Z84C0020PEC Z80 at its rated 20 MHz clock speed. It pairs a Z80 processor with a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W to run CP/M without a ROM chip.

The Z80 runs from 64 KiB of SRAM (plus 64 KiB of banked SRAM). The Pico handles clocking, boot loading and verification, terminal and disk I/O, random numbers, and timers. Phase 10 also provides network services. Four persistent CP/M drives live in the Pico's onboard flash. Phase 9 uses a USB terminal; Phase 10 adds a browser-based WebSocket terminal. After bring-up, the Phase 9 automatic loader starts CP/M on Pico reset, ready for a later picocom connection.

This guide covers the hardware, firmware, and phased tests needed to reproduce the build. Validate your own wiring and operation as you go; clock-rate qualification and timing margins require measurements on your build.

docs.title: Start building
docs.text:
Install the software listed in Toolchain, including the complete Arm compiler, Python, Pico SDK and USB utilities.

  1. Check the parts inventory and read the breadboard and meter basics.
  2. Follow the implementation plan in order, from power checks through SRAM loading, CP/M, and terminal and disk testing.
  3. Use the firmware build and flashing guide to build and load the firmware for your current phase.

The hardware chapters are detailed references; you do not need to understand every firmware excerpt before starting. Use the glossary for unfamiliar terms.

docs.title: How does it boot without ROM?
docs.text:
The Pico feeds the Z80 instructions that make it write and verify its own boot image in SRAM. After verification, the Z80 is reset and starts executing that image from RAM. The Pico never drives the memory address bus or writes SRAM directly.

See the loader sequence for the protocol and timing, and Phase 6 for the implementation and hardware checks.

docs.title: System architecture
docs.text:
The Pico 2 W is a multicore I/O controller: core 0 configures the nominal 20 MHz Z80 clock and owns assisted SRAM loading and Z80 I/O. Phase 10 uses PIO for clock generation and SRAM bank-select writes. Core 1 owns USB, runtime storage, Wi-Fi and network clients. Bounded console rings and request/result mailboxes separate the two cores. The Z80 itself writes SRAM during loading and executes CP/M directly from SRAM after verification and reset. USB supervisor commands request Z80 actions through a bounded queue; USB interrupts and endpoint operations remain on core 1.

Open or download the full-size SVG. The diagram follows the maintained Phase 10 implementation, which compiles the Phase 9 automatic-loader application with networking enabled.

docs.title: Working and tested breadboard implementation
docs.text:
The breadboard implementation shown below has been built and tested, running the Z80 at 20 MHz with CP/M executing from SRAM. It brings together the Z80, Pico 2 W, SRAM, and interface logic across three BB830 breadboards.

Follow the staged implementation plan to reproduce the build and validate each stage, from power and clock checks through ROMless boot loading, terminal access, and persistent disk I/O.

docs.title: Explore further
docs.text:
• USB CP/M terminal and flash storage - load CP/M, reach the prompt, and test persistent disk I/O.
  • System operation - virtual I/O, flash storage, and runtime coordination.
  • I/O ports and services - the terminal and disk interface, plus ROMLESS-SVC/1 timers, clock, utilities and persistent environment variables.
  • CP/M documentation - boot-image construction, disk media, and software compatibility.
  • Firmware testing - host tests, Z80 emulation, and hardware validation boundaries.
  • Pico flashing and USB supervisor tools - device selection, verified updates, clean stop, and journal diagnostics.
  • Source index - maintained firmware, tools, and implementation guides.

docs.title: Related projects
docs.text:
Two related projects provide a C development toolchain and a collection of CP/M applications and disk images for this computer. Together, they offer a path from C source on a modern development machine to applications running under CP/M on this project's real Z80.

C Compiler & toolchain DCC C Compiler Build C applications on your computer. Run them on a Z80 under CP/M. Explore DCC ↗ 8800 Applications & disk images Altair 8800 AI Edition Explore CP/M applications and build disk images for this Z80 computer. Explore Altair ↗

The disks supplied with this project already include a default set of applications. The system boots 64K CP/M 2.2, a custom version of the original Burcon CP/M 2.2 and BIOS, modified and optimised for the Z80 and this board. You can use these supplied disks when you reach the CP/M phases; building or importing additional applications is optional.

This is the application-development goal for the later stages of the project. Start with the staged hardware bring-up, completing the documented electrical checks and tests in Phases 0–8 before proceeding to CP/M disk deployment. Those phases establish correct power, clock, bus, SRAM, and I/O operation on your board.

Phase 9 introduces flash-backed disks, Z80 CP/M booting, and applications through the USB terminal. Phase 10 adds the WebSocket terminal. The deployment example below describes the completed Phase 10 system; follow each phase's own firmware and validation instructions as you reach it.

docs.title: DCC C Compiler
docs.text:
The DCC C Compiler builds Z80 CP/M .COM applications on Windows, macOS, and Linux. It supports C89 with selected C99/C11 features, making it possible to write C applications with modern development tools for a CP/M target. Its documentation includes a C conformance guide describing supported features and target exceptions.

DCC translates C source into M80 assembly, then uses M80 and L80 to assemble and link the executable. Its dccmake command coordinates the build, and its runtime provides console and file I/O and other C library facilities suited to CP/M. See this project's CP/M and DCC compatibility overview for the runtime environment provided by the Z80 ROMless SBC.

docs.title: Altair 8800 AI Edition
docs.text:
Altair 8800 AI Edition includes a collection of CP/M/Z80 applications in its Apps folder. The collection includes C applications built with DCC and tooling to package applications into Altair 88-DCDD disk images. These images can also supply applications for the Z80 ROMless SBC.

Once the earlier bring-up tests pass and you reach Phases 9–10, use the following workflow to bring applications across from the Altair project.

docs.title: In the ESP32 Altair 8800 AI Edition project
docs.text:
1. Build the desired C application in the Altair project's Apps collection using its DCC build instructions, and create the corresponding 88-DCDD .dsk image.
  2. Find the source disk images in the Altair project's /esp32-altair-8800/disks folder, then copy the desired .dsk image into Z80ROMlessSBC/src/disks/source-altair/.

docs.title: In the Z80ROMlessSBC project
docs.text:
These steps target the completed Phase 10 hardware and firmware setup. When first bringing up Phase 9, use its USB CP/M and flash storage instructions and complete its tests before moving on to Phase 10.

  1. Open the Z80ROMlessSBC project folder in VS Code. Choose Terminal → Run Task and select one of the disk deployment tasks listed below. The task automatically prepares the copied disk images and installs them into the Pico's flash storage.
  2. After deploying the disks, choose Terminal → Run Task → Build and flash Pico - Phase 10 firmware to build and deploy the Pico firmware for the Z80 boot process. This task preserves the disks you just installed.
  3. With both the disks and Pico firmware deployed, boot CP/M on the real Z80 and access the installed applications on the configured drives A: through D:.

The Pico serves the flash-backed disks while the Z80 executes CP/M and its applications. Disk conversion and provisioning are handled by the dedicated VS Code disk deployment tasks; no manual conversion commands are required. See the disk provisioning details for how this works. The firmware uses native 524,288-byte images rather than the original 88-DCDD sector framing.

docs.title: VS Code disk deployment tasks
docs.text:
The tasks in .vscode/tasks.json use the following source images from src/disks/source-altair/:

Task Disks replaced Source image Flash Pico - All disks (A-D) A: through D: All four images listed below Flash Pico - Drive A A: cpm63k.dsk Flash Pico - Drive B B: bdsc-v1.60.dsk Flash Pico - Drive C C: escape-posix.dsk Flash Pico - Drive D D: blank.dsk

Copy an updated disk image using the filename expected by its task, or update the task's source path to select a different application image. The A: tasks regenerate the board-native boot disk; the B:–D: tasks convert the selected Altair images at flash time. The tasks replace the selected disks without backups and preserve firmware and ENV settings. All disks (A-D) also validates and installs the newly built boot package with Drive A. Individual drive tasks preserve the installed boot package; Drive A checks compatibility. Follow the task's confirmation prompt before deployment.

Drive A: also contains the boot system and needs the board-native BIOS and matching boot package. Drives B: through D: can hold application disks converted from validated Altair images. See Phase 9: USB CP/M and flash storage for the storage design and the disk media README for conversion commands, the default source-image mapping, and selective installation of application disks.

docs.title: Toolchain
docs.text:
Install these tools before building the Pico firmware. The Arm compiler builds the Pico application; a separate Z80 assembler builds the programs that run on the Z80. Python runs the build helpers, embeds the browser terminal in firmware, and prepares CP/M disk images.

Run project commands from the repository root. The checked-in VS Code tasks use macOS/Linux shell syntax. Native Windows setup and its current limitations are described below.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Tool Used for When required Git Checkout, Pico SDK and recursive submodules All firmware builds Complete Arm GNU Toolchain (arm-none-eabi) Pico C/C++ compilation, linking and binary utilities; includes Newlib and the C++ runtime All firmware builds CMake and Ninja Configure and build the firmware All firmware builds Native C/C++ compiler Build host tools such as pioasm; run native firmware tests SDK tools and host tests Python 3.11 or newer, with pip and venv Build scripts, embedded HTML, CP/M image generation and USB utilities All firmware builds Raspberry Pi Pico SDK, including submodules RP2350, USB and Pico 2 W Wi-Fi libraries All firmware builds picotool Generate RP2350 firmware outputs and program/verify the Pico over USB Firmware builds and flashing z80asm Assemble Z80 diagnostics, BIOS, CCP/BDOS and AUTORUN Top-level firmware CMake configuration, Phase 6 scope/soak targets and CP/M images z80dasm Independent Z80 binary disassembly and assembly/disassembly checks Optional inspection and CP/M audit work Bundled disassemble_cpm64.py Disassemble/audit the preserved CP/M image and generate its Z80 source port CP/M source regeneration/audit; Python standard library only cpmtools (cpmcp, cpmrm) Install native CP/M programs into disk images CP/M image generation picocom, or a Windows serial terminal USB console and supervisor commands Hardware bring-up and USB console use pyserial Discover and communicate with USB serial devices from Python Project USB utilities lsof and ps Check serial ownership and release picocom before flashing Project flash/supervisor scripts on macOS/Linux VS Code Editor and convenient build/flash tasks Optional MkDocs and the project's documentation packages Build or preview this website Documentation work only

picotool is Raspberry Pi's device/binary utility. picocom is a serial terminal. They serve different purposes; installing one does not install the other. The utility's command is picotool, singular.

docs.title: macOS
docs.text:
Install Apple's Command Line Tools if absent, then install the host packages using Homebrew:

xcode-select --install
brew install git cmake ninja python picotool picocom z80asm cpmtools

The Command Line Tools supply the native Clang compiler and developer tools. Install the complete Arm compiler separately using the next section. The Homebrew arm-none-eabi-gcc formula alone lacks the Newlib runtime required by this project; the project has encountered missing -lc and -lg link errors with that installation.

docs.title: Linux (Debian/Ubuntu)
docs.text:
Install the host tools and USB development library:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install build-essential git cmake ninja-build python3 python3-venv \
  python3-pip picocom z80asm cpmtools lsof pkg-config libusb-1.0-0-dev

Check python3 --version is at least 3.11. Install the complete Arm toolchain below, then install a current RP2350-capable picotool from Raspberry Pi's prebuilt SDK tools, or follow its source build instructions. Put the directory containing picotool on PATH. Follow those instructions for Linux USB permissions/udev rules as well; serial access may also require your distribution's serial-device group membership.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
Install Git for Windows, CMake, Ninja, and the complete Arm toolchain described below. Enable the installers' PATH options, or add the directories containing their executables to your user Path. Install a native C/C++ build environment, such as Visual Studio Build Tools with its C++ desktop workload, for SDK host tools. Use its Developer PowerShell when those tools need the native compiler.

Windows needs a Python installation in addition to the Arm compiler. Install the Python install manager from Python.org, then install a runtime and check it in a new PowerShell window. The example uses Python 3.14; the project requires 3.11 or newer:

py install 3.14
py -3.14 --version
py -3.14 -m pip --version

For an existing Python installation, py -3 --version and py -3 -m pip --version check the selected interpreter. Follow the official Windows Python guide if py or python is not found; reopen VS Code after changing Path.

Install picotool from Raspberry Pi's SDK tools releases. Make picotool.exe and its supplied runtime dependencies available together, and follow the picotool documentation for Windows USB driver setup. Use a Windows serial terminal such as PuTTY for the Pico's COM port; picocom is used in the macOS/Linux examples.

The checked-in flash tasks and pico_flash.py/pico_supervisor.py workflows currently depend on POSIX shell commands, lsof and ps. Installing Python does not make those workflows native Windows compatible. The automatic toolchain checks in pico_build.py also currently use Unix executable names. With a compatible z80asm also available on PATH, use direct CMake commands for native Windows firmware builds, and copy the built UF2 to the Pico’s BOOTSEL removable drive for initial programming. Follow the board power requirements. Use a Linux environment for the documented z80asm/cpmtools CP/M image workflow; USB access from a virtual Linux environment needs separate configuration.

docs.title: Z80 assembly and disassembly tools
docs.text:
The project's external assembler is NonGNU z80asm. The tested installation reports Z80 assembler version 1.8. build_images.py invokes it with z80asm -o <binary> <source>; CMake also invokes it for the Phase 6 scope/soak and Phase 9/10 disk-diagnostic programs. The checked-in source uses this assembler's syntax and directives. Other assemblers, including the separate z88dk assembler, should not be substituted solely because their executable names look similar.

The top-level CMake project includes the Phase 9/10 definitions during configuration. Their disk-diagnostic generation requires z80asm, so install it before configuring even when your selected build target is an earlier phase. cpmtools is additionally required when generating CP/M disk images: cpmcp and cpmrm install/replace the native AUTORUN.COM on Drive A. Both are included in the macOS/Linux installation commands above.

z80dasm is an optional independent Z80 disassembler, used for the disassembly/assembly round-trip check recorded in the CP/M audit. The current firmware build and Python image scripts do not invoke it automatically. Add it when inspecting binaries or repeating those independent checks:

# macOS
brew install z80asm z80dasm

# Debian/Ubuntu
sudo apt install z80asm z80dasm

Check the installed tools:

z80asm --version
z80dasm --help

The repository also includes src/cpm/disassemble_cpm64.py. This Python tool decodes the preserved Burcon CP/M image, emits an Intel 8080 listing and a Z80 source port, and generates the audit report. It uses Python's standard library and does not require a disassembler package from pip or the z80dasm executable. Its default outputs are checked-in source/report files; pass output paths when generating a separate review copy. Inspect its options with:

python3 src/cpm/disassemble_cpm64.py --help

The arm-none-eabi-objdump and arm-none-eabi-objcopy utilities are supplied with the Arm toolchain. Pico SDK builds use them to produce listings and binary outputs for the Pico firmware. Use z80dasm for inspecting Z80 code.

docs.title: Install the complete Arm GNU toolchain
docs.text:
Use the official Arm GNU Toolchain releases and Arm's installation guide. Select the arm-none-eabi bare-metal target, with both C and C++ support. Match the download's host to the computer doing the build:

Build computer Host package to select Target Apple Silicon Mac darwin-arm64 arm-none-eabi Intel Mac darwin-x86_64 arm-none-eabi Linux PC x86_64 Linux arm-none-eabi 64-bit Linux on Raspberry Pi/Arm aarch64 Linux arm-none-eabi Windows PC Windows installer/archive for the supported host architecture arm-none-eabi

The host architecture does not change the target: the Pico 2 W build uses RP2350 Arm Cortex-M33 code. Select arm-none-eabi rather than the Linux-target or AArch64-target toolchains. Arm GNU Toolchain 15.3.Rel1 / GCC 15.3.1 has passed the project's Phase 6 and Phase 10 builds; the VS Code tasks do not pin that release.

docs.title: macOS and Linux archive installation
docs.text:
1. Download the matching .tar.xz archive from the release page.
  2. Extract it into an empty toolchain directory. The example below uses a stable directory name so your shell configuration need not contain a release number.
  3. Add its bin directory to PATH and verify the runtime libraries.

Replace the archive path with the actual downloaded filename:

arm_archive="$HOME/Downloads/arm-gnu-toolchain-RELEASE-HOST-arm-none-eabi.tar.xz"
arm_install="$HOME/.local/share/arm-gnu-toolchain"
mkdir -p "$arm_install"
tar -xJf "$arm_archive" -C "$arm_install" --strip-components=1
export PATH="$arm_install/bin:$PATH"

Use a fresh directory when installing a different release to avoid mixing toolchains. A versioned name such as arm-gnu-toolchain-<release> also works. To keep the example installation on PATH, add this line to ~/.zshrc on macOS or your Linux shell's startup file, then open a new terminal:

export PATH="$HOME/.local/share/arm-gnu-toolchain/bin:$PATH"

The macOS .pkg installer is an alternative. If you use it, add its installed bin directory to PATH; it may be under /Applications/ArmGNUToolchain/.

docs.title: Windows installer or ZIP installation
docs.text:
Run Arm's Windows installer, or extract the Windows ZIP archive into a chosen directory. Keep the entire directory tree, including the libraries beside bin. Add the directory containing arm-none-eabi-gcc.exe to your user Path, then open a new PowerShell window. For a temporary session, replace the example below with the actual installation directory:

$armBin = 'C:\Tools\ArmGNUToolchain\bin'
$env:Path = "$armBin;$env:Path"

docs.title: Verify the compiler and runtimes
docs.text:
Run these checks after updating PATH; the same commands work in PowerShell:

arm-none-eabi-gcc --version
arm-none-eabi-g++ --version
arm-none-eabi-gcc -mcpu=cortex-m33 -mthumb -mfloat-abi=softfp -print-file-name=libc.a
arm-none-eabi-gcc -mcpu=cortex-m33 -mthumb -mfloat-abi=softfp -print-file-name=libg.a
arm-none-eabi-g++ -mcpu=cortex-m33 -mthumb -mfloat-abi=softfp -print-file-name=libstdc++.a

The last three commands must print paths to installed library files. An output of just libc.a, libg.a or libstdc++.a means the selected compiler cannot find that runtime. Check which compiler is selected with command -v arm-none-eabi-gcc on macOS/Linux, or Get-Command arm-none-eabi-gcc in PowerShell.

docs.title: Checkout and Pico SDK
docs.text:
Clone the project and its WebSocket library submodule:

git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/gloveboxes/Z80ROMlessSBC.git
cd Z80ROMlessSBC

For an existing checkout, use git submodule update --init --recursive. Install a complete Pico SDK, including its submodules, if one is not already installed. For macOS/Linux:

mkdir -p "$HOME/GitHub/pico"
git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/raspberrypi/pico-sdk.git \
  "$HOME/GitHub/pico/pico-sdk"
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DPICO_BOARD=pico2_w \
  -DPICO_SDK_PATH="$HOME/GitHub/pico/pico-sdk"

For native Windows, run the equivalent from the project root in PowerShell:

git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/raspberrypi/pico-sdk.git "$env:USERPROFILE\GitHub\pico\pico-sdk"
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DPICO_BOARD=pico2_w "-DPICO_SDK_PATH=$env:USERPROFILE\GitHub\pico\pico-sdk"

Reuse an existing SDK by passing its directory to -DPICO_SDK_PATH; the repository's default path belongs to the author's machine. Configure with your own path explicitly. For example, build the first-phase firmware with:

cmake --build build --target z80_stage01_supervisor -j

Choose the target matching your hardware's current phase using the firmware target table.

docs.title: Python packages and USB console
docs.text:
Create a separate Python environment for the project USB utilities. On macOS/Linux, run:

python3 -m venv .venv-flash
.venv-flash/bin/python -m pip install -r scripts/requirements-flash.txt
.venv-flash/bin/python -c 'import sys, serial; print(sys.executable)'

The dependency is pyserial; its Python import name is serial. The VS Code flash tasks activate this environment. Native Windows uses a different environment layout; for Python dependencies and serial-library checks:

py -3 -m venv .venv-flash
.\.venv-flash\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -r scripts/requirements-flash.txt
.\.venv-flash\Scripts\python.exe -c "import sys, serial; print(sys.executable)"

For a USB terminal, select 115200 baud, 8 data bits, no parity, one stop bit and no flow control. Identify the Pico's actual serial port first. A macOS example is:

picocom --baud 115200 --databits 8 --parity n --stopbits 1 --flow n /dev/cu.usbmodemXXXX

Linux commonly uses /dev/ttyACM0; Windows uses a COM port. Replace these examples with your discovered port. Exit picocom with Ctrl+A, then Ctrl+X. See USB console setup and the Pico utilities guide for device discovery, flashing and the board's required power sequence.

docs.title: VS Code builds and final checks
docs.text:
On macOS/Linux, choose Terminal → Run Task → Build and flash Pico - Phase 10 firmware to build and deploy Phase 10 firmware while preserving disks and ENV. This task uses scripts/pico_build.py for its build step. It searches an explicit ARM_GNU_TOOLCHAIN_BIN override, the build's cached compiler, complete toolchains on PATH, then ~/.local/share/arm-gnu-toolchain*/bin. It checks the runtimes before building. For an installation outside these locations, set the override before starting VS Code, for example:

export ARM_GNU_TOOLCHAIN_BIN="$HOME/.local/share/arm-gnu-toolchain/bin"

An existing CMake build keeps its selected compiler. Use a new build directory when switching toolchains. An explicit cmake --fresh configure also resets the cache; pass your SDK path and keep the desired compiler first on PATH.

Check the host tools without a Pico attached:

git --version
cmake --version
ninja --version
picotool version

Also check z80asm --version before configuring firmware. For CP/M image generation, check that cpmcp and cpmrm are available. For independent binary inspection, check the optional z80dasm --help (its header includes the version). No attached Pico is needed to build firmware.

Continue with firmware build and provisioning, firmware testing, or building the documentation. Documentation dependencies are listed separately in docs/docs/requirements.txt.

docs.title: Appendix D: CP/M BIOS and dcc Compatibility
docs.text:
This software reference is optional for hardware assembly. The host emulator lets you try CP/M without a Pico; physical buses, flash recovery, and timing require hardware testing.

The system runs 64K CP/M 2.2 with a custom BIOS assembled from src/cpm/z80_bios.asm. The BIOS maps standard console and disk operations to Pico-serviced I/O, keeping the WebSocket terminal and flash storage transparent to applications.

dcc produces compatible Z80 .COM programs. Its runtime uses standard CP/M page-zero vectors; BDOS handles console and file services, and the BIOS handles hardware transfers.

docs.title: In this section
docs.text:
For the compiler, C library, and CP/M APIs, see the DCC documentation.

  • Image provenance and machine boundary
  • CP/M memory map and entry points
  • Z80 I/O with the PIO engine
  • Custom BIOS responsibilities
  • Bank-1 fixed-address DCC library
  • Compatibility boundaries
  • Validation requirements
  • Automated end-to-end test
  • Interactive CP/M test

docs.title: Implemented layout
docs.text:
Bank 1 owns CP/M disk allocation and directory state. Bank-0 BDOS calls enter bank 1 through the shim at EE00h; bank-1 C code calls its own 0005h BDOS vector. Bank-0 console calls remain local. One DCC library can be loaded at 0100h at a time.

Bank-1 address Purpose 0000h–00FFh CP/M vectors and page zero 0100h–(heap_base-1) Fixed library image, static data and BSS heap_base–(C800h-stack-1) Library DCC malloc heap (C800h-stack)–C7FFh Library call stack, configured by the .LIB header C800h–DDFFh General bmalloc pool, 5,632 bytes DE00h–E5FFh BDOS proxy, loader, exports and service stack E600h–EDFFh Pinned extent allocator and metadata EE00h–FB3Fh Authoritative CP/M 2.2 BDOS FB40h–FB7Fh Mirrored warm-boot return and extent lookup FB80h–FEFFh BIOS buffer and core FF00h–FFFFh Mirrored bank-switch gateway

The library image, C stack, and allocator are pinned. breset resets only the general pool; it does not unload the library or reset its DCC heap.

docs.title: Library memory layout
docs.text:
A library owns the fixed region 0100h–C7FFh (50,944 bytes). Its image, BSS, DCC malloc heap and call stack share that region; only the stack size is chosen explicitly. Everything from C800h up is outside the library: the shared bmalloc pool, then pinned resident code loaded and verified by the firmware at boot.

0000h  +-----------------------------+
       | CP/M page zero              |  0005h = bank-1 BDOS vector
0100h  +-----------------------------+  ---- library region ----
       | Image: code and data        |  .LIB image length, loaded verbatim
       +-----------------------------+  0100h + image length
       | BSS                         |  zeroed by the loader
       +-----------------------------+  heap_base (linked __hstart)
       | DCC malloc heap             |  __brk = heap_base at load
       |            ...              |
       +-----------------------------+  __hlimit = C800h - stack
       | Call stack                  |  256..2048 bytes, grows down
C800h  +-----------------------------+  ---- shared pool ----
       | bmalloc pool                |  5,632 bytes, 22 x 256-byte extents
DE00h  +-----------------------------+  ---- pinned resident services ----
       | BDOS proxy                  |  E=6, used by the bank-0 BDOS shim
DE8Eh  | Loader, search, request and |  library request record at DF20h,
       | library context state       |  library DMA/search context at DF80h
E000h  | Library loader              |  validates the header, copies image
E300h  | Export table, capability    |  capability record at E360h,
       | record, descriptor helpers  |  descriptor helpers at E390h
E400h  | DMA buffer, FCB staging,    |  call token at E4D6h, library FCB
       | mailboxes, service stacks   |  at E500h, private stacks to E5FFh
E600h  | Dispatcher, allocator       |  dispatcher at E640h, tables at
       | tables, context hooks       |  E700h, context hooks at E780h
E800h  | Extent allocator            |  E=0..5
EC00h  | Capabilities and library    |  E=7 query, E=8 LOAD/INVALIDATE/
       | control                     |  QUERY/CALL
EE00h  +-----------------------------+  ---- CP/M ----
       | CP/M 2.2 BDOS               |  authoritative disk and allocation state
FB40h  | Warm-boot trampoline,       |  mirrored; warm-boot return and
       | extent lookup               |  checked-transfer lookup at FB48h
FB80h  | BIOS buffer and core        |
FF00h  +-----------------------------+  ---- mirrored in both banks ----
       | Bank-switch gateway         |  READ/WRITE/INFO/service entries;
FFFFh  +-----------------------------+  FFF0h-FFFFh private workspace

The library may call its own BDOS through 0005h. It accesses pool memory only through what the host passes it: the copied call frame, or a pool extent the host leases to it and validates, such as ISAM's bulk buffer. It must not call the gateway or touch resident service memory; DE00h–FFFFh is reserved for system code. Growth of the resident services never reduces the library region.

Region Start End (exclusive) Set by Image 0100h 0100h + image length Linked by l80c; copied by the loader BSS Image end heap_base Linked by l80c; zeroed by the loader DCC heap heap_base C800h − stack __brk and __hlimit initialized by the loader Call stack C800h − stack C800h dcc-stack-bytes, recorded in the .LIB header

docs.title: Size rules
docs.text:
The image, BSS and at least one heap byte must fit below the stack: heap_base < C800h − stack, with heap_base at or above the end of both the image and the BSS. There is no separate image-size cap; a larger image leaves less heap. The stack must be 256–2,048 bytes in 256-byte units.

These rules are enforced at every stage:

  • dccmake rejects an invalid dcc-stack-bytes, or one smaller than the compiler's computed stack requirement.
  • l80c --lib fails with "bank-1 heap overlaps the configured stack" if the image, BSS and heap do not fit, and records heap_base and the stack size in the header.
  • The loader rejects a header that breaks the same rules with FORMAT status before copying the image.
Stack Heap limit Image + BSS + heap Largest image (no BSS, 1-byte heap) 256 C700h 50,688 50,687 bytes, through C6FEh 512 C600h 50,432 50,431 bytes, through C5FEh 1,024 C400h 49,920 49,919 bytes, through C3FEh 2,048 C000h 48,896 48,895 bytes, through BFFEh

docs.title: Loader initialization
docs.text: After validating the header and copying the image, the loader zeroes the BSS from the image end up to heap_base, sets the linked DCC __brk to heap_base and __hlimit to C800h minus the stack. The heap is not cleared. A library linked without the DCC runtime records FFFFh for both variable offsets and uses its image end as heap_base.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Library Image BSS Heap Stack LIBDEMO DATA.LIB 8,863 bytes, 0100h–239Eh 4 bytes 41,565 bytes, 23A3h–C5FFh 512 bytes, C600h–C7FFh ISAM ISAM.LIB 43,006 bytes, 0100h–A8FDh 1,104 bytes 5,810 bytes, AD4Eh–C3FFh 1,024 bytes, C400h–C7FFh

Exact figures follow each build. Use DCC's meminfo() inside the library to report heap capacity, committed bytes and remaining growth at run time.

docs.title: Library file and linker
docs.text:
DCC's native l80c --lib, maintained in its src/l80c/l80c.c, links a fixed-origin image at 0100h and emits one library format: a 26-byte header, up to eight 12-byte export entries, then the image. Every export has a canonical signature. Like a CP/M .COM, the image is loaded verbatim without a checksum.

Byte offset Bytes Meaning 0 4 B1LB 4 1 Format version 1 5, 6, 7 3 ABI major 1, minor 0, call revision 1 8 2 Origin 0100h 10 2 Image length 12 2 Export count, 1–8 14 2 Reserved, zero 16 2 Stack bytes, 256–2,048 in 256-byte units 18 2 Header length, 26 + 12 × exports 20, 22 4 __brk and __hlimit image offsets, or FFFFh without the DCC runtime 24 2 Absolute heap base (__hstart) after the image and BSS

Each export entry is:

Entry offset Bytes Meaning 0 8 Zero-padded export name 8 2 Adapter offset relative to image origin 10 2 Canonical signature string offset relative to image origin

All eight entries fit in the first 128-byte disk record. Signature strings are nonempty, NUL-terminated ASCII, at most 255 characters, inside the image. The full string is compared, not a short hash that could collide. The loader validates both offsets against the image.

LIBDEMO separates host/ and lib/, each with its own dccmake.txt and build/. Its root configuration contains dcc-projects=lib,host; one root dccmake invocation builds the library first, then its host. The library configuration selects dcc-output-format=lib, automatic exports, and DCC's native l80c through l80c-tool. With dcc-library-api=auto, compiler-derived public definitions generate host/generated/API.H, host wrappers and bank adapters. Buffer rules live in the library source; no handwritten API header or JSON interface is needed. Run dccmake dcc-contract-only=true in the root to generate the client contract without assembly or linking; COM children are skipped. Normal builds refresh it automatically. Clients include the generated header and compile the generated wrappers with BANKLIB/BIOSBANK. dccmake -help describes the workflow. A header path instead of auto validates a handwritten contract against the same discovered, signed exports. M80 public symbols are limited to six characters; generated adapter names are unique within that limit.

ABI 1.0 clients discover the versioned library service through BIOS operation 7 and submit LOAD/INVALIDATE/QUERY/CALL requests through operation 8. They do not inspect loader-private mailboxes or allocator tables. See the exact capability/control records. The linker writes, and the loader requires, format 1, ABI 1.0 and call revision 1. An invalid header or read failure leaves the module uncallable, with distinct FORMAT/IO status. The SDK runs onload/onunload automatically; these C lifecycle hooks are SDK policy, not CP/M BDOS functions.

The resident dispatcher publishes a per-call two-byte token at the public E4D6h ABI data address. The runtime never reuses a token within its lifetime: after 65,534 invocations it returns BL_EXHAUSTED rather than wrapping, reserving the last token for unload cleanup. Bank-1 object constructors may use the token as an opaque handle.

The LIBDEMO example builds DATA.LIB, an ordinary DCC C data service, and DATATEST.COM, its bank-0 client. The host runs eight numbered end-to-end checks with explicit PASS/FAIL results. Ordinary-looking add16, upper, filerd, blknew, blkread and blkfree calls demonstrate scalar values, copied in/out text, file open/read/close, flat record IN/OUT/INOUT transfers, and chunked reads from a 4 KiB bank-owned block. The two lifecycle hooks complete the eight exports. The tests also cover export/signature enumeration, malformed calls, buffer bounds, stale handles, reload invalidation, directory-search preservation, transfer-pool recovery, and unloading an open block with no committed DCC heap left behind. The emulator also executes a DCC library with a 32 KiB malloc/free and a zero-initialized 2 KiB BSS. Its library source is the maintained example.

docs.title: Typed calls and object ownership
docs.text:
The SDK's preferred C names are descriptive: bank_library_open, bank_library_call, bank_library_last_error, bank_memory_allocate and the other bank_library_*, bank_memory_* and bank_bios_* operations. Header aliases map them to six-character M80/L80 public symbols, which the text below and generated wrappers also use; aliases add no wrapper call.

Shared client-side support lives in examples/BANKSDK, separate from runnable examples. The reusable host runtime lives in BANKLIB.H and its matching C implementation; BANKMEM and BIOSBANK provide checked memory access and the BIOS calling-convention adapter. blname and blsig enumerate loaded exports without a manifest. blcall checks the expected complete signature before executing anything. blerr reports transport, format, signature, allocation, bounds, lifecycle, and cleanup failures separately from an exported function's ordinary result.

Open reserves one 512-byte bank-1 extent, first for FCB staging and then reused for bounded call frames; close and failed open release it. Successful steady-state calls perform no allocations/frees. Generated wrappers retain one four-byte binding per export, checking its complete canonical signature once per module generation. Raw blcall still validates the signature every time. Invalidation/reload advances generation; RESET advances pool epoch. The SDK queries both before writing a cached frame, and resident CALL validates them again. Stale ownership returns BL_STALE and never frees or overwrites a possibly reassigned extent. Metadata is immutable while loaded: raw debug writes require invalidate/reload.

A two-byte frame-length prefix lets the generated adapter reject malformed or truncated requests before accessing arguments. The body is at most 256 bytes; allocations and transfers are rounded to 16-byte BIOS bursts. On successful dispatch the result frame is read back before outputs are published. Failed calls retain the workspace for retry/close and do not publish modified outputs. Calls are synchronous and non-reentrant.

Host/library DMA and directory-search continuation are independent. Search Next rereads its directory sector because the directory buffer is shared. Current drive/user and allocation state remain shared. Tests interleave searches across drives and check drive/user changes in both directions.

The typed ABI supports integer values, declared counted byte buffers and single named, pointer-free flat structs through annotated pointers. #pragma dcc bank_record FUNCTION ARG in|out|inout uses a 1-based argument index and requires a complete struct of unqualified 8/16/32-bit integers or fixed one-dimensional integer arrays. The compiler emits resolved field metadata; dccmake generates complete struct definitions and compile-time size, offset and integer-width checks in the client contract. Typedef aliases resolve to the underlying named struct; generated prototypes use its tag. Anonymous/nested structs, pointer members, const/volatile members, unions, bitfields and by-value aggregate arguments/results are rejected.

Records use the DCC packed, little-endian layout and bounded bulk copies, not per-field serialization. Fixed-size wrappers use exact-size local frames, constant offsets and one adapter length check. The canonical DIRECTION:rec1le:TAG[SIZE]{FIELD:TYPE@OFFSET;ARRAY:TYPE[COUNT]@OFFSET} signature includes full field names, order, widths/signedness, array lengths, offsets and size; comparing just a tag or size is insufficient. Records and buffers share the 256-byte body limit and 255-character signature limit. No loader, linker format or firmware ABI change is needed.

Record pointers cannot be NULL; const pointers support only IN. OUT records start zero-filled. Outputs are copied back only after successful dispatch, even when the ordinary C result reports an operation failure. Transport rejection leaves caller outputs unchanged. Copied arguments are independent snapshots; overlap involving a record is rejected if either argument is writable. A library must not retain a frame-local pointer after returning.

Buffer direction and bounds must be explicit. Caller addresses never appear in the bank-1 frame; adapters form bank-1-local pointers into copied bytes. Pointer graphs, callbacks, varargs, and implicit deep serialization are not supported.

Large objects stay in the bank that owns them. The sample exposes a validated opaque handle to a 4 KiB allocation and reads at most 128 bytes per call. Closing an object invalidates its handle; opening another object uses a fresh token. Unload closes outstanding objects and files. Handles are meaningful only to the owning library and host runtime, not persistent identifiers, memory addresses, or a security boundary.

docs.title: BDOS and bank switching
docs.text:
The bank-0 shim copies FCBs and DMA records through resident staging buffers, returns CP/M results, and mirrors pointer-returned disk tables in bank 0. Bank 1 retains the authoritative allocation vectors. A bank-0 directory search can continue after a bank-1 library file operation; the proxy keeps a separate search continuation snapshot. Calls are sequential; the gateway masks interrupts during a bank switch. Library code must not re-enter the bank-switch allocator, call bank-0 addresses, or use a bank-0 pointer directly.

The bank-1 BIOS warm-boot vector enters the mirrored FB40h trampoline and returns to bank-0 warm boot. The same slot holds the extent lookup used by checked bread/bwrite transfers. Drive A's system tracks contain the bank-0 BDOS shim so warm boot restores the same arrangement. The firmware holds the bank-1 BDOS/loader image; the CP/M boot image supplies the bank-0 shim and matching gateway. Flash both firmware and CP/M system image for this ABI.

docs.title: Current limits
docs.text: There is one library slot, no runtime relocation, and no nested bank calls. Library exit, abort, program chaining, and transient-program startup paths are outside the supported runtime subset. The host must call its unload export before invalidating a library with open files. Direct bank-0 BIOS disk calls bypass the BDOS shim; ordinary CP/M applications use BDOS. The emulator covers cold/warm boot, bank-0 directory and file reads, a bank-1 file read, interrupted directory search, header rejection, and restoration of bank 0 after calls. Physical board validation remains necessary.

docs.title: D.4 Custom BIOS Responsibilities
docs.text:
The BIOS implements CP/M 2.2’s standard 17-entry jump table for BDOS and dcc’s direct-BIOS functions.

CP/M BIOS operation Board implementation BOOT Initialize CP/M and page-zero vectors; enter CCP WBOOT Flush writes, reload CCP/BDOS from Drive A, and enter CCP CONST Return 0xFF when terminal status port 0x01, bit 0, reports input ready CONIN Wait for input on port 0x00; return a 7-bit character CONOUT Wait for status bit 1 (transmit room); write C to port 0x00 READER Return text EOF (0x1A) LIST / PUNCH Discard output LISTST Return not ready HOME Set track to zero SELDSK Return the disk parameter header for A–D, or zero for an invalid drive SETTRK / SETSEC / SETDMA Store track, sector, and software buffer address; no hardware DMA READ / WRITE Transfer 128-byte records through ports 0x10–0x14, preserving CP/M write-type semantics SECTRAN Return the sector unchanged; images use linear sector order

BDOS handles filenames, FCBs, directories, allocation, and record selection. The BIOS handles drives and records, so dcc file APIs need no custom backend. See the I/O port map for port decoding and aliases.

docs.title: Banked-memory BIOS extension (ABI 1.0)
docs.text:
The mirrored FF00h page is present in both banks. Check BMX1 at FF09h, major 1 at FF0Dh, minor 0 at FF0Eh, and INFO success before calling it. Firmware and the CP/M system image must be updated together.

Address Entry Contract FF00h READ HL=bank-0 buffer, DE=bank-1 address, BC=length FF03h WRITE HL=bank-0 buffer, DE=bank-1 address, BC=length FF06h INFO HL=0100h, DE=C800h, BC=1600h on success FF10h Service E selects the operation below

READ and WRITE use multiples of 16 bytes; both ranges must end at or below the exclusive limit FF00h without wrapping. Raw transfers into resident memory are for system code; application handles are allocated only in C800h–DDFFh. The bank-0 C wrappers bread and bwrite provide byte-granular transfers using discovered BIOS byte-copy helpers (F800h READ, F803h WRITE). These helpers retain the register convention above, accept arbitrary byte counts, and return A=0/carry clear or A=2/carry set for an invalid range. Zero count succeeds without dereferencing either address. For positive counts, the bank-0 buffer must start at or above 0100h; the raw bank-1 address has no equivalent lower-bound check and can include page zero. Both ranges must end at or below FF00h, without wrapping. This does not make reserved bank-1 memory available to applications. Full-range validation precedes copying; partial writes preserve neighbouring bytes. IX/IY, stack and interrupt state are preserved.

bread and bwrite call the checked entries F806h READ and F809h WRITE. They take A=handle page (a handle's high byte; handles are 256-byte aligned), DE=bank-1 address, HL=bank-0 buffer and BC=byte count. The bank-0 shim maps the page to its allocator extent: pool pages C8h–DDh, the pinned library at page 01h and its stack at C0h. With interrupts masked, the shim calls a mirrored helper at FB48h that selects bank 1, reads the live extent length and allocated marker, and reselects bank 0 without touching the stack. A free, unused or unknown page returns A=3/carry set. A range starting below the handle or ending beyond the extent returns A=2/carry set. Otherwise the call continues as F800h/F803h. Every call checks the live tables, so a handle freed or invalidated by RESET is rejected; no bounds are cached.

Counts divisible by 16 dispatch directly to the raw gateway, without setting up tail storage. The gateway's 237-byte mirrored code retains the low count and direction in A and saves the advancing source SP in that source bank's private FFF0h word. Only D0 of bank-select OUT data is significant; the other bits may contain the counter. Group bookkeeping happens once per 256 bytes, while each 16-byte burst still performs exactly two bank-select OUTs. The main carry flag survives the register payload and avoids a second direction test. No allocation metadata is cached. FF06h delegates to a bank-0-only INFO helper at FA00h inside the BDOS shim. Deploy matching firmware, boot package and drive A system records together. See MEMPERF for the repeated-workload methodology and emulator cycle measurements, which exclude hardware wait time.

Resident allocator operations have a short dispatch path and save SP directly. Metadata-table selectors preserve AF with bit operations; SIZE still validates the current extent length and allocated marker on every call. Private host and library context snapshots store nine bytes: the DMA word plus the actual search state at FB14h, FB18h–FB1Ah and FB29h–FB2Bh. The host search proxy uses the same packed seven-byte search layout. Adjacent shared disk-geometry scratch is never copied as per-domain state.

docs.title: Allocation and direct entry calls
docs.text: E Operation Arguments and result 0 ALLOC HL=requested bytes; returns a 256-byte-aligned handle or zero 1 FREE HL=handle; returns 1 on success 2 SIZE HL=handle; returns rounded size or zero 3 AVAILABLE Returns free bytes, initially 5,632 4 RESET Invalidates general-pool handles and restores the free extent 5 CALL HL=live code handle, BC=distinct live stack handle, IX=entry offset, IY=context; returns code's HL 6 BDOS proxy Resident bank-0 BDOS shim service 7 CAPABILITIES Returns bank-1 address of a 48-byte versioned descriptor, or zero 8 LIB CONTROL HL=discovered request address; returns status independently of results 9 LAST STATUS Returns last resident-service status without clearing it

docs.title: Capability and library control records
docs.text:
After INFO succeeds, use bank_bios_query() rather than inspecting allocator signatures or private tables. The descriptor contains 24 little-endian words:

Word Meaning 0-3 Size (48), descriptor revision (1), ABI (0100h), feature mask (003Fh) 4-7 Pool start, capacity, allocation unit, raw burst size 8-11 Byte READ/WRITE entries, library request address and size 12-15 Export table address, image origin, pinned code and stack handles 16-19 Call-token address, maximum body bytes, exports and signature characters 20-23 Call revision (1), checked READ/WRITE entries, one reserved zero word

Feature bits 0-5 advertise byte transfers, library control, detailed status, DMA/search contexts, generation/epoch validation and checked handle transfers, respectively. bank_bios_library_control() copies the request to its discovered address, dispatches operation 8 and retrieves the response. All fields are 16-bit words:

Byte offset Meaning 0, 2 Request size (32), revision (1) 4, 6 Action (0 LOAD, 1 INVALIDATE, 2 QUERY, 3 CALL), output status 8, 10 Expected/current module generation, zero-based export index 12, 14 Live FCB staging/frame handle, per-call token 16, 18, 20 Ready flag, export count, entry size 22, 24, 26, 28 Image bytes, export table address, image origin, stack handle 30 Expected/current pool epoch

LOAD copies a padded 48-byte FCB from a live pool allocation. QUERY reports authoritative descriptors without changing ownership. CALL requires a live 512-byte extent, a body length prefix in 1..256, a typed export and matching module generation/pool epoch. INVALIDATE makes the module uncallable even at generation exhaustion. Generations and epochs never wrap: further LOAD/RESET fails with EXHAUSTED rather than reviving stale state.

BIOS status codes are:

Code Status Meaning 0 OK The BIOS operation succeeded; an invoked function's result is separate. 1 UNAVAILABLE The banked-memory capability or matching resident service is unavailable. 2 ARGUMENT An argument, range, length, request field or operation is invalid. 3 HANDLE A required allocation handle is not live or does not meet the operation's requirements. 4 MEMORY No free extent can satisfy the allocation request. 5 PINNED An attempt was made to free a pinned library or stack extent. 6 DISPATCH A typed library adapter did not return its required success value of 1. 7 FORMAT The library header is invalid. 8 IO A library load encountered a file open or read failure. 9 STALE The module is not ready, or the expected module generation or pool epoch does not match. 10 EXHAUSTED A non-wrapping module-generation or pool-epoch counter cannot advance.

Raw CALL returns arbitrary function HL, including valid zero; status is separate. bank_memory_last_error() and bank_bios_last_error() use the BIOS codes above. bank_library_last_error() uses the separate BL_* codes defined in BANKLIB.H; for example, BL_IO is 2 and BL_STALE is 12.

bmalloc and bfree run in the bank-1 extent allocator. Free-list and physical-extent tables occupy the pinned E600h–EDFFh region; returned handles never point at metadata. Allocation searches free extents and splits one; free coalesces adjacent extents. SIZE and AVAILABLE read tables directly. breset preserves the pinned library, stack, loader and allocator. Four compact 32-byte metadata tables preserve the entire 5,632-byte pool; service growth does not reduce the library's DCC heap or stack.

The 0100h library image and C000h stack are pinned handles for CALL. For an ordinary allocated code block, the caller supplies its entry offset. The BIOS validates the code and stack handles and offset; it cannot verify that the offset is an instruction boundary. CALL places IY on the bank-1 stack as one 16-bit DCC C argument. A function using the normal DCC frame prologue reads it at IX+4 and returns a 16-bit value in HL.

docs.title: Stack switch and return
docs.text:
1. The mirrored gateway saves the bank-0 interrupt state and selects bank 1.
  2. Resident code saves the bank-0 SP in bank-1 workspace and uses its private service stack. CALL then switches to the exclusive end of the supplied, distinct live stack allocation and rejects BC=0.
  3. The function returns with RET. Resident code restores SP, and the gateway selects bank 0, restores interrupt state and returns to C.

The bank-1 function never dereferences the bank-0 stack. IX and IY are restored; HL carries the function result. Calls are sequential and cannot re-enter the gateway from bank 1. Interrupt handlers and NMI during a bank switch are unsupported.

DMA and search continuation belong separately to the host and library domains. Only search fields are restored, not shared disk-geometry scratch variables. Search Next refreshes the shared directory buffer before resuming; this adds a directory read. Current drive/user and disk allocation state remain shared.

docs.title: Bank-1 CP/M and C library
docs.text:
Bank 1 holds the authoritative BDOS and drive allocation state. The bank-0 BDOS disk/file shim forwards calls and marshals FCBs and DMA records. A bank-1 library may call its own BDOS for console and file I/O. Its DCC malloc heap starts at the linked end of its image and BSS (__hstart); its upper limit is C800h minus the configured stack size. The loader clears BSS and obtains the heap base from the library header. The fixed linked image begins at 0100h; the separate general bmalloc pool begins at C800h.

The bank-0 shim saves its caller's stack pointer, uses a private stack at F600h–F7FFh while forwarding a call, then restores the caller's stack. The CCP's own stack is too close to its code for nested bank transfers.

The resident LIB loader validates a .LIB header, reads the image into 0100h, initializes DCC heap bounds, and exposes export offsets. The bank-0 BANKLIB runtime copies the length-prefixed call frame with bank_bios_write(), then invokes LIB CONTROL (operation 8, action 3 CALL). The resident service validates the module generation, pool epoch, frame allocation and typed export before invoking CALL internally. After successful dispatch, BANKLIB reads the result frame with bank_bios_read() and publishes it to the caller. Direct CALL is available for lower-level code but does not replace the typed library-control checks. The bank-1 library design describes ownership and limits. LIBDEMO is the maintained C example; SPREADS shows the smaller hand-written-code path.

The example has two parts: the bank-0 host builds DATATEST.COM, and the bank-1 library builds DATA.LIB. DCC generates the shared API header and call wrappers from the library source. The host exercises scalar values, copied buffers, flat records, file I/O, bank-owned blocks and library lifecycle. Its HOSTCHK.C helper handles test setup, memory reports and cleanup checks.

Bank-0 host: LIBDEMO/host/DATATEST.C 
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

#include "API.H"
#include "BANKLIB.H"
#include "HOSTCHK.H"

static unsigned int previous_handle;

static unsigned int check_values(void)
{
    unsigned int left = 120, right = 23, result;
    result = add16(left, right);
    if (result != 143 || bank_library_last_error() != BL_OK || left != 120 || right != 23)
        return 0;
    printf("add16(120, 23) = %u; caller values unchanged.\n", result);
    return add16(65535U, 1) == 0 && bank_library_last_error() == BL_OK;
}

static unsigned int check_text(void)
{
    unsigned char text[128];
    unsigned int i;
    memset(text, 0xA5, sizeof(text));
    memcpy(text, "Bank 1", 7);
    if (upper(text, 6) != 6 || bank_library_last_error() != BL_OK ||
        memcmp(text, "BANK 1", 7))
        return 0;
    for (i = 7; i < sizeof(text); ++i)
        if (text[i] != 0xA5)
            return 0;
    printf("upper(\"Bank 1\") = \"%s\".\n", text);
    memset(text, 'a', sizeof(text));
    if (upper(text, sizeof(text)) != sizeof(text) || bank_library_last_error() != BL_OK)
        return 0;
    for (i = 0; i < sizeof(text); ++i)
        if (text[i] != 'A')
            return 0;
    if (upper(text, 129) != 0 || bank_library_last_error() != BL_BOUNDS)
        return 0;
    for (i = 0; i < sizeof(text); ++i)
        if (text[i] != 'A')
            return 0;
    return upper(0, 1) == 0 && bank_library_last_error() == BL_ARGUMENT;
}

static unsigned int check_file(void)
{
    unsigned char data[130], first;
    unsigned int i, checksum = 0;
    memset(data, 0xA5, sizeof(data));
    if (filerd(data + 1, 128) != 128 || bank_library_last_error() != BL_OK ||
        data[0] != 0xA5 || data[129] != 0xA5)
        return 0;
    first = data[1];
    for (i = 1; i <= 128; ++i)
        checksum += data[i];
    printf("Read 128 bytes from A:AUTORUN.COM in bank 1; byte sum %u.\n",
           checksum);
    return filerd(data + 1, 1) == 1 && bank_library_last_error() == BL_OK &&
           data[1] == first && data[0] == 0xA5 && data[129] == 0xA5;
}

static unsigned int check_exports(void)
{
    unsigned int i, j, found;
    unsigned char frame[19];
    char name[9], signature[BL_SIGNATURE_MAX + 1];
    if (bank_library_export_count() != 8)
        return 0;
    found = 0;
    for (i = 0; i < bank_library_export_count(); ++i)
    {
        if (!bank_library_export_name(i, name) || !bank_library_export_signature(i, signature, sizeof(signature)))
            return 0;
        printf("Export %s: %s\n", name, signature);
        if (!strcmp(name, "ADD16"))
        {
            found = 1;
            memset(frame, 0xA5, sizeof(frame));
            if (bank_library_call(name, "void()", frame, sizeof(frame)) ||
                bank_library_last_error() != BL_SIGNATURE)
                return 0;
            if (bank_library_call(name, signature, frame, 1) ||
                bank_library_last_error() != BL_DISPATCH)
                return 0;
            if (bank_library_call(name, signature, frame, BL_FRAME_MAX + 1) ||
                bank_library_last_error() != BL_BOUNDS)
                return 0;
            for (j = 0; j < sizeof(frame); ++j)
                if (frame[j] != 0xA5)
                    return 0;
        }
        if (!strcmp(name, "BLKFREE"))
        {
            char *field = strstr(signature, "state:i8@8");
            if (!field)
                return 0;
            memset(frame, 0xA5, sizeof(frame));
            *field = 'x';
            if (bank_library_call(name, signature, frame, sizeof(frame)) ||
                bank_library_last_error() != BL_SIGNATURE)
                return 0;
            *field = 's';
            if (bank_library_call(name, signature, frame, sizeof(frame) - 1) ||
                bank_library_last_error() != BL_DISPATCH)
                return 0;
            for (j = 0; j < sizeof(frame); ++j)
                if (frame[j] != 0xA5)
                    return 0;
        }
    }
    return found;
}

static unsigned int create_block(unsigned int seed, struct BlockInfo *info)
{
    struct BlockSpec spec;
    unsigned char saved[sizeof(spec)];
    unsigned int handle;
    spec.seed = seed;
    memcpy(spec.label, "BANKDATA", sizeof(spec.label));
    memcpy(saved, &spec, sizeof(spec));
    handle = blknew(&spec, info);
    if (memcmp(saved, &spec, sizeof(spec)) ||
        bank_library_last_error() != BL_OK || !handle ||
        info->handle != handle || info->size != 4096 ||
        info->byte_sum != 522240UL || info->state != 1 ||
        memcmp(info->label, "BANKDATA", sizeof(info->label)))
        return 0;
    return handle;
}

static unsigned int check_blocks(void)
{
    unsigned int handle, replacement, i;
    unsigned char data[130];
    struct {
        unsigned char before;
        struct BlockInfo info;
        unsigned char after;
    } guarded;
    struct BlockInfo other;
    struct BlockSpec spec;
    memset(&guarded, 0xA5, sizeof(guarded));
    spec.seed = 91;
    memcpy(spec.label, "BANKDATA", sizeof(spec.label));
    if (blknew(0, &guarded.info) || bank_library_last_error() != BL_ARGUMENT ||
        blknew(&spec, 0) || bank_library_last_error() != BL_ARGUMENT ||
        blknew((const struct BlockSpec *)&guarded.info, &guarded.info) ||
        bank_library_last_error() != BL_ARGUMENT ||
        blkfree(0) || bank_library_last_error() != BL_ARGUMENT)
        return 0;
    for (i = 0; i < sizeof(guarded); ++i)
        if (((unsigned char *)&guarded)[i] != 0xA5)
            return 0;
    handle = create_block(37, &guarded.info);
    if (!handle || bank_library_last_error() != BL_OK)
        return 0;
    memset(&other, 0xA5, sizeof(other));
    if (blknew(&spec, &other) != 0 || bank_library_last_error() != BL_OK)
        return 0;
    for (i = 0; i < sizeof(other); ++i)
        if (((unsigned char *)&other)[i] != 0)
            return 0;
    memset(data, 0xA5, sizeof(data));
    if (blkread(handle, 1023, data + 1, 128) != 128 ||
        bank_library_last_error() != BL_OK || data[0] != 0xA5 || data[129] != 0xA5)
        return 0;
    for (i = 0; i < 128; ++i)
        if (data[i + 1] != (unsigned char)(37 + 1023 + i))
            return 0;
    puts("Read a 128-byte slice of a 4096-byte bank-owned block.");
    memset(data, 0xA5, sizeof(data));
    if (blkread(handle, 0, data + 1, 129) || bank_library_last_error() != BL_BOUNDS)
        return 0;
    for (i = 0; i < sizeof(data); ++i)
        if (data[i] != 0xA5)
            return 0;
    if (blkread(handle, 4095, data + 1, 2) != 0 || bank_library_last_error() != BL_OK ||
        blkread(handle, 4096, data + 1, 1) != 0 || bank_library_last_error() != BL_OK ||
        blkread(handle, 65535U, data + 1, 2) != 0 || bank_library_last_error() != BL_OK ||
        blkread(0, 0, data + 1, 1) != 0 || bank_library_last_error() != BL_OK ||
        !blkfree(&guarded.info) || bank_library_last_error() != BL_OK ||
        blkread(handle, 0, data + 1, 1) != 0 || bank_library_last_error() != BL_OK ||
        blkfree(&guarded.info) != 0 || bank_library_last_error() != BL_OK ||
        guarded.info.handle || guarded.info.size || guarded.info.byte_sum ||
        guarded.info.state != -1 ||
        memcmp(guarded.info.label, "BANKDATA", sizeof(guarded.info.label)) ||
        guarded.before != 0xA5 || guarded.after != 0xA5)
        return 0;
    puts("PASS: flat record in/out/inout, 32-bit values, arrays and guards.");
    replacement = create_block(91, &guarded.info);
    if (!replacement || replacement == handle || bank_library_last_error() != BL_OK ||
        blkread(handle, 0, data + 1, 1) != 0 || bank_library_last_error() != BL_OK ||
        blkread(replacement, 0, data + 1, 1) != 1 || bank_library_last_error() != BL_OK ||
        data[1] != 91)
        return 0;
    /* Unloading, rather than blkfree, must retire this live handle. */
    previous_handle = replacement;
    return 1;
}

static unsigned int check_reload(void)
{
    unsigned int handle, result, cleanup;
    unsigned char data[1];
    struct BlockInfo info;
    if (!hsopen())
        return 0;
    handle = create_block(12, &info);
    result = handle && handle != previous_handle && bank_library_last_error() == BL_OK;
    if (result)
        result = blkread(previous_handle, 0, data, 1) == 0 &&
                 bank_library_last_error() == BL_OK &&
                 blkread(handle, 4095, data, 1) == 1 &&
                 bank_library_last_error() == BL_OK && data[0] == (unsigned char)(12 + 4095);
    /* Leave this block open to exercise the unload hook's cleanup. */
    cleanup = hsclos();
    return result && cleanup;
}

int main(void)
{
    unsigned int step, loaded;
    puts("DATATEST: ordinary C calls, separate banks.");
    puts("[1/8] Load DATA.LIB and run onload");
    loaded = hsopen();
    step = 1;
    if (!loaded)
        goto failed;
    puts("PASS: load and lifecycle.");

    step = 2;
    puts("[2/8] Integer arguments and results");
    if (!check_values())
        goto failed;
    puts("PASS: scalar values and 16-bit wraparound.");

    step = 3;
    puts("[3/8] Counted text buffer (inout)");
    if (!check_text())
        goto failed;
    puts("PASS: text copy-back, limits and null-pointer rejection.");

    step = 4;
    puts("[4/8] File I/O in bank 1 (out)");
    if (!check_file())
        goto failed;
    puts("PASS: file read, reopen and buffer guards.");

    step = 5;
    puts("[5/8] Export discovery and rejected calls");
    if (!check_exports())
        goto failed;
    puts("PASS: eight exports, signatures and malformed-frame rejection.");

    step = 6;
    puts("[6/8] Flat records, bank-owned blocks and opaque handles");
    if (!check_blocks())
        goto failed;
    puts("PASS: chunk data, bounds, stale handles and double-free rejection.");

    step = 7;
    puts("[7/8] Unload and check shared runtime state");
    loaded = 0;
    if (!hsclos())
        goto failed;
    puts("PASS: directory search preserved and transfer memory recovered.");

    step = 8;
    puts("[8/8] Reload, reject old handles and clean up an open block");
    if (!check_reload())
        goto failed;
    puts("PASS: reload isolation and unload cleanup.");
    puts("PASS: all 8 bank-1 library checks.");
    return 0;

failed:
    printf("FAIL: step %u (transport error %u).\n", step, bank_library_last_error());
    if (loaded && !hsclos())
        puts("FAIL: library cleanup.");
    return 1;
}
Bank-1 library: LIBDEMO/lib/DATA.C 
#include <ctype.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>

#include "BANKLIB.H"

struct BlockSpec {
    unsigned int seed;
    unsigned char label[8];
};

struct BlockInfo {
    unsigned int handle;
    unsigned int size;
    unsigned long byte_sum;
    signed char state;
    unsigned char label[8];
};

#pragma dcc bank_buffer upper 1 inout 2 128
#pragma dcc bank_buffer filerd 1 out 2 128
#pragma dcc bank_buffer blkread 3 out 4 128
#pragma dcc bank_record blknew 1 in
#pragma dcc bank_record blknew 2 out
#pragma dcc bank_record blkfree 1 inout

static unsigned char *block_data;
static unsigned int block_handle;

#define BLOCK_BYTES 4096

static void library_report_memory(void)
{
    meminfo_t info;
    meminfo(&info);
    printf("Bank 1 DCC heap: %u bytes capacity, %u committed, %u growth; stack: %u bytes\n",
           info.heap_capacity, info.heap_committed, info.heap_growth, info.stack_size);
}

unsigned int onload(void)
{
    library_report_memory();
    return 1;
}

unsigned int onunload(void)
{
    meminfo_t info;
    if (block_data)
    {
        free(block_data);
        block_data = 0;
        block_handle = 0;
    }
    meminfo(&info);
    if (info.heap_committed)
    {
        printf("Bank 1 cleanup left %u committed heap bytes.\n", info.heap_committed);
        return 0;
    }
    return 1;
}

unsigned int add16(unsigned int left, unsigned int right)
{
    return left + right;
}

unsigned int upper(unsigned char *data, unsigned int count)
{
    unsigned int i;
    if (!data || !count || count > 128)
        return 0;
    for (i = 0; i < count; ++i)
        data[i] = (unsigned char)toupper(data[i]);
    return count;
}

unsigned int filerd(unsigned char *data, unsigned int count)
{
    FILE *file;
    unsigned int result, failed;
    if (!data || !count || count > 128)
        return 0;
    file = fopen("A:AUTORUN.COM", "rb");
    if (!file)
        return 0;
    result = fread(data, 1, count, file);
    failed = ferror(file);
    if (fclose(file) || failed)
        return 0;
    return result;
}

unsigned int blknew(const struct BlockSpec *spec, struct BlockInfo *info)
{
    unsigned int i;
    if (block_data)
        return 0;
    block_data = (unsigned char *)malloc(BLOCK_BYTES);
    if (!block_data)
        return 0;
    for (i = 0; i < BLOCK_BYTES; ++i)
        block_data[i] = (unsigned char)(spec->seed + i);
    /* A runtime token is a handle, never a bank-1 pointer. */
    block_handle = *(unsigned int *)BANK_LIBRARY_CALL_TOKEN_ADDRESS;
    info->handle = block_handle;
    info->size = BLOCK_BYTES;
    /* Each full 256-byte cycle contains all byte values, regardless of seed. */
    info->byte_sum = (BLOCK_BYTES / 256UL) * 32640UL;
    info->state = 1;
    memcpy(info->label, spec->label, sizeof(info->label));
    return block_handle;
}

unsigned int blkread(unsigned int handle, unsigned int offset,
                     unsigned char *data, unsigned int count)
{
    if (!handle || handle != block_handle || !block_data ||
        !data || !count || count > 128 || offset >= BLOCK_BYTES ||
        count > BLOCK_BYTES - offset)
        return 0;
    memcpy(data, block_data + offset, count);
    return count;
}

unsigned int blkfree(struct BlockInfo *info)
{
    if (!info->handle || info->handle != block_handle || !block_data)
        return 0;
    free(block_data);
    block_data = 0;
    block_handle = 0;
    info->handle = 0;
    info->size = 0;
    info->byte_sum = 0;
    info->state = -1;
    return 1;
}

docs.title: Boot and deployment
docs.text: The Pico loads and verifies bank 0, then loads and verifies 8,960 bank-1 bytes, including the loader, allocator, BDOS, BIOS and mirrored gateway. Bank-1 warm boot switches back to bank 0. Drive A's system tracks contain the bank-0 BDOS shim, so warm boot restores the same gateway. Deploy matching firmware, CP/M system image, and rebuilt .COM and .LIB files together. Libraries carry format 1, ABI 1.0 and call revision 1 in their header.

docs.title: D.6 Compatibility Boundaries
docs.text:
• Programs must fit within the 0x0100-0xE5FF TPA after runtime, globals, heap, and stack requirements are included.
  • The installed operating system is CP/M 2.2. Optional CP/M 3 or emulator-only BDOS extensions are not supplied by this BIOS/BDOS image. In particular, software should treat dcc's BDOS-105-backed clock functions as unavailable unless separately demonstrated on this target.
  • CP/M filenames and disks retain CP/M 2.2 semantics: 8.3 names, FCB-based access, 128-byte logical records, and Ctrl-Z text-file conventions where the dcc API documents them.
  • The terminal data port returns 0x00 if read while empty. Correct software must test status bit 0 first; BDOS and the custom BIOS already do so.
  • Status bit 7 reports WebSocket client connection state to direct-port software, but CP/M and dcc do not require it for their standard console ABI.
  • dcc's own emulator and physical-Z80 test history establishes general CP/M runtime portability, but it does not by itself qualify this board's Pico trap, custom BIOS, flash backend, or electrical timing.

docs.title: D.8 Image Build and End-to-End Test
docs.text: The deployed image assembles cpm64_z80.asm (CCP/BDOS) and z80_bios.asm (board BIOS). The immutable Burcon binary remains the audit reference. See image provenance and the memory map.

docs.title: Build images
docs.text:
Requires Python 3, z80asm, cpmtools, and the converted disks in src/disks/generated/. Run from the repository root:

python3 src/cpm/build_images.py --output-dir build/cpm

Outputs include bios.bin, the 64 KiB z80boot.img, CRC-protected z80boot.pkg, AUTORUN.COM, four 512 KiB disk images, and manifest.json. Drive A receives the native system tracks and AUTORUN utility/configuration; Drives B–D are unchanged copies of the converted images.

To also create a complete 4 MiB z80romless-flash.bin, supply Phase 10 firmware:

python3 src/cpm/build_images.py --output-dir build/cpm \
  --firmware build/src/stage10_websocket_terminal/z80_stage10_websocket_terminal.bin

docs.title: Run tests
docs.text:
Check reference reproducibility, resident layout, BIOS ABI, package CRCs, disk construction, and flash-region boundaries:

python3 -m unittest discover -s src/cpm -p 'test_*.py' -v

Build the project-owned Z80 host, then run the end-to-end test with Python 3.10 or newer:

cmake -S src/cpm/z80_debug_host -B build/cpm/z80_debug_host \
  -DZ80_DEBUG_HOST_BUILD_EXAMPLES=OFF -DBUILD_TESTING=OFF
cmake --build build/cpm/z80_debug_host
python3 src/cpm/test_z80_debug_host.py \
  --host build/cpm/z80_debug_host/z80-debug-host

The test builds fresh images and executes the board BIOS through emulated console/disk ports. It checks boot to A>, CLEAR, DIR, LS.COM exit and warm reload, multi-extent ATTNC11.COM loading, and cross-drive PIP copies. Warm boot reloads 44 CCP/BDOS records (5,632 bytes) from Drive A.

These tests establish host/emulator behavior. Physical bus timing, Pico I/O, flash fault recovery, and power-cycle persistence require the hardware qualification checks.

docs.title: D.1 CP/M Image Provenance
docs.text: The system boots 64K CP/M 2.2: a Z80-optimised port of Burcon CP/M 2.2 with a custom BIOS for this board.

docs.title: Original system
docs.text:
• Source: Burcon CP/M 2.2 for the Altair 88-DCDD controller.
  • Reference image: src/cpm/cpm64_system.bin, the 5,632-byte CCP/BDOS region captured after the matching Burcon MOVCPM 64 and SYSGEN tools produced a bootable system in the Altair emulator.
  • Integrity: The image builder checks its SHA-256 fingerprint. This reference binary is preserved unchanged.
  • Original layout: CCP at 0xE300, BDOS at 0xEB00, and BIOS at 0xF900, with a 0x0700-byte BIOS reservation.

To regenerate the reference, use the matching Burcon utilities and MOVCPM instructions. The generator reports SAVE 38; preserve the BIOS reservation and verify relocated entry vectors.

docs.title: CPM Customisations
docs.text:
• Added the CLEAR command to clear the terminal screen.
  • Removed Ctrl+S flow control and printer support from CP/M.

docs.title: Changes for this board
docs.text:
• Z80 CP/M port: src/cpm/cpm64_z80.asm replaces the original CCP/BDOS at build time. Optimisations and removed features leave 246 bytes of padding (54 in CCP, 192 in BDOS) after adding CLEAR. Section sizes are unchanged; CCP and BDOS move upward by 0x0300. See the memory map for the running system's layout.
  • Custom BIOS: src/cpm/z80_bios.asm replaces the Altair BIOS and cold loader. It uses the board's Pico-serviced terminal and flash-disk ports, rather than the Altair controller's ports 0x08–0x0A. See Custom BIOS.
  • Validation: The port's unoptimised mode reproduces the reference byte-for-byte. Host tests check relocation and Z80 instructions, plus cold boot, DIR, program loading, and warm boot.
  • Audit details: src/cpm/cpm64_i8080.asm and src/cpm/cpm64_i8080_audit.md record the original disassembly and findings.

For supplied applications, DCC builds, and disk deployment, see Related projects.

docs.title: D.9 Interactive CP/M Test
docs.text: Run the optimized CP/M image and board BIOS with host-backed console and disk I/O. Requires CMake, a C/C++ compiler, Python 3.10+, z80asm, and cpmtools.

docs.title: Start in VS Code
docs.text:
1. Open Run and Debug, select Interactive CP/M emulator, and press Start.
  2. Wait for 64K CP/M 2.2 and the A> prompt.
  3. Enter CP/M commands. Press Ctrl+] to stop the session.

The pre-launch task builds the project’s Z80 host, I/O adapter, and images in build/cpm. The launcher loads the 64 KiB payload from z80boot.pkg and attaches Drives A–D. No Pico or external Altair checkout is needed.

docs.title: Try the software path
docs.text:
A>CLEAR
A>DIR
A>LS
A>C:
C>ATTNC11
C>A:PIP D:ATTNC11.COM=C:ATTNC11.COM
C>A:PIP D:ATTN.WTS=C:ATTN.WTS
C>D:
D>DIR

This exercises console output, directories, transient loading and exit, BIOS warm reload, multi-extent programs, and cross-drive writes.

Disk changes are saved to the generated files in build/cpm. The preparation task regenerates them on the next launch; copy out results you want to retain.

The terminal maps arrow keys to Ctrl-E/X/D/S, Insert/Delete to Ctrl-O/G, Page Up/Down to Ctrl-R/V, and Backspace to Ctrl-H. Standalone Escape uses a 30 ms grace period to distinguish it from ANSI key sequences.

docs.title: Optional HTTP(S) file-transfer test
docs.text:
The host adapter also emulates Altair file-transfer, time/timer, utility, weather, environment-variable, and chat ports. Network features require curl support and relevant configuration; they do not establish Pico support.

With curl development headers/libraries installed, build the host and adapter:

cmake -S src/cpm/z80_debug_host -B build/cpm/z80_debug_host \
  -DZ80_DEBUG_HOST_BUILD_EXAMPLES=OFF -DBUILD_TESTING=OFF
cmake --build build/cpm/z80_debug_host
cmake -S src/cpm/dcc_io_adapter -B build/cpm/dcc_io_adapter
cmake --build build/cpm/dcc_io_adapter
python3 src/cpm/test_http_ft.py --https

The test requires FT.ASM from the sibling ESP32 Altair checkout (default: ../esp32/esp32-altair-8800/Apps/FT/FT.ASM; override with --ft-source). It assembles FT with CP/M MAC/LOAD, tests local HTTP binary/text transfers, empty files, error recovery, and prompted filenames. --https also downloads LOVE.BAS and runs it in MBASIC.

Artifacts, hashes, and transcripts go to build/cpm-http-ft; ordinary build/cpm disks remain unchanged. The adapter uses the production HTTP mailbox/parser with a native curl transport.

When using cpmtools directly, use build_images.cpm_diskdefs(): its explicit logicalextents 1 is required for files larger than 16 KiB.

These are emulator tests. Pico loading, flash journaling and power-loss recovery, electrical behavior, and bus timing require hardware qualification.

docs.title: D.2 CP/M Memory Map and Entry Points
docs.text:
The reset-ready SRAM image uses the following upper-memory layout:

Region Address range Role Page zero 0x0000-0x00FF CP/M vectors, default FCBs, DMA buffer, and command tail Transient Program Area (TPA) 0x0100-0xE5FF .COM program, dcc runtime, static data, heap, and stack CCP 0xE600-0xEDFF Console Command Processor, reloaded after a warm boot BDOS shim and tables 0xEE00-0xFB3F Bank-0 console and disk/file proxy; entry at 0xEE06 BDOS shim private stack 0xF600-0xF7FF 512-byte stack inside the bank-0 BDOS slot; protects the CCP code below its small stack Mirrored trampoline 0xFB40-0xFB7F Bank-1 warm-boot return and checked-transfer extent lookup (0xFB48) Reserved BDOS padding 0xFB80-0xFBFF 128-byte BIOS directory buffer BIOS core 0xFC00-0xFEFD 766-byte Z80-optimized boot, console, disk, translation and startup-report routines Spare padding 0xFEFE-0xFEFF 2 bytes BIOS bank extension 0xFF00-0xFFFF READ/WRITE/INFO/HEAP entry points, mirrored code and private workspace

The TPA contains 0xE500 bytes, or 58,624 bytes, before the CCP boundary. A dcc program and every runtime block selected for it must fit in this space together with its stack and heap. The CCP occupies 0x0800 bytes and the BDOS slot occupies 0x0E00 bytes; the BDOS slot's final 128 bytes are reserved as the BIOS directory buffer. The dcc runtime reads the installed JP 0xEE06 vector at 0x0005 to locate BDOS; application memory must still remain below the CCP boundary at 0xE600. Required CCP/BDOS workspace, the allocation vectors, disk state, and internal stacks remain inside their relocated resident regions.

The BIOS cold boot installs JP instructions at 0x0000 and 0x0005 for warm boot and BDOS respectively. A dcc program normally starts at 0x0100 and returns to CP/M through the warm-boot vector. The custom warm boot reloads the 44 CCP/BDOS system records before returning to the command prompt, restoring the resident image. The supported TPA above excludes the CCP.

The complete 1,024-byte bios.bin includes the core, two bytes of padding, and the extension page. The public BIOS API is installed in both SRAM banks. Production bank 0 contains a BDOS disk/file shim in the EE00h–FB3Fh slot; the authoritative BDOS resides in bank 1. The Drive A system tracks contain that shim for warm boot.

The bank-0 shim saves the caller's stack pointer and switches to its private stack before forwarding disk calls. It restores the caller's stack before returning. This keeps nested bank transfers away from the CCP instructions immediately below the CCP stack.
