Bank-1 address Role 0000h–00FFh CP/M page zero 0100h–(heap_base-1) Fixed DCC library image, statics and BSS heap_base–(C800h-stack-1) DCC library malloc heap, starting after linked BSS (C800h-stack)–C7FFh Pinned library stack; size comes from the .LIB header C800h–DDFFh General bmalloc pool, 5,632 bytes DE00h–E5FFh Resident loader, proxy and service workspace E600h–EDFFh Extent allocator metadata/code EE00h–FB3Fh Authoritative CP/M BDOS FB40h–FB7Fh Mirrored warm-boot return and extent lookup FB80h–FEFFh BIOS buffer and core FF00h–FFFFh Mirrored bank-switch gateway

Boot loads and verifies bank-1 page zero and every byte from DE00h through FFFFh. The 0100h–DDFFh application, library stack, and shared heap range is not cleared at boot; those regions are written by their owners before use.

Bank 0 cannot dereference bank-1 addresses. It uses the BIOS transfer calls for parameter blocks and the library-control request for exported functions. See the library memory layout for the image, BSS, heap and stack rules. Firmware and the CP/M system image must match when the bank-1 resident layout changes.

docs.title: D.3 Z80 I/O with the PIO Engine
docs.text: The Z80 executes CP/M directly from SRAM; only IN and OUT instructions reach the Pico. In Phases 9 and 10 every one of those I/O cycles is completed by the RP2350's PIO hardware. Core 0 never touches the bus during a cycle: it only applies a written byte or supplies a byte to read. This page explains the terms, what each PIO block does, and why this makes Z80 I/O fast.

docs.title: PIO terminology
docs.text: Term Meaning PIO block A programmable I/O peripheral. The RP2350 has three: PIO0, PIO1 and PIO2. Each has 32 words of instruction memory shared by its state machines. State machine (SM) A tiny independent processor inside a block (four per block). It executes one PIO instruction per system clock: 8.33 ns at the 120 MHz supervisor clock, so its timing is exact and repeatable. Scratch and shift registers Each SM has X and Y scratch registers, an output shift register (OSR) for data going to pins, and an input shift register (ISR) for data read from pins. Pin mappings Each SM is configured with windows of GPIOs: IN reads from them, OUT and SET drive them, side-set drives a pin in the same instruction as other work, and JMP PIN branches on one pin. FIFOs Two four-word queues per SM. The SM pushes to the RX FIFO for the ARM cores to read; the ARM cores put words in the TX FIFO for the SM to pull. Autopush pushes the ISR automatically when it is full. IRQ flags Eight flags per block that SMs set, clear and wait on. They can interrupt an ARM core, and on the RP2350 IRQ PREV sets a flag in the neighbouring (previous) block.

docs.title: The role of each PIO block
docs.text:
Block Program Role PIO0 banked_clock, 4 words Generates the 20 MHz Z80 clock (3 ticks HIGH, 3 LOW) on GP2. It stops in a LOW phase whenever PIO0 IRQ flag 1 (I/O hold) or flag 2 (core-0 hold) is set. It shares PIO0 with the matrix display's I²C program. PIO1 banked_io, 29 words The I/O engine. Claimed exclusively; it recognises, completes and times every Z80 IN and OUT, and drives the data bus, buffer enables, WAIT release and SRAM bank select (A16). PIO2 (not used by the Z80) Left for the CYW43 Wi-Fi driver, whose SPI bus claims the highest free PIO block.

PIO1's engine holds the Z80 clock through PIO0 with IRQ PREV, so the clock and the I/O engine cooperate without any ARM involvement.

docs.title: PIO1 pin windows
docs.text:
Mapping GPIOs Signals IN GP10 upwards D0-D7, A0/A1/A2/A4, RD#, WR# OUT (10 pins) GP8-GP17 A16 bank select, IO_RELEASE, D0-D7 SET (2 pins) GP6-GP7 UP_OE# (Pico drives the Z80 bus), DOWN_OE# (Pico reads the Z80 bus) Side-set GP9 IO_RELEASE: releases the hardware WAIT# JMP PIN GP27 RD#: distinguishes IN from OUT

The HCT32 asserts WAIT# in hardware as soon as IORQ# falls, so the Z80 is already waiting before PIO sees the cycle.

docs.title: How PIO data reaches core 0
docs.text:
The I/O engine exchanges one 32-bit word per cycle with core 0 through its FIFOs:

Direction Instruction Word contents PIO1 → core 0 (RX) in pins, 32 with autopush A snapshot of the pins: data in bits 0-7, A0/A1/A2/A4 in bits 8-11, RD# in bit 17, WR# in bit 18 Core 0 → PIO1 (TX) pull, out pins, 10, out pindirs, 10 The reply for an IN: pin levels for GP8-GP17 (A16 unchanged, IO_RELEASE LOW, D0-D7) in bits 0-9, then the pin directions to use while driving (bits 10-19) and when idle (bits 20-29)

An RX-not-empty interrupt runs core 0's handler, which takes snapshots in bus order: each OUT becomes a device write and each IN a device read whose byte goes back in the TX FIFO (see Division of work). The handler and the device code it calls run from SRAM.

docs.title: An OUT cycle
docs.text:
1. IORQ# falls; PIO sets the I/O hold so the clock stops at its next LOW phase, and JMP PIN sees RD# HIGH.
  2. PIO enables the receive buffer (DOWN_OE#) and lets it settle for eight ticks.
  3. For port 07h it drives D0 onto A16, switching the SRAM bank. For any other port it autopushes the snapshot to core 0.
  4. It releases WAIT# while CLK is still LOW, clears the hold so the clock runs freely, waits for IORQ# to rise, then isolates the buffer and rearms WAIT#.

The Z80 continues as soon as PIO completes the cycle; core 0 applies the write afterwards. If four writes are already queued, PIO waits before releasing WAIT#, so the Z80 simply pauses rather than losing data.

docs.title: An IN cycle
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Z as Z80
    participant P1 as PIO1 I/O engine
    participant P0 as PIO0 clock
    participant C0 as Core 0
    Z->>P1: IORQ# + RD# LOW (WAIT# already LOW)
    P1->>P0: IRQ PREV: hold CLK LOW
    P1->>C0: Request snapshot (RX FIFO, IRQ)
    C0->>P1: Reply byte + pin directions (TX FIFO)
    P1->>Z: Drive D0-D7, enable UP_OE#, release WAIT#
    P1->>P0: Run exactly two clocks
    Z->>Z: TW sees WAIT# HIGH, T3 samples data
    P1->>P1: IORQ# HIGH: isolate bus, data pins to inputs
    P1->>P0: Release hold: next instruction fetch

After the reply arrives, PIO places the byte on D0-D7, enables the buffer toward the Z80 and releases WAIT#. It then lets the clock run exactly two cycles: in the first the Z80 sees WAIT# released, and at the falling edge of the second (T3) it samples the data. PIO re-asserts the hold at precisely the right instruction, so the clock stops in T3's LOW phase. Only after the bus is isolated does the clock resume into the next opcode fetch, so the Pico can never still be driving the bus when the Z80 reads its next instruction.

docs.title: Division of work
docs.text: Owner Responsibility PIO0 + PIO1 All Z80 bus timing: the 20 MHz clock, cycle detection, buffer enables, data drive and sampling, WAIT# release and A16 bank select Core 0 The Z80's supervisor and the device logic behind its I/O ports Core 1 USB, Wi-Fi and network services, the web terminal, flash programming and the disk read-ahead

docs.title: Core 0: PIO1 interrupt
docs.text:
The RX-not-empty interrupt is core 0's only per-cycle work. It takes each snapshot in bus order, applies OUT bytes and computes IN replies:

Ports Work 00h-01h console Queue output to the shared ring for core 1 (USB or WebSocket), return input bytes, report status without taking the lock 10h-14h disk Latch drive and LBA, run commands, serve reads from the SRAM read-ahead or flash, collect 128-byte write records and hand them to core 1 02h-04h service ABI Collect requests for core-1 workers and return their replies 17h timers Countdown timers and stopwatches 15h-16h HTTP Filename and chunk handshakes with the core-1 HTTP worker 05h, 06h Boot markers and disk-diagnostic results 07h (IN) SRAM bank status; OUT 07h completes entirely in PIO

Measured cost is about 1 µs per IN and 1.2-1.3 µs per OUT. Even at about 266,000 polled INs per second this is roughly a quarter of core 0's time (excluding interrupt entry and exit), and most of it answers console-status polls. Anything slow is handed to core 1 through bounded queues and mailboxes.

docs.title: Core 0: main loop
docs.text:
• Flash grants. When core 1 must program flash, core 0 parks the Z80 with BUSREQ#, applies queued OUTs and pauses the I/O engine. Afterwards it rearms the engine and returns the bus.
  • Watchdog. A cycle that makes no progress for 500 ms holds the CPU in reset.
  • Supervisor commands from core 1 (the Ctrl-] menu): load and verify, start, status ([pio], [iolat], [disk]), stop, reboot, fault arming, and configuration or web reboots.
  • Run monitoring. BIOS and CCP boot markers, the boot timeout, disk-diagnostic progress, and holding the CPU on a fatal storage error.
  • Orderly stop. Request a flush from core 1, park the Z80, apply queued OUTs and check disk quiescence, then hold RESET# or resume.
  • State publication for core 1.

docs.title: Core 0: boot
docs.text:
Before CP/M starts, core 0 recovers the flash journal, validates the boot image and loads all 64 KiB into SRAM by injecting instructions on a slow, software-stepped clock, then reads every byte back. It prepares bank 1 and only then arms the I/O engine and starts the 20 MHz PIO clock. This loader is the only use of stepped clocking.

Core 0 does no bus timing, clock stopping or stepping during a cycle, and no USB, network or flash programming. Between cycles it is idle in its main loop.

docs.title: Why it is fast
docs.text:
• Hardware timing. Every bus step is a PIO instruction with 8.33 ns resolution. There are no software delays, timer polls or clock stepping in the I/O path.
  • Core 0 does only the data work. About 1 µs per IN in the measured workload, and an OUT never makes the Z80 wait for core 0 unless four writes are already queued.
  • High throughput. Polled IN cycles run at about 225,000-266,000 per second on the 20 MHz Z80, which directly speeds up console polling, every INIR disk record transfer, and service and HTTP replies.
  • Bank switching at bus speed. OUT 07h never involves an ARM core.
  • Isolated from Wi-Fi. The handler runs from SRAM and does no network or flash work, so core-1 activity cannot stretch a Z80 I/O cycle.
  • Ordered and backpressured. One FIFO preserves the Z80's bus order: an IN always observes every earlier OUT. A full FIFO holds WAIT# instead of dropping data.

Ctrl-] s reports the engine state ([pio]), core-0 cost per IN and OUT ([iolat]) and disk read-ahead hits ([disk]).

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
• Snapshots with neither or both of RD# and WR# active hold the CPU in reset through the watchdog.
  • A cycle that makes no progress for 500 ms fails closed the same way.
  • During a flash bus grant the board's pull-ups keep IORQ#, RD# and WR# inactive, and core 0 drains the FIFO before the grant and before a supervisor stop.

Source: banked_io.pio (both PIO programs), banked_pio.c (allocation, FIFO service) and io_trap.c (device dispatch). Hardware details: PIO acceleration.

docs.title: Host coverage
docs.text:
• Image tests: Check the Burcon reference fingerprint, assembled CCP/BDOS and BIOS layout, page-zero reset target, package headers and CRCs, disk geometry, and complete 4 MiB flash layout.
  • DCC host test: Executes the optimized image and board BIOS through emulated I/O, covering boot, CLEAR, DIR, LS.COM, warm reload, multi-extent loading, and cross-drive file copies.
  • Banked-memory tests: Check the BIOS transfer ABI, bank isolation, allocator, and heap operations in Z80 emulation.

See the automated tests and interactive emulator. Host tests do not establish physical bus timing, Pico I/O behavior, or flash power-loss recovery.

docs.title: Required hardware qualification
docs.text:
Complete Phase 8, Phase 9, and Phase 10, including logic-analyzer, all-LBA disk, and flash fault-injection checks. Run representative dcc .COM programs covering:

  1. Output: printf/puts, literal $, CR/LF, buffering, and fflush.
  2. Input: getchar, scanf, kbhit, getch, Ctrl-Z, and browser reconnects.
  3. Files: Create, close/reopen, sequential/random I/O, rename, delete, directory updates, disk-full handling, and warm boot.
  4. Persistence: Read/write all drives A–D; repeat writes, power-cycle, and compare recovered data byte-for-byte with the host.
  5. Memory: Exercise stack/heap near the TPA limit (0xE600 exclusive) and confirm reliable exit and CCP reload.

Hardware console and file-I/O compatibility requires these checks to pass.

docs.title: Building the documentation
docs.text: The MkDocs source lives in docs/docs/en, with navigation in docs/docs/mkdocs.yml. It is the single source of truth for the complete engineering specification; do not recreate a monolithic copy in the project README.

docs.title: Build the website
docs.text:
From docs/docs, create an environment, install the documentation dependencies, and run a strict build:

python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
.venv/bin/mkdocs build --strict

The generated website is written to docs/site from the repository root.

docs.title: Source-backed phase code
docs.text:
Phase 1-10 use the existing include-markdown plugin's plain include directive inside fenced code blocks and collapsed ??? example sections. Each section includes one complete maintained file from src/; do not paste firmware into Markdown or use line-number slices that drift when code changes. Use include, not include-markdown, for source code so Markdown link and heading transformations do not alter it.

Paths are relative to the phase page. From en/implementation/, the repository source tree is ../../../../src/; the BIOS page includes its example from ../../../../examples/. Keep the source path in the section title and retain links to related headers and build definitions in the source index.

Every documentation build reads the current checkout. The MkDocs configuration explicitly watches ../../src and ../../examples during mkdocs serve, so source edits continue to trigger preview rebuilds even if the include plugin loses its per-file watches after a rebuild. A published site reflects its last deployed revision, not subsequent local changes. Build from the complete repository so the included sources are available; a missing include is a build error.

docs.title: Deferred PCB documentation
docs.text: The historical PCB pages remain in docs/docs/en/pcb/, but exclude_docs in the MkDocs configuration excludes them from generated pages and search. They are also absent from navigation. Keep them hidden until PCB migration is separately reviewed; do not regenerate the historical PCB or fabrication artifacts as part of a documentation build.

docs.title: Serve locally
docs.text:
.venv/bin/mkdocs serve

MkDocs prints the preview URL, normally http://127.0.0.1:8000/.

docs.title: Deploy
docs.text: .github/workflows/docs.yml performs a strict build and publishes the site to the gh-pages branch whenever main changes. It can also be run manually with the GitHub Actions workflow_dispatch control.

docs.title: Hardware Design
docs.text:
The hardware chapters progress from the bill of materials through pin-level wiring, address generation, physical construction, buffering, and final bus isolation. For a first build, read the inventory and construction basics, then follow the phased implementation plan. Consult the other hardware chapters when a phase refers to them; their chapter order is not the chip-installation order.

Chapter Purpose 0. Project inventory Parts, passive components, power distribution, and required bench equipment 1. Reference pin mapping Authoritative IC pin maps, signal ownership, and logic-domain checks 2. Address interface Current 128 KiB SRAM address map, bank select, Z80-assisted loading, and four-bit port monitoring 3. Physical construction Breadboard topology, socket placement, and jumper routing 4. Output buffer AHCT244 channel allocation and enable behavior 5. Bus isolation Address, data, and control transceiver operating modes

The historical PCB documentation is hidden while migration is deferred. The existing PCB, BOM, and fabrication files are unchanged and incompatible with this assisted-loader revision. Do not manufacture that package for this build.

The instrument procedures are cross-cutting qualification references rather than additional hardware chapters. Use the RIGOL DHO814 capture plan for analogue integrity and exact timing, and the DSLogic Plus capture plan for bus-wide digital state and event ordering. Individual implementation pass gates name the captures required at each phase.

docs.title: 2. SRAM Loading and Bank Switching
docs.text:
The Z80 alone drives SRAM addresses and write strobes. The Pico loads and verifies memory by supplying instructions under a slow clock, then releases the Z80 to execute from SRAM. BUSREQ/BUSACK pauses the CPU for flash work; it does not permit Pico memory mastering.

For wiring, use the implementation checklists: Phase 3 control/port monitor, Phase 4 address trunk and bank select, and Phase 6 SRAM loading.

docs.title: Banked 128 KiB SRAM
docs.text: The AS6C1008 provides two 64 KiB banks. GP8 controls A16 through U4 AHCT244; port 0x07 selects the bank. Switching affects all addresses, including code, stack, and vectors, so applications must use the BIOS transfer API.

docs.title: Physical bank-select path
docs.text: The Phase 4 checklist owns the GP8–U4–A16 wiring and R24 pull-down. GP8/J2 pin 1 is reserved for bank selection.

docs.title: PIO acceleration
docs.text:
Phases 9 and 10 complete every Z80 I/O cycle in PIO with a 120 MHz supervisor clock. A PIO0 state machine (4 words, beside the matrix display) generates the 20 MHz Z80 clock. PIO1 is claimed exclusively for the I/O engine (29 words) and holds that clock through PIO0 IRQ 1 with the RP2350's IRQ PREV. PIO2 is left to the CYW43 SPI driver, which takes the highest free block. PIO1 owns GP6-GP17 while CP/M runs: SET drives UP_OE#/DOWN_OE#, OUT drives A16, IO_RELEASE and D0-D7 (with their pin directions), side-set drives IO_RELEASE and JMP PIN tests RD#. The board's 10 kOhm IORQ#/RD#/WR# pull-ups keep a granted bus inactive, so the engine needs no BUSACK# recheck after IORQ#.

Every cycle holds CLK LOW at its next LOW phase, then:

  • OUT: PIO enables U10, samples after at least eight system ticks, releases WAIT and lets CLK free-run; U10 only drives the Pico side. OUT 07h drives D0 onto A16 while SRAM is deselected. Other ports autopush a 32-bit snapshot (data bits 0-7, A0/A1/A2/A4 bits 8-11, RD# bit 17, WR# bit 18) into the 4-entry RX FIFO; when it is full, PIO stalls before WAIT release.
  • IN: PIO pushes a request snapshot and waits on its TX FIFO. Core 0 replies with the OUT pin word (A16 unchanged, IO_RELEASE LOW, D0-D7) and the driving and idle pin directions. PIO drives D0-D7, enables U9 and releases WAIT with CLK still LOW for at least eight ticks, then runs exactly two clocks: TW samples WAIT inactive and T3's falling edge samples the data. It clears the hold, sets it again eight ticks later, and the clock SM sees it at T3's LOW-phase check, never TW's, whatever the IRQ PREV latency. After IORQ# rises, PIO isolates U9, rearms WAIT, returns D0-D7 to inputs and only then resumes CLK. The next opcode fetch therefore never sees the Pico driving the bus; there is no race against the 50 ns T3-to-T1 window.

Core 0 services both FIFOs from the PIO1 RX-not-empty IRQ in bus order, so an IN always observes every earlier OUT; it also drains them before granting the bus or deciding a stop. Snapshots with neither or both strobes fail closed. The fixed HCT32 WAIT circuit remains required.

If either PIO resource cannot be allocated, CP/M start fails closed. Without verified bank hardware, PIO1 keeps GP8/A16 on SIO, so other I/O continues but banking reports unavailable. The backend requires 20 MHz Z80 / 120 MHz supervisor clocks. Stuck transactions trigger fail-closed recovery after 500 ms.

docs.title: Firmware and port contract
docs.text:
Loading probes bank isolation, initializes/verifies bank-1 metadata and the mirrored BIOS page, and restores bank 0. Failed banking checks allow the base 64 KiB loader to continue. A new image load resets the banked heap; warm boot preserves it.

Operation Meaning IN A,(07h) B4h: bank 0 ready; B5h: bank 1 ready; 00h: unavailable OUT (07h),A PIO selects A & 1; ignored without active PIO

Status reads use the firmware trap. Port aliases follow address & 0x17; see the port reference. INT#/NMI# remain inactive on this board; the transfer API preserves maskable interrupt state but does not support NMI or reentrant calls.

docs.title: dcc banked heap example
docs.text:
examples/BANKED provides bmalloc/bfree handles and bread/bwrite through base-bank buffers. Handles are not C pointers. Capacity is 65,024 bytes in 256-byte allocations; the metadata block and top BIOS page are reserved.

The BIOS copies 16-byte bursts; the C library buffers partial transfers. See the memory map and BIOS ABI for bounds and register conventions. Deploy matching firmware, boot package, and Drive A system records. Changes to src/common/banked_transfer.asm require regenerating its supervisor header with scripts/build-banked-transfer.py.

docs.title: Loader Sequence
docs.text:
1. Isolate both data paths, stop the execution clock, and reset the Z80.
  2. Inhibit SRAM reads while supplying LD HL,nn and LD (HL),n bytes. The Z80 performs each memory write.
  3. Verify with injected LD A,(HL), enabling SRAM reads and the downward buffer only for the read cycle. Compare every byte.
  4. On success, reset to PC zero, isolate the Pico data paths, enable normal SRAM reads, and start execution. On failure, hold RESET# LOW and stop CLK.

Slow steps include settling delays; boot duration depends on software and buffer turnaround as well as clock pulses. See maintained sram.c and cpu.c. These are loader operations, not runtime DMA.

docs.title: Board verification and recovery
docs.text:
The board has passed repeated 20 MHz PIO boots and BANKED.COM, including 32 KiB copies, bounds, reuse, exhaustion, and the final heap byte. This establishes operation on that board; copy throughput and electrical margins have not been measured.

Use Build and flash Pico - Phase 10 firmware, confirm the CP/M prompt, run BANKED, then inspect Ctrl-] s for [pio] active=1 running=1. Firmware-only updates preserve the matching CP/M package, disks, and ENV.

Host regressions cover PIO instruction timing, bus grants, console handoff, and an interrupt during clock startup. Clock frequency is published before PIO starts so an early BIOS interrupt can resume it correctly. Host models complement physical CLK/WAIT#/A16/SRAM-control captures.

docs.title: 5. Bus Translation and Isolation
docs.text: The Z80 is the sole address-bus driver. Two fixed-direction transceivers separate its 5 V data bus from the Pico. Both must be disabled before changing Pico data GPIO direction or value. Never enable both at once.

docs.title: 5.1 Data Paths
docs.text:
Device Supply DIR pin 1 A pins 2-9 B pins 18-11 OE# pin 19 U9 SN74AHCT245N +5 V at pin 20 +5 V, A to B GP10-GP17 D0-D7 HCT32 pin 8 U10 SN74LVC245AN +3.3 V at pin 20 GND, B to A GP10-GP17 D0-D7 GP7

Both devices use common GND at pin 10 and local 100 nF bypass capacitors. Use the Phase 5 wiring tables for individual data-bit connections.

Mode GP6 upward request GP7 downward OE# Upward path Downward path Isolated / run 1 1 Off Off Injected read / IN reply 0 1 On only while RD# LOW Off SRAM verification / OUT 1 0 Off On

U3 gates U9 OE# with raw RD# and GP6; GP7 controls U10 OE# directly. Both GPIOs have 10 kOhm pull-ups to 3.3 V. Firmware isolates both paths before changing direction, waits at least 1 us before driving, and preloads output data or configures inputs before enabling a path. This is software exclusion: driving GP6 and GP7 LOW together is prohibited.

Software-serviced I/O steps the clock until the strobes release, isolates both paths, and rearms WAIT before resuming execution. PIO handles SRAM bank-select writes directly; see bank switching. RD# gating alone does not prevent contention if GP6 remains asserted into a later memory read.

Do not substitute TXS/TXB auto-direction parts, BSS138, or resistor-divider modules for this push-pull multi-load bus. The AHCT245 lacks data-port power-off protection: apply external +5 V before USB and remove USB before +5 V. Disabling its OE does not eliminate its input clamp paths.

docs.title: 5.2 CPU-Only Address Ownership
docs.text: Only the Z80 drives A0-A15; SRAM, pulls, and four input-monitor taps share the trunk. Loading requires the Z80 running under injected instructions, not held in reset. BUSACK is retained for flash quiescence, never Pico DMA.

docs.title: 5.4 Implementation Wiring Index
docs.text:
• Pico connections
  • Fixed logic and output buffer
  • Control and port monitor
  • Data paths
  • SRAM and CPU insertion

docs.title: 3. Construction and Breadboard Topology
docs.text: Build the phase sequence; leave later devices absent until instructed. Every pin map is a top view. Matching schematic net labels mean an electrical connection even without a continuous drawn wire.

docs.title: Before You Wire
docs.text:
On each BB830, A-E at one numbered row are one connection; F-J at that row are a separate connection. The center ravine isolates them. Adjacent numbered rows are not connected. Check power-rail continuity with a meter: stripes do not prove internal continuity or voltage.

Wire one named source pin to one named destination pin, then check continuity at the actual socket contacts and shorts to adjacent contacts. GP2 is Pico header pin 4, not header pin 2. A0-A15 means sixteen independent nets. Strip only enough insulation to seat the jumper, with no exposed bridges.

docs.title: Use the Meter Safely
docs.text: Use resistance/continuity only with external power and USB disconnected and capacitors discharged. Do not discharge capacitors by shorting them. In voltage mode, black COM goes to circuit GND and red goes to the named pin. Measure IC supply contacts, not only the supply entry. Prefer the supply current readout; an ammeter goes in series, never across +5 V and GND. Return its lead to the voltage socket after any current measurement. Attach clips with power off.

docs.title: Board Roles and Placement
docs.text: Place Memory, Core, and Peripheral boards left-to-right with long edges parallel, row 1 at the top, A-E left and F-J right. Do not mirror a board. Keep the AHCT244 next to the Z80 so CLK never crosses a board boundary. Signal-group placement is a routing aid, not a wire-length-matching requirement.

docs.title: 3.1 Package Orientation and Pin 1
docs.text:
Board / device Rows Orientation Pin 1 Opposite corner Memory / HCT32 5-11 Notch up E5 Pin 14 at F5 Memory / SRAM 18-33 Notch up Left pin-row side, row 18 Pin 32 right, row 18 Core / AHCT244 8-17 Notch down F17 Pin 20 E17 Core / Z80 19-38 Notch up Left pin-row side, row 19 Pin 40 right, row 19 Peripheral / Pico 1-20 USB up Header 1 left, row 1 Header 40 right, row 1 Peripheral / LVC244 22-31 Notch up E22 Pin 20 F22 Peripheral / AHCT245 33-42 Notch down F42 Pin 20 E42 Peripheral / LVC245 44-53 Notch down F53 Pin 20 E53

Narrow 7.62 mm DIPs straddle the ravine in E/F. Dry-fit the Z80/SRAM wide 15.24 mm sockets in columns matching their actual pin-row spacing; do not bend them into E/F. Both sides must remain electrically isolated. Reserve Core rows 1-3 for supply-module clearance; if the module needs more, mount it off-board rather than compressing the clock/CPU region.

Memory uses 23 terminal rows for ICs, Core 30, and Peripheral 50. Leave gaps, keep bypass capacitors near supply pins, and place address pulls by the SRAM trunk and Pico data pulls beside U9/U10 A pins. No reset transistor is fitted.

docs.title: Power Distribution
docs.text:
Feed the three +5 V rails from one supply-entry star, with multiple short common-GND links near bus crossings. The Peripheral +3.3 V rail is supplied only by Pico header 36 and powers U7/U10. Do not connect a plug-in module's 3.3 V output to it. Fit seven local 100 nF capacitors, three 22 uF board capacitors, and one 100 uF entry capacitor. Observe electrolytic polarity; the 1N5819 band faces VSYS.

All installed 5 V ICs must be powered whenever the 5 V rail is on. Pulls do not isolate installed unpowered devices. Follow Phase 0.

docs.title: 3.2 KiCad Electrical Schematic
docs.text:
The native schematic and net manifest are generated by build-kicad-schematic.py. Current validation: zero ERC violations, 71 real nets, 284 pin endpoints. This establishes connectivity, not bench timing or supply-transient safety.

The existing PCB, session, Gerbers, drills, and PCB assembly outputs are unchanged and belong to the previous circuit. Do not manufacture them for the assisted-loader revision. Do not run the full PCB regeneration pipeline until a separate PCB migration is authorized.

docs.title: 0. Project Inventory
docs.text:
This is the eight-active-package assisted-loader design, excluding the power diode. No PLD, PLD programmer, address expander, or reset transistor is needed. Match the complete part number and PDIP package before ordering.

Tick an item when you have the full listed quantity available, including the specified socket or headers where applicable. These are inventory checks, not installation or electrical-test results. Progress is saved in this browser on this device, separately from the implementation-phase checklists.

docs.title: Permanent breadboard resistors
docs.text:
Use 40 individual (discrete) 10 kOhm resistors. No resistor-network packages are fitted on the breadboard. Each resistor connects one signal to its specified supply rail or GND; signal wires must not be joined together. A resistor to a supply is a pull-up, and a resistor to GND is a pull-down. These establish defaults when no active output drives a signal.

The group checks below divide the same 40 resistors listed above; they are not additional parts. Tick each group when its quantity is set aside.

Install all permanent resistors in Phase 0, following the installation table. This is before fitting any active devices.

Temporary test resistors are additional bench items, not part of the 40 permanent branches. Later phases specify when to fit and remove 1 kOhm test resistors and extra 10 kOhm data-pattern pulls. Keep spares for those tests. No 4.7 kOhm or 47 kOhm reset-transistor parts remain.

Reserve one five-pin header for the future PCB; it adds no active packages and is not required for the Phase 0-10 breadboard build. No peripheral pull-ups or LED resistors are included. The existing PCB BOM, routing, and fabrication package are for the previous design and must not be used to manufacture this circuit. PCB updates are deferred. Use the revised native schematic and these breadboard instructions.

docs.title: DreamSourceLab DSLogic Plus Capture Plan
docs.text: A logic analyser is optional for building the board. Use one to investigate bus activity and capture digital signal ordering; use a scope for voltage and analogue timing measurements.

docs.title: Purpose and instrument limits
docs.text:
The DSLogic Plus proves simultaneous digital state, event ordering, bus values, and control sequencing. It complements the RIGOL DHO814: the logic analyzer answers what happened and in what order, while the oscilloscope proves voltage margin, rise/fall time, ringing, overshoot, and close analogue timing. Never use a logic-analyzer HIGH or LOW display as proof that a receiving device's datasheet voltage limits were met.

A displayed bus value is only as correct as the channel mapping: label the channels before capture and put bit 0 at the least-significant position. The analyzer samples rather than recording every instant; at 100 MHz, samples are 10 ns apart, so a shorter pulse may be missed. A clean-looking digital trace is not proof that the analog waveform has no glitch.

The official DSLogic Plus data sheet specifies:

Property DSLogic Plus limit Digital channels 16, CH0-CH15 Buffer Mode sample rate 400 MHz / 4 channels, 200 MHz / 8 channels, 100 MHz / 16 channels Stream Mode sample rate 100 MHz / 3 channels, 50 MHz / 6 channels, 25 MHz / 12 channels, 20 MHz / 16 channels Hardware memory 256 Mbits Buffer depth without RLE 256 Mbits divided by enabled channel count Maximum stream depth 16G samples Input threshold 0-5 V, adjustable in 0.1 V steps Input impedance 250 kOhm in parallel with approximately 13 pF Protected CH0-CH15 range -30 V to +30 V with the supplied fly wires 100 MHz sample interval 10 ns; sampling and threshold uncertainty limit edge timing

Use 16-channel, 100 MHz Buffer Mode for the complete address bus. At the board’s 20 MHz clock this gives only five samples per period, below the 10× sampling recommendation for phase-sensitive measurements. It is useful for bus values and coarse ordering, but cannot prove tight setup/hold margins. Use fewer channels at a higher sample rate or the scope for detailed timing.

Sixteen-channel Stream Mode runs at 20 MHz: only one sample per 20 MHz clock period. Reserve it for slow state/fault searches, not 20 MHz timing evidence.

docs.title: Safety and connection preparation
docs.text:
1. Install the current DSView release from the DreamSourceLab download page. Connect DSLogic Plus directly to a reliable USB port. Open DSView and require the hardware indicator to turn green and the device selector to identify DSLogic Plus before attaching it to the circuit.
  2. The probe grounds are connected through USB to the host computer ground. Connect them only to the SBC's common GND. Never attach a ground lead to +3.3 V, +5 V, a signal, or a floating/hot DUT. If the host is mains-grounded, DSLogic ground is earth-referenced.
  3. Power off the SBC before attaching or moving clips. Connect ground leads first, then signal leads. Remove signal leads first when disconnecting.
  4. Use the supplied shielded fly wires. Each active channel has an independent ground return; connect those returns to nearby common-GND points. The Z80 runs at 20 MHz with fast edges, so use the guide’s high-frequency connection method rather than one long shared ground lead.
  5. Probe the physical destination pin listed below, not a distant jumper end. Sixteen inputs add meaningful capacitive loading to a solderless breadboard. Recheck operation at 1 MHz after connecting each group, and do not stack a scope probe on the same node unless that combined loaded condition is the test being qualified.
  6. Do not connect CK, TI, or TO for the standard project captures. CK and TI are limited to the 0-3.3 V domain; attaching either to a 5 V Z80 signal violates the hardware data sheet. CH0-CH15 provide every trigger used here.

docs.title: Baseline DSView configuration
docs.text:
1. Press O or open Options. Select Logic Analyzer and Buffer Mode, with Upload captured data as the stop option.
  2. Select Use 16 Channels (Max 100 MHz), enable CH0-CH15, set Sample Rate = 100 MHz, and begin with Sample Duration = 100 ms. The official maximum at 100 MHz with 16 channels is approximately 167.77 ms.
  3. Set Filter Targets = None. The 1 Sample Clock filter suppresses pulses shorter than one sample interval and must not be used as pass evidence.
  4. Disable RLE Compress for baseline qualification so capture depth is fixed and reproducible. A separately labelled RLE capture may be used to search for sparse events, but it does not replace the baseline capture.
  5. Set the single device threshold for the selected group: 3.5 V for Group A, 2.2 V for Group B, or 1.6 V for mixed 3.3 V/TTL Groups C and D. These thresholds make transitions visible at useful digital decision levels; the DHO814 still proves device-specific $V_{IH}$/$V_{IL}$ margins.
  6. Select Single Capture and Normal Capture. Do not use Instant Capture as pass evidence because it ignores trigger settings. Repetitive Capture is useful only as additional evidence for repeatable events.
  7. Press T to open Trigger. Use Simple Trigger unless a scenario below requests a bus pattern. Clear every stale channel condition first: multiple Simple Trigger conditions are ANDed at the same sample point.
  8. Start with the trigger position at 30% to retain the cause and more post-trigger response. Use 50% when equal pre/post context is useful. Stream Mode fixes the trigger close to the start and is not used for these gates.
  9. Rename every channel to the signal shown in its group before capture. Use cursors and edge snap to measure ordering; record the sample count between relevant edges as well as the displayed time.
  10. Save the complete .dsl capture and DSView session, export a VCD or raw CSV, and save a PNG screenshot. Include phase, clock rate, stimulus, group, threshold, sample rate, duration, filter, RLE state, and trigger in the name.

docs.title: Group A: complete SRAM address bus
docs.text:
Use threshold 3.5 V. This group proves all address bits simultaneously at the SRAM receiver pins.

DSLogic channel Signal Physical probe point CH0 A0 SRAM pin 12 CH1 A1 SRAM pin 11 CH2 A2 SRAM pin 10 CH3 A3 SRAM pin 9 CH4 A4 SRAM pin 8 CH5 A5 SRAM pin 7 CH6 A6 SRAM pin 6 CH7 A7 SRAM pin 5 CH8 A8 SRAM pin 27 CH9 A9 SRAM pin 26 CH10 A10 SRAM pin 23 CH11 A11 SRAM pin 25 CH12 A12 SRAM pin 4 CH13 A13 SRAM pin 28 CH14 A14 SRAM pin 3 CH15 A15 SRAM pin 31

docs.title: Group B: memory data and controls
docs.text:
Use threshold 2.2 V. Group B correlates the complete byte with the CPU and SRAM control cycle. The analogue scope captures remain responsible for proving the SRAM's stricter write-data HIGH margin.

DSLogic channel Signal Physical probe point CH0-CH7 D0-D7 in ascending order SRAM pins 13, 14, 15, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21 CH8 CLK Z80 pin 6 CH9 MREQ# Z80 pin 19 CH10 RD# Z80 pin 21 CH11 WR# Z80 pin 22 CH12 SRAM CE# SRAM pin 22 CH13 SRAM OE# SRAM pin 24 CH14 SRAM WE# SRAM pin 29 CH15 M1# Z80 pin 27

docs.title: Optional DSView Z80 decoder cross-check
docs.text: After preserving the raw Group B capture, add DSView's Z80 protocol decoder and bind D0-D7 to CH0-CH7, M1# to CH15, RD# to CH10, WR# to CH11, and optional MREQ# to CH9. Leave IORQ# and A0-A15 unbound for this group. The decoder can annotate opcode fetches and memory read/write bytes, but it cannot report the full address and must not replace manual inspection of the raw controls. Group C remains authoritative for trapped I/O, and Group A remains authoritative for the complete address bus.

docs.title: Group C: trapped I/O and data-path exclusion
docs.text:
Use threshold 1.6 V. Repeat for IN with RD# on CH10 and OUT with WR# on CH10. Data-path exclusion is a firmware rule, not a hardware interlock. In Phases 9-10 every cycle completes in PIO: OUTs with a free-running clock, INs with exactly two clocks after WAIT release and CLK held LOW until U9 is isolated. Capture them as separate categories and confirm on raw captures that U9 disables before CLK resumes into the next opcode fetch. Capture A16 separately when checking OUT 07h bank switching, following the PIO reference.

DSLogic channel Signal Physical probe point CH0-CH7 D0-D7 in ascending order SRAM pins 13, 14, 15, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21 CH8 CLK Z80 pin 6 CH9 IORQ# Z80 pin 20 CH10 RD# for IN; WR# for OUT Z80 pin 21; repeat at pin 22 CH11 WAIT# Z80 pin 24 CH12 IO_RELEASE Pico GP9, header pin 12 CH13 PICO_DATA_UP_OE# request Pico GP6, header pin 9 CH14 Pico-to-bus transceiver OE# SN74AHCT245 pin 19 CH15 Bus-to-Pico transceiver OE# SN74LVC245 pin 19

docs.title: Group D: SRAM boot inhibit and control propagation
docs.text:
Use threshold 1.6 V. This mixed group follows CPU controls through the AHCT244 and HCT32 to SRAM, and checks injected loading and flash quiescence.

DSLogic channel Signal Physical probe point CH0 RESET# Z80 pin 26 CH1 BUSREQ# Z80 pin 25 CH2 BUSACK# Z80 pin 23 CH3 Z80 MREQ# Z80 pin 19 CH4 Z80 RD# Z80 pin 21 CH5 Z80 WR# Z80 pin 22 CH6 Buffered MREQ# / SRAM CE# AHCT244 pin 12 CH7 Buffered RD# AHCT244 pin 7 CH8 Buffered WR# / SRAM WE# AHCT244 pin 9 CH9 SRAM CE# SRAM pin 22 CH10 SRAM OE# SRAM pin 24 CH11 SRAM WE# SRAM pin 29 CH12 BOOT_READ_DISABLE Pico GP5, header pin 7 CH13 PICO_DATA_UP_OE# request Pico GP6, header pin 9 CH14 DATA_DOWN_OE# Pico GP7, header pin 10 CH15 CLK Z80 pin 6

docs.title: Trigger and expected outcomes
docs.text:
Purpose Group and trigger Expected result Address integrity Group A. Set all 16 Simple Trigger levels to match 0000, FFFF, 5555, or AAAA; all conditions are ANDed. Repeat for each fixed pattern and trigger on 0000 for walking/CPU-read sequences. Each sampled test address matches its expected pattern; walking-one/zero patterns select the intended bit, and no address transition occurs during the active sampling interval of a memory cycle. Repeat at every qualified clock rate. Opcode fetch Group B, CH15 M1# falling. M1#, MREQ#, RD#, CE#, and OE# assert in the expected active-LOW sequence; WE# remains HIGH and D0-D7 contain the fetched opcode before the Z80 sampling edge. SRAM read Group B, CH10 RD# falling with CH9 MREQ# LOW. CE# and OE# assert once, WE# remains HIGH, and all eight data bits settle to the expected byte before the sampling edge. No extra control transition is permitted. SRAM write Group B, CH11 WR# falling with CH9 MREQ# LOW. D0-D7 meet the SRAM’s setup/hold requirements around write completion; CE# and WE# assert once and OE# remains HIGH. DSLogic screens pulse presence and ordering only; the DHO814 must prove the exact 45 ns minimum WE# LOW width. Reset and restart Group D, CH0 RESET# rising, trigger position 30%. RESET# was LOW for six complete clocks. Injection starts with inhibit HIGH after the two exit clocks. Normal restart has both data paths isolated and inhibit LOW; CPU controls alone operate SRAM. Verify real reset-exit phase before accepting the cycle model. Flash quiescence Group D, CH2 BUSACK# falling for acquisition; repeat rising for release. BUSREQ# falls before BUSACK#. CPU address/control outputs float; pulls make SRAM controls inactive. Pico does not drive memory. Trap is armed before BUSREQ# release. Injected loading Group D, CH12 inhibit and CH4 RD# edges. SRAM OE# stays HIGH during injected instructions. It falls only for a deliberate SRAM read, with Pico output isolated. SRAM WE# follows CPU writes, never a Pico-generated write pulse. Trapped IN Group C with RD# on CH10; trigger CH9 IORQ# falling. WAIT# falls before sampling. Only AHCT245 OE# falls; the Pico supplies the reply byte. GP9 releases WAIT after preload. Phases 6-8: slow clocks complete the cycle. Phases 9-10: exactly two 20 MHz clocks (TW, T3), then CLK stays LOW. In both, both OEs are HIGH and GP9 LOW before the execution clock resumes into the next fetch. Trapped OUT Group C with WR# on CH10; trigger CH9 IORQ# falling. WAIT# falls first. Only LVC245 OE# falls; the Pico samples the CPU byte. GP9 releases WAIT. Phases 6-8: stepped completion isolates/rearms before execution resumes. Phases 9-10: CLK free-runs after release; isolation/rearm follows IORQ# rising. The two OE# signals are never LOW together.

For the final frequency claim, save Group A, B, C-IN, C-OUT, and D captures at each tested rate. The separate groups must use the same firmware build, clock rate, and deterministic stimulus. A 16-channel DSLogic Plus cannot establish simultaneous whole-address, whole-data, and control ordering in one acquisition; do not imply otherwise in qualification records.

docs.title: Authoritative documents
docs.text:
• DSLogic Plus Data Sheet
  • DSView User Guide
  • DreamSourceLab DSLogic product page

docs.title: Multimeter — Essential
docs.text: A good-quality digital multimeter is essential for building this board. It is used throughout the implementation phases to check wiring, power rails, pull resistors, and static signal levels. An oscilloscope and logic analyser are optional diagnostic tools.

docs.title: Useful features
docs.text:
• Reliable continuity indication for checking wires and socket contacts.
  • Resistance measurement for pull resistors and unexpected shorts.
  • DC voltage measurement with clear resolution around 3.3 V and 5 V.
  • Fine, insulated probe tips for reaching IC contacts without bridging pins.

docs.title: Use during construction
docs.text:
1. Disconnect external power and USB before continuity or resistance tests.
  2. Check each connection at the actual socket contacts, then check isolation from adjacent pins. Tick the implementation checklist only after checking.
  3. Before fitting ICs, follow the phase instructions to verify supply polarity, rail voltages, grounds, and fixed logic levels.
  4. Repeat the specified voltage checks as devices and wiring are added.

Keep the black lead in COM and the red lead in the voltage/resistance socket for these checks. Never put a meter in current mode across a power rail. A running clock may display an average voltage; use the phase’s static test mode for meter checks, or a scope to inspect the waveform.

See breadboard and meter basics for handling and probing guidance. The implementation pages remain the step-by-step build instructions and define the expected readings.

docs.title: RIGOL DHO814 Capture Plan
docs.text: An oscilloscope is optional for building the board. Use one to investigate signal quality and measure electrical timing margins.

docs.title: What to measure
docs.text:
• Use the scope for voltage, pulse widths, edge shape, ringing, and timing at receiving pins. Use DSLogic for whole-bus ordering.
  • The horizontal axis is time; the vertical axis is voltage relative to GND. Trigger levels align captures; they are not logic pass thresholds.
  • Arm Single before issuing a test command. If it keeps waiting, check source, edge, level, and whether the stimulus ran.

docs.title: Probe and instrument preparation
docs.text:
1. Bond the DHO814 chassis to protective earth with its supplied ground cable before connecting probes. USB-C power does not earth it. Probe grounds/BNC shells are common: connect them only to circuit GND, never a signal or rail.
  2. Power down before attaching or moving probes: disconnect USB before +5 V; restore +5 V before USB. Stopping acquisition does not remove circuit power.
  3. Set each probe and channel to 10X. Compensate each probe on the scope’s calibration output. Prefer ground springs; keep wire grounds under 20 mm.
  4. Set active channels to 1 MOhm, DC coupling, Invert OFF, Delay 0, bandwidth limit OFF. Use full 100 MHz bandwidth for edge/timing evidence.
  5. Use Normal acquisition, not Average. Use Normal trigger sweep for repetition or Single for one-off events; Auto sweep is not pass evidence.
  6. Start at 1 V/div for 3.3 V nodes or 2 V/div for 5 V. Keep GND and both levels visible. Trigger on CH1 at approximately 1.65 V or 2.5 V respectively.
  7. Use Auto memory for repetitive clocks; for single shots select the largest depth available. Disable unused channels for better sample rate:
Active channels Maximum depth Maximum sample rate 1 25 Mpts 1.25 GSa/s 2 10 Mpts 625 MSa/s 3–4 5 Mpts 312.5 MSa/s
  1. Place the trigger around 40% across the screen. Measure frequency, period, duty, HIGH/LOW widths, extrema, rise/fall, and relevant inter-channel delays. Confirm automatic readings with cursors and visible edges.
  2. Save screenshots and waveforms, recording firmware identity, phase, stimulus, clock rate, probe points/ratios, bandwidth, sample rate, memory depth, rail voltages, and measured minima/maxima.

Settings follow the RIGOL DHO800 User Guide. For supply noise, a separately labelled bandwidth-limited capture may supplement full-bandwidth evidence.

docs.title: 20 MHz no-I/O clock measurement
docs.text:
Use the Phase 6 no-I/O scope diagnostic. Unlike the reporting screens/soaks, it does not pause CLK for I/O reports.

  1. Deploy Flash Pico - Phase 6 20 MHz scope diagnostic.
  2. Prepare/earth the scope as above. With board power off, connect CH1 to Z80 CLK pin 6, ground spring to nearby common GND. U4 pin 18 is an accessible buffered-output alternative; GP2/header 4 measures only the 3.3 V source before U4.
  3. Enable CH1 only: 10X, DC, 1 MOhm, full bandwidth, 2 V/div, 20 ns/div, Normal acquisition, Auto depth. Trigger CH1 rising at approximately 2.5 V.
  4. Restore +5 V, then USB. Send f + Enter and wait for RUN; exclude the slow load/verify/reset interval from measurements.
  5. Measure frequency, period, duty, and HIGH/LOW widths. At 20 MHz the period is 50 ns. Inspect adjacent edges, levels, ringing, and missing pulses.
  6. Save waveform/screenshot and metadata. Repeat at GP2 and U4 pin 18 if comparing source, buffer, and interconnect; power down before moving probes.
  7. Send x to stop and read the SRAM mailbox. Exclude this slow readback from the capture interval. A mismatch HALTs Z80 code but leaves PWM running, so a clock alone does not prove the test is progressing.

docs.title: Recorded project capture
docs.text:
• Cursor frequency/period: 20.0000 MHz / 50.000 ns.
  • Duty/HIGH/LOW: 49% / 24.5 ns / 25.5 ns.
  • Across 482 counter readings: average 19.929 MHz, range 9.9502–20.202 MHz.
  • The low counter reading needs waveform review before claiming missing-edge or jitter qualification. Frequency alone does not qualify receiving-pin voltage or signal integrity.

docs.title: Four-channel connections and expected results
docs.text:
Connect the channels exactly as listed, using the physical IC pin as the probe point. CH1 is the normal trigger source unless the row explicitly names another source. Where a row lists alternatives, repeat the capture for every alternative while leaving the other channels in place where possible.

Purpose CH1 / trigger CH2 CH3 CH4 Trigger and expected outcome Clock translation Pico GP2, header pin 4 AHCT244 pin 18 Z80 CLK pin 6 Z80 RESET# pin 26 CH1 rising. At 1 kHz, 100 kHz, 1 MHz, and each qualification rate, CH1 is about 0-3.3 V and CH2/CH3 about 0-5 V. CH2 and CH3 match frequency and duty cycle, contain no extra edges, and differ only by interconnect delay. RESET# stays HIGH while running. Reset sequence Z80 RESET# pin 26 Z80 CLK pin 6 Z80 M1# pin 27 Z80 MREQ# pin 19 CH1 rising, Single. RESET# remains LOW for at least three complete clocks. After release, M1# and MREQ# produce valid active-LOW opcode-fetch activity with no runt RESET# or CLK pulse. Flash quiescence Z80 BUSREQ# pin 25 Z80 BUSACK# pin 23 Z80 RESET# pin 26 Z80 CLK pin 6 CH1 falling, Single. BUSACK# subsequently falls for flash erase/program, not memory DMA. Pico data paths remain isolated. Trap is rearmed before release; clocks contain no runt edges. SRAM write control Z80 CLK pin 6 Z80 MREQ# pin 19 Z80 WR# pin 22 SRAM WE# pin 29 CH1 rising. During CPU writes, including injected LD (HL),n, SRAM WE# follows WR# through AHCT244. WE# has no extra pulse and its LOW width is at least 45 ns. SRAM read timing Z80 CLK pin 6 Z80 MREQ# pin 19 SRAM OE# pin 24 One SRAM data pin D0-D7: pins 13-15, 17-21 CH1 rising. Repeat CH4 for all eight bits and the 00/FF/55/AA patterns. MREQ# and OE# assert LOW once per read; CH4 reaches the expected 0 V or 5 V state and is stable before the Z80 sampling edge. Use the DSLogic Group B capture to prove the complete byte and digital ordering. Address integrity Z80 CLK pin 6 SRAM A0 pin 12 or A7 pin 5 SRAM A8 pin 27 SRAM A15 pin 31 CH1 rising. Repeat with A0 and A7 on CH2 at 1, 2, 3, and 4 MHz, then at every frequency-qualification rate. For 0000/FFFF/5555/AAAA and walking patterns, each observed line matches the commanded bit, reaches valid 0/5 V levels, is stable during the active memory control interval, and has no double edge or excessive ringing. The DSLogic Group A capture proves A0-A15 together. Boot-read inhibit BOOT_READ_DISABLE at GP5, header pin 7 Buffered RD# at AHCT244 pin 7 SRAM OE# pin 24 Z80 CLK pin 6 CH1 edge, Single. Inhibit HIGH keeps OE# HIGH throughout injected instruction reads. Lower it only with Pico output isolated for intentional SRAM reads or normal execution. Repeat CH1 at AHCT244 pin 14. No unintended OE pulse is permitted. Data-path exclusion GP6 up-OE request, header pin 9 GP7 down-OE, header pin 10 AHCT245 OE# pin 19 LVC245 OE# pin 19 CH1 edge, Single; repeat CH2 edge and RD# at pin 21. Both OEs default HIGH. Up OE is GP6 OR RD#; down OE follows GP7. Both actual OEs must never be LOW together. This is a firmware rule with RD qualification, not an all-state hardware interlock; do not force both requests LOW. I/O trap and WAIT# Z80 IORQ# pin 20 Z80 WAIT# pin 24 Z80 CLK pin 6 IO_RELEASE at GP9, header pin 12 CH1 falling, Single. HCT32 asserts WAIT before the sampling edge. GP9 rises only after the data path is ready. Slow clocks complete I/O, then isolate/rearm before the execution clock resumes. WAIT must not reassert while IORQ/strobe remain active. Repeat CH4 at RD#, WR#, and both actual OEs. Supply integrity +5 V logic-rail entry at the 100 uF bulk capacitor Farthest-board +5 V rail Pico 3V3 header pin 36 Z80 CLK pin 6 Trigger on CH4 rising for repetitive operation; use Single on commands. Repeat at idle, injected RAM patterns, Z80 memory loop, disk write, and Wi-Fi traffic. CH1/CH2 remain 4.75-5.25 V; CH3 meets the Pico rail specification. No capture may show more than 250 mV droop or reset/clock disturbance. Keep DC-coupled full-bandwidth pass evidence.

docs.title: Accept or investigate
docs.text:
• Compare LOW/HIGH levels and setup/hold times with the receiving device’s datasheet limits, not the trigger voltage.
  • Investigate rail overshoot/undershoot, multiple threshold crossings, runt pulses, and ringing. Probe loading/ground leads can introduce artifacts.
  • Rise/fall readings near 4.2 ns approach the combined 100 MHz scope/150 MHz probe response; do not interpret them as exact device edge times.
  • Keep DSLogic whole-bus captures for final digital/frequency qualification.

docs.title: MCP Acceptance Runner
docs.text: scripts/scope-acceptance.mjs collects Phase 2/8 evidence; it does not flash or certify the board. Reports remain qualified=false until manual gates pass. Its single-pause evaluator cannot qualify stepped I/O completion: review raw clocks, data enables, and WAIT rearming manually.

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
1. Build the correct cumulative firmware and pass preceding phases. Phase 2 uses the empty Z80 socket; Phase 8 requires the assisted-loader board at the 1 MHz baseline.
  2. Power off before changing probes. Use compensated 10X probes, full bandwidth, DC coupling, 1 MOhm inputs, verified deskew and common circuit ground. Scope ground clips are not floating inputs.
  3. Install Node.js 20 or later and run npm ci. Build the current rigol-mcp image in the selected runtime and initialize its capture volume using that project's instructions.
  4. Stop the registered Rigol MCP server yourself and close the Pico serial terminal. The runner starts one dedicated server and calls it sequentially. --exclusive-session is your acknowledgement, not automatic proof that no other client is connected.
  5. Use a new output directory under build/bench/. The runner checks firmware identity and scope readbacks before collecting evidence, and asks for board/probe/datasheet provenance.

docs.title: Phase 2 Clock Translation
docs.text:
Connect CH1 to Pico GP2 (3.3 V), CH2 to Z80 socket CLK pin 6 (5 V), and CH3 to the Z80 VCC supply node. Repeat a separate capture on AHCT244 pin 18 to distinguish buffer delay from interconnect delay. Keep the Phase 2 reset state; do not release a CPU merely to obtain a clock measurement.

mkdir -p build/bench
npm run scope:acceptance -- --mode stage2 --runtime container \
   --ip 192.168.1.43 --port /dev/cu.usbmodemYOUR_DEVICE \
   --output build/bench/stage2-first --exclusive-session --bench-confirmed
  • Use --runtime docker for Docker.
  • The runner checks calculated frequency within 1%, duty 45–55%, supply 4.75–5.25 V, and settled clock HIGH against measured VCC minus 0.5 V.
  • Missing/sentinel readings are inconclusive. The frequency tolerance checks gross errors, not oscillator accuracy or jitter.
  • Inspect extrema, threshold crossings, and first/last pulses manually. Firmware DONE means the stimulus completed, not that the waveform passed.

docs.title: Phase 8 Clock Stop and Resume
docs.text:
Connect CH1=Z80 IORQ# pin 20, CH2=WAIT# pin 24, CH3=CLK pin 6, CH4=Pico IO_RELEASE GP9 (header pin 12). Thresholds are 2.5 V on the 5 V side and 1.65 V on the Pico side. Verify actual rails separately. Set these variables using the CPU datasheet and approved latency/pause budget; the runner has no guessed limits:

npm run scope:acceptance -- --mode stage8 --runtime container \
   --ip 192.168.1.43 --port /dev/cu.usbmodemYOUR_DEVICE \
   --output build/bench/stage8-first \
   --minimum-high-ns "$MIN_CLK_HIGH_NS" --minimum-low-ns "$MIN_CLK_LOW_NS" \
   --maximum-last-edge-us "$MAX_LAST_EDGE_US" --maximum-pause-us "$MAX_PAUSE_US" \
   --duration 60 --captures 3 --exclusive-session --bench-confirmed
  • The runner starts the RAM/USB checker, captures events, checks fault counters, and holds reset on exit. --duration 60 is not a one-hour pass; use 3600 and observe the firmware’s one-hour PASS for a full run.
  • Exercise USB traffic separately. Wi-Fi/storage workloads require later-phase evidence; discrete captures cannot exclude faults between records.
  • Retain inconclusive results for stepped completion. Check every completion clock, data setup/hold, both OEs HIGH, and GP9 LOW before execution resumes.
  • Repeat CH4 at RD#, WR#, GP6/GP7, and actual OEs; retain DSLogic groups A–D.
  • Last-edge delay includes clock-phase uncertainty; it is not exact ISR latency. Exclude deliberate pauses from jitter statistics. The 500 ms watchdog deadline is not a CPU timing limit.

docs.title: Reports and Restoration
docs.text:
1. Retain reports, serial.log, raw captures, and saved setup. Record source revision, flashed firmware identity, settings, thresholds, counters, and sample metadata; the current checkout does not identify the flashed UF2.
  2. After the workload stops, choose whether to restore the saved scope setup. Check readback and the final SCPI error queue. Declined/failed restoration produces a nonzero exit and does not restart the previous workload.
  3. If interrupted, hold reset or power down and inspect state before retrying. Restart the registered MCP server only after the dedicated runner exits.

docs.title: Fault Injection
docs.text:
Run host simulation first:

npm run test:control
npm run test:scope

Host tests check production control/loader/trap behavior against models; they do not qualify electrical faults or real timing.

Fault Required observed behavior BUSACK never asserts Request timeout, BUSREQ HIGH, Pico data isolated, no flash programming. The request-timeout path leaves the CPU running. BUSACK stuck LOW on release RESET LOW, Pico data isolated, boot inhibit HIGH, clock stopped. Capture translated SRAM controls too. IORQ or selected RD/WR stuck LOW Release deadline expires; isolate, assert reset, supply reset clocks and reboot via watchdog. Capture the transient recovery, not just the final pins. Injected image verification failure Hold RESET LOW, both data OEs HIGH, inhibit HIGH and clock stopped; do not execute an unverified image. Early IO_RELEASE or overlapping transceiver OEs Reject qualification; capture GP9, both actual OEs, and data setup at the CPU sampling edge.

Physical fault injection needs an approved interposer that disconnects the real driver before forcing a level, power-off fixture changes, and explicit operator approval. Never short active push-pull outputs, bypass voltage translation, or leave installed 5 V ICs unpowered while driven. No electrical fault injection is automated here. Persistent faults may reboot repeatedly. Record recovery at receiving pins and repeat baseline qualification after wiring changes.

docs.text: Pico header and expansion reference. Step-by-step wiring lives in the implementation phases.

docs.title: 1.0 Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W Header Pin Map
docs.text:
GPIO numbers are not physical header positions. All incoming 5 V signals pass through the 3.3 V-powered LVC244 or LVC245, including GP27/GP28, which are not 5 V-tolerant pads. Do not rely on GP0-GP25 FT tolerance during power-off.

Connect GND header pins 3,8,13,18,23,28,38 and AGND pin 33 to common GND. Header pin 36 supplies the two LVC devices and 3.3 V pull-ups. Connect external +5 V through a 1N5819 to VSYS pin 39; the band faces VSYS. Leave VBUS pin 40, RUN pin 30, 3V3_EN pin 37, and ADC_VREF pin 35 open. GP23/24/25/29 are reserved by Pico 2 W wireless hardware.

docs.title: J2 Peripheral Expansion
docs.text:
The schematic exposes the three expansion GPIOs, plus Pico 3.3 V and common GND, on a 1x5, 2.54 mm through-hole header. Its assigned KiCad footprint is Connector_PinHeader_2.54mm:PinHeader_1x05_P2.54mm_Vertical, ready for the future PCB migration. The existing PCB does not yet include this header.

J2 pin Net Pico physical header pin Use 1 PICO_GP8 11 SRAM bank-select output; reserved by supervisor 2 PICO_GP22 29 GP22 digital GPIO / Phase 10 matrix SDA 3 PICO_GP26 31 GP26 digital GPIO or ADC0 / Phase 10 matrix SCL 4 +3V3 36 Pico 3.3 V output; not an external supply input 5 GND 3,8,13,18,23,28,33,38 Common ground

These are 3.3 V-only peripheral connections, with no level shifting, protection, or LED series resistors fitted. GP8 has R24, a 10 kOhm pull-down at Pico physical pin 11, and is reserved for bank selection. GP22/GP26 have no fixed pulls on the board. Do not apply 5 V or drive them while the Pico is unpowered. Use an external current-limiting resistor for each LED. External I2C pull-ups must go to 3.3 V, not 5 V. Any peripheral powered from J2 shares the Pico regulator's remaining current budget with Wi-Fi, the LVC devices, and existing pulls; do not back-feed pin 4 or assume a dedicated peripheral power allowance.

Matrix wiring is documented in Phase 10; GP8 bank-select wiring is documented in Phase 4. GP3 is RESET#, not a fourth spare pin. As defined in the RP2350 GPIO function table, GP8, GP22, and GP26 offer SDA functions but no hardware I2C SCL, and do not form a full-duplex hardware SPI pin set. Use software or PIO implementations for I2C or SPI on this header, within the three-signal limit. A conventional four-signal SPI peripheral with separate clock, MOSI, MISO, and chip select needs another GPIO or a separate design change; do not borrow supervisor bus/control pins. Keep future peripheral handling outside timing-critical supervisor paths and qualify it separately.

docs.title: SRAM Address and Data Trunks
docs.text:
Use the maintained wiring checklists:

  • Phase 3: control and address-monitor taps
  • Phase 4: Z80–SRAM address trunk
  • Phase 4: A16 bank selection
  • Phase 5: SRAM, translators, and Pico data connections

docs.title: Memory Control
docs.text: See Phase 2 output-buffer and fixed-logic wiring and Phase 5 supplies, directions, and enables. The PIO bank-select backend controls GP7/GP8/GP9 during bank writes.

docs.title: Power and Fixed Pins
docs.text: Phase 0 owns IC grounds, fixed pins, supplies, pull resistors, and the power sequence. See the native schematic for the complete netlist.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
Scope: the three-BB830 breadboard prototype. Phase 0-10 below describe incremental socket installation, jumper wiring, and breadboard bring-up. PCB migration is deferred and its historical documentation is hidden from this site. The existing PCB is incompatible with the current firmware; do not substitute its BOM, placement, routing, or speed target into these steps.

Bring-up means proving a small part of the circuit works before adding the next part. Treat each phase like an integration test with a hardware fixture: the installed chips, wiring, firmware, and supply settings are all part of the test. A successful firmware upload alone does not prove the wiring.

Read the construction guide before handling the boards, then complete Phase 0 onward in order. Use the hardware pages as references, not as an instruction to wire and populate the whole computer at once. Prepare the firmware build tools before Phase 1; use the maintained phase programs rather than assembling displayed source files into your own test firmware.

Phase 4 includes the current SRAM A16 bank-select wiring and its power-off continuity checks. Phase 6 installs the SRAM and CPU, then qualifies both banks with the loader and CP/M tests.

For each phase:

  1. Power off: disconnect external power and USB before moving a wire, inserting a chip, or using the meter's continuity mode.
  2. Wire and inspect: follow that phase's wiring steps, verify chip orientation, then check each new connection end to end with a multimeter.
  3. Power and test: use the specified current limit and firmware; measure the named signals with the appropriate instrument.
  4. Record and decide: save the firmware version, rail voltages, idle current, test output, and any required captures. Advance only when every required test passes. If a result differs, stop at this phase and check the most recent wiring before changing firmware or adding more hardware.

A failing power check is a stop condition

A collapsed rail, unexpected current, or warm chip is not a software problem to debug while powered. Disconnect power first. Do not increase the current limit just to make the board start.

docs.title: Phase sequence
docs.text:
Phase Proves 0 - Power distribution Sockets, rails, protection, and passive defaults 1 - Pico supervisor Safe startup levels and GPIO routing 2 - Fixed logic and clock HCT32 OR gates, buffered controls, clock quality 3 - Control and port monitor Eight buffered inputs and independent WAIT release 4 - Address bus Passive address-trunk wiring; CPU remains absent 5 - Data bus Bidirectional translation and contention prevention 6 - Z80-assisted loading Fit CPU/SRAM, qualify injection, run CPU/RAM diagnostics CPU reset, fetch and bus grants Phase 6 receiving-pin measurements and physical BUSREQ/BUSACK qualification 20 MHz arithmetic and SRAM soak Optional one-hour resident CPU/stack/SRAM workload after earlier bring-up and frequency screens No-I/O 20 MHz scope test Separate continuous CPU/SRAM workload for scope captures; results retrieved from SRAM only after stopping 8 - Bidirectional I/O and USB terminal IN replies, port aliases, terminal round-trip and repeated boot/I/O integration 9 - USB CP/M and flash storage Controlled load/verify, 20 MHz scope-measured execution, USB terminal, all-record disk diagnostic and journal recovery 10 - WebSocket terminal Final multicore network terminal and disk integration Frequency qualification Measured operating limit and complete timing evidence

The former Phase 7 CPU checks are consolidated into Phase 6. There is no separate Phase 7 target; Phase 8-10 retain their numbers and target names.

Build and test one functional block at a time. Do not install the next chip until the current phase passes. Use sockets for all DIP devices, place a 100 nF ceramic capacitor directly across each IC's supply pins, and fit at least one 22 uF bulk capacitor per breadboard. Use a current-limited 5 V supply, multimeter, oscilloscope, and a DSLogic Plus logic analyzer using the documented capture groups. Start each first power-up of populated hardware at a 100 mA current limit. For the empty-board Phase 0 check, a regulated USB-C breadboard supply and multimeter are sufficient after the unpowered checks pass; adjustable current limiting is recommended extra protection. Remove power immediately if a rail falls by more than 5%, the supply's overcurrent indicator activates (if present), or a device becomes warm.

Each phase owns the signal wiring first required by that phase. Install and continuity-check those jumpers with the affected active devices removed, then insert only the devices named by the phase. The wiring diagrams are included from the consolidated hardware pages, which remain the authoritative subsystem references; the implementation plan presents the same source in construction order rather than maintaining duplicate diagrams.

Fit the specified pull-ups and pull-downs so every signal has its defined state before firmware starts. Use temporary 1 kOhm series resistors when first connecting two potentially driven nodes. Record idle current after each populated phase; Phase 0 needs only resistance and voltage readings. Unless stated otherwise, keep all chips from later phases out of their sockets.

Phase 1-10 embed the complete maintained applications and relevant shared modules in collapsed Maintained Source sections. Expand a file to read the code compiled by the firmware build; MkDocs includes it directly from src/ on every documentation build. Test plans include both existing diagnostic commands and manual measurements or test-only fault setups; they are not all automated. A command printing PASS does not replace the listed electrical checks. Record any test not performed as not verified, rather than inferring a pass.

docs.title: Saved phase checklists
docs.text:
The Done boxes and inline checkboxes on Phase 0-10 save progress in your browser on this device. Each phase has its own Clear checklist button with confirmation; clearing one phase does not clear another. Progress is not synced across devices and is removed if you clear the site's browser data. If storage is blocked or full, a warning appears and the checkboxes still work without reliable saving.

Tick wiring/setup items only after completing their instructions, and tick test or pass-gate items only after measuring and recording the required result. A saved tick is a personal record, not automated verification, permission to skip a prerequisite, or evidence that hardware timing is qualified. Leave deferred, optional, or unperformed tests unticked.

The source index links the public headers, shared modules, and build definitions. Build each phase from the repository, not by compiling the displayed files as standalone programs.

PIN_BUSACK_N is GP0, driven from Z80 BUSACK# pin 23 through the SN74LVC244 input buffer. IORQ#, RD#, WR#, and A0/A1/A2/A4 use the same buffer, so no 5 V output reaches the Pico directly. GP5 is BOOT_READ_DISABLE, GP6/GP7 are active-low data enable requests, and GP9 independently releases WAIT. GP23 on the Pico 2 W is dedicated to the CYW43439 wireless module's control interface (shared with GP24/GP25/GP29) and must never be repurposed. PIN_DATA_0-PIN_DATA_7 occupy GP10-GP17. The CPU alone drives SRAM address and write controls; there is no memory-source selector. PIN_WR_N is GP28, buffered through the same SN74LVC244; io_trap_handler() reads both PIN_RD_N and PIN_WR_N to resolve cycle intent.

docs.title: VS Code tasks
docs.text:
Choose Tasks: Run Task, then Build Pico - Phase 6 20 MHz scope diagnostic to build only, or Flash Pico - Phase 6 20 MHz scope diagnostic to build and deploy. The flash task force-enters BOOTSEL; save work and finish running tests first. Follow the hardware and power prerequisites below.

z80_stage06_scope_20mhz is an isolated diagnostic for observing the clock, instruction fetches and SRAM activity without Z80 I/O reports or clock pauses. It is separate from both the full-memory frequency screens and the one-hour arithmetic soak.

Building this target does not deploy it. Do not flash, disconnect serial, or attach/move probes during another running test. Finish and retain that test's results first.

docs.title: Purpose and limits
docs.text:
After slow loading and verification, the Pico generates continuous nominal 20 MHz PWM while the Z80 repeatedly checks arithmetic, flags, comparisons, loops, stack behavior and SRAM data. No Z80 IN, OUT, block-I/O instruction, or Pico I/O-trap handler participates in the running workload.

The Pico USB console still accepts commands. This is no Z80 port I/O, not an absence of USB communication with the Pico. s and h do not pause PWM or inspect live SRAM. There are no periodic result reads, bank reloads, BUSREQ transactions or automatic one-hour stops.

Property Scope diagnostic Target z80_stage06_scope_20mhz Supervisor clock 120 MHz, selected before USB and Z80 execution Z80 clock 20 MHz, scope-measured; PWM divider 1, period count 6, three HIGH/three LOW Runtime Continuous until explicit stop, disconnect, or power loss SRAM work area 2000h-FFFFh, 56 KiB Live CPU result reports None Results Reserved SRAM mailbox, retrieved only after stopping Detected Z80 mismatch Save first failure, enter HALT; PWM keeps running Operator stop x immediately stops PWM, then reads the mailbox with assisted clocks Console disconnect Fail closed; reconnect and explicitly request result retrieval Automatic PASS Never

The configured clock is not a measured frequency. A continuously switching CLK does not prove that arithmetic or memory checks are still advancing: the CPU might have halted, stalled or branched incorrectly. This target intentionally gives up the soak's live progress timeout and result supervision to provide an uninterrupted measurement interval.

docs.title: Maintained sources
docs.text:
• scope_test.c: Pico controller
  • scope_test.asm: no-I/O assembly selection
  • math_workload.asm: shared checked workload
  • scope_test_program.h: image/mailbox definitions and validation
  • math_soak_program.h: independent C reference answers
  • CMakeLists.txt: isolated firmware target

The original soak selects the same assembly workload with port reports enabled; the scope image selects SRAM reports instead. The original soak's assembled bytes are preserved by this separation.

docs.title: What the Z80 tests
docs.text:
The soak guide's arithmetic and instruction descriptions also describe the shared scope workload:

  1. Check 16 nested CALL levels, HL/DE/BC preservation, SP recovery and the lower stack guard.

  2. Perform 16 passes through 128 fixed operand pairs:

    • 16-bit ADD, ADC with carry, and SBC with/without borrow.
    • Result and documented arithmetic-flag assertions.
    • Shift/add multiplication, checking the low 16 product bits.
    • Signed and unsigned less/equal/greater decisions.

  3. Check every vector-table end pointer and the outer repetition count.

  4. Fill the entire 56 KiB work area, then read and compare the entire area.
  5. Commit a completed-phase count in SRAM and advance to the next pattern.

Patterns are low address byte, high address byte, complemented low byte and complemented high byte. Four phases make a cycle. Each complete phase credits 57,344 SRAM-byte checks, 22,528 arithmetic assertions, five stack checks and 17 loop checks: 79,894 logical checks.

Additional scope-reporting instructions include LD HL,(nn), LD (nn),HL, LD (nn),IX, and LD (nn),DE. They update memory only. The normal/failure OUT blocks are excluded by assembly selection.

docs.title: Memory map
docs.text:
Address Purpose 0000h-0EFFh Code and local loop state; assembler rejects overlap with mailbox 0F00h-0F1Fh 32-byte scope result mailbox 0F20h-0FFFh Unused resident reserve 1000h-19FFh 128 independent expected-answer records 1A00h-1FFFh Stack reserve; lower guard at 1A00h 2000h-FFFFh Destructive SRAM work area

The Pico builds, loads and verifies the complete lower 8 KiB image once. Only the Z80 addresses and accesses SRAM, including assisted loading and post-stop reads. Neither the mailbox nor code/table/stack regions receive the destructive work-area sweeps; this is not full-64-KiB pattern coverage.

docs.title: Build without deploying
docs.text:
From the repository root, with the firmware toolchain and z80asm available:

export PATH="$HOME/.local/share/arm-gnu-toolchain-15.3.rel1/bin:$PATH"
cmake -S . -B build/scope20 -G Ninja -DPICO_BOARD=pico2_w
cmake --build build/scope20 --target z80_stage06_scope_20mhz

Output:

build/scope20/src/stage06_sram_dma/z80_stage06_scope_20mhz.uf2

This separate build directory leaves the earlier soak/screen UF2s intact. Normal firmware retains its existing clock limit. The scope target uses the isolated 20 MHz clock/CPU chain and does not install an I/O trap.

The VS Code Flash Pico - Phase 6 20 MHz scope diagnostic task force-flashes the UF2 without a Phase 9 stop/flush handshake. Use it only when interrupting the current firmware is safe and the populated board has external +5 V applied before USB.

docs.title: Later deployment and console operation
docs.text:
The following is a later manual procedure, not part of building.

  1. Finish the current test and save its final results. Close its serial owner; never open competing USB serial readers.
  2. For the current circuit, all eight active packages must be installed and powered. Apply external 5 V before USB; disconnect USB before removing external 5 V. Never program the populated board with only USB power.
  3. Attach the scope probes with the board powered off, following the 20 MHz clock measurement procedure.

  4. Identify the intended Pico with picotool info -a. With exactly one intended Pico attached, flash and verify:

    picotool load -v -x \
  build/scope20/src/stage06_sram_dma/z80_stage06_scope_20mhz.uf2 -f

    If multiple devices are attached, select the current --bus and --address explicitly. Require flash verification success.

  5. Open the Pico USB serial connection with DTR asserted. For example:

    picocom -b 115200 /dev/cu.usbmodem1101

    Use the actual port on your host. Check the no-I/O diagnostic banner and clk_sys=120000000Hz; boot/reconnect never starts the test.

  6. Send f + Enter. Wait for RUN: nominal=20000000Hz before measuring. Loading, verification and startup reset clocks are not the continuous scope interval.

Command Behavior f + Enter Start a fresh load, verification and continuous run; stopped state only s + Enter Report controller state, not live CPU progress h + Enter Show help without disturbing the running clock x immediately During RUN, stop and retrieve results; during assisted operations, abort r + Enter Read the stopped mailbox after a previously started run, including after reconnect

x discards the remainder of its input line. Press Enter before another command. A serial disconnect stops safely without retrieving results or restarting. After reconnect, use r + Enter; SRAM must have remained powered. Results survive reset, not loss of SRAM power, and a fresh f replaces them.

docs.title: Scope captures
docs.text:
Use the DHO814 20 MHz setup to measure at Z80 CLK pin 6, not just Pico GP2.

The project prototype capture in the oscilloscope guide shows a 20.0000 MHz cursor reading and 50.000 ns period. Its statistics also include a 9.9502 MHz minimum; inspect the waveform for that low reading before using the capture to qualify missed edges or jitter. Capture only after RUN and before x/disconnect. There should be no deliberate reporting-related clock gaps during that interval.

For SRAM work, use the existing read/write capture groups. The first part of each phase performs arithmetic and stack traffic, followed by a full work-area fill and verification. Not every observed write is a work-area write: stack and mailbox updates are also legitimate memory cycles. Repeat captures with the logic analyzer as needed to identify addresses/data.

On a detected mismatch, HALT leaves the Pico PWM running; Z80 HALT can still produce fetch/refresh activity. Do not interpret either as continuing useful work. Stop and retrieve the mailbox after your captures.

docs.title: Interpreting stopped results
docs.text:
x stops PWM and asserts RESET before starting slow Z80-assisted reads. These readback clocks are outside the measurement interval. Retrieval finishes with RESET asserted, SRAM inhibited and Pico data paths isolated. Do not assume a stopped PWM signal is physically LOW.
