Mailbox offset Meaning 00h-03h ASCII SCP1, format identifier 04h 00h prepared/not started, 01h started, E1h committed mismatch 05h Busy flag: 01h while committing progress/failure, 00h when stable 06h-09h Completed phases, unsigned 32-bit little-endian 0Ah Last completed pattern, 0-3; FFh before any completion 0Bh Reserved 0Ch, 0Dh Failure stage and vector/context 0Eh-0Fh Failure address, little-endian 10h-11h Actual value, little-endian 12h-13h Expected value, little-endian 14h-1Fh Reserved

The busy flag is written first and cleared last for both progress and failure commits. A stop during an update yields INCONCLUSIVE, rather than crediting a potentially torn count or failure record. An invalid magic, state, last-pattern/count relationship or failure record is also inconclusive. The 32-bit phase counter must not be allowed to wrap; counts after wrap are not meaningful.

Example of eight completed phases:

SNAPSHOT: phases=8 completed_cycles=2 sram_byte_checks=458752 math_vectors=16384 completed_phase_checks=639152
RESULT: no mismatch recorded in retrieved mailbox; not proof of live progress, not a timed PASS or timing qualification

Only completed phases are credited. A stable started mailbox with zero phases is inconclusive. A positive count proves that those completions were recorded, not that the CPU was still advancing at the moment you stopped it.

Failure stages and field meanings match the soak failure identifiers, but this target stores the fields in SRAM instead of emitting a packet. The Z80 commits failure data before setting the failure state and clearing busy, then HALTs. HALT itself is not monitored by a Pico input.

Loader, clock, verification and readback faults print explicit FAIL messages. An incomplete/invalid mailbox never becomes a PASS. There is no automated duration criterion or live first-fault notification in this scope target.

docs.title: Host validation
docs.text:
With the optional pinned emulator environment configured as in the soak host-validation guide:

cmake -S src/common/tests -B build/host-control -G Ninja \
  -DSOAK_EMULATOR_PYTHON="$PWD/build/math-soak-emulator/bin/python"
cmake --build build/host-control --target scope_test math_soak_test math_soak_14h_test
ctest --test-dir build/host-control -R '^(scope_|math_soak_)' --output-on-failure

Controller tests cover DTR/manual gating, verification, quiet RUN behavior, post-stop readback, disconnect/reconnect, invalid/torn mailboxes and failures. The independent Z80 core executes the actual scope image through two cycles and rejects any IN or OUT, including failure paths. It checks mailbox commit ordering, a 16-bit counter carry into the high word, all arithmetic failure stages, the stack guard and first/middle/last SRAM corruption.

The original soak controller and instruction tests remain regression checks. Host validation and an ARM build are not physical scope measurements or a bench pass for this newly built target.

docs.title: One-Hour 20 MHz Z80 Arithmetic and SRAM Soak Test
docs.text:
This diagnostic makes the physical Z80 execute and check its own workload from SRAM, while the Pico supplies a scope-measured 20 MHz clock, receives result reports and supervises a one-hour run. It is not a Pico simulation of the Z80, an empty clock loop, or a test of only one SRAM address.

The workload combines 16-bit arithmetic and flags, signed and unsigned comparisons, software multiplication, nested loops, subroutine calls, stack traffic and repeated write/read/compare sweeps of a 56 KiB work area.

There are two separately built durations. The original one-hour target remains unchanged in behavior; z80_stage06_math_soak_14h_20mhz runs the same resident workload for at least 14 hours, then finishes on a complete four-pattern cycle. Unless specified otherwise, the examples below describe the one-hour target.

Property Configuration Firmware target z80_stage06_math_soak_20mhz Z80 program Resident assembly starting at 0000h Z80 clock 20,000,000 Hz scope-measured on the project prototype; 50% duty configured Pico system clock 120 MHz Minimum run 3600 seconds of execution-phase elapsed time Completion boundary A complete four-pattern cycle Arithmetic corpus 128 operand pairs, repeated 16 times per phase SRAM work area 2000h-FFFFh, 57,344 bytes Result channel Z80 OUT (06h),A Stop policy First detected mismatch, control fault or progress timeout Operator start USB serial with DTR, then f + Enter

A passing soak is functional evidence under the tested conditions, not an analogue timing qualification or a guaranteed system rating. The earlier full-64-KiB frequency screen is a separate test and remains useful.

docs.title: Sources and related documentation
docs.text:
The maintained implementation, rather than the explanatory examples here, is authoritative:

  • Z80 assembly entry: math_soak.asm
  • Shared checked workload: math_workload.asm
  • Pico controller: math_soak_test.c
  • Reference answers and memory layout: math_soak_program.h
  • Assembly and embedding rules: CMakeLists.txt
  • Hardware I/O trap: io_trap.c
  • Buffered data-bus access: bus.c

See also the Phase 6 SRAM bring-up specification and frequency-qualification plan. The full text of this README is also included in the MkDocs soak-test page.

For uninterrupted clock/SRAM captures, use the separate no-I/O 20 MHz scope diagnostic. It selects the same checked assembly workload but stores results in SRAM instead of using OUT; retrieval occurs only after stopping, with no live or timed PASS. It does not replace or alter this one-hour soak.

docs.title: Hardware, power and clock prerequisites
docs.text:
This is for the current breadboard circuit with all eight active packages:

  • Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W.
  • Z84C0020PEC Z80.
  • AS6C1008-55PCN SRAM; grounded A16 selects the accessible lower 64 KiB.
  • SN74HCT32N fixed logic.
  • SN74AHCT244N control/clock buffer.
  • SN74AHCT245N Pico-to-Z80 data buffer.
  • SN74LVC245AN Z80-to-Pico data buffer.
  • SN74LVC244AN control/port monitor.

Complete the earlier wiring, isolation, assisted-loading and clock-speed checks before using this soak. The historical PCB is not equivalent to this circuit.

Every installed 5 V IC must be powered. Apply external 5 V before USB; disconnect USB before removing external 5 V. Do not flash a populated board on USB power alone. Do not change wiring or insert/remove ICs while powered.

Only this isolated diagnostic chain opts into the 20 MHz limit. Before USB initialization, with Z80 reset asserted, it configures PLL_SYS with a 1200 MHz VCO and post-dividers 5 and 2, giving 120 MHz clk_sys. PWM uses integer divider 1 and period count 6, with three counts HIGH and three LOW. USB keeps its separate 48 MHz PLL. No supervisor-clock retuning occurs during execution.

The controller refuses to start if the system clock is not 120 MHz or the selected PWM clock is not 20 MHz. Displayed frequencies are nominal configured values, not oscilloscope measurements.

docs.title: Loading and memory layout
docs.text:
The Pico first builds an 8192-byte resident image containing assembled Z80 instructions, reference records and initialized stack space. The Z80 itself writes and reads this image using the existing slow, instruction-injected loader. Every image byte is verified before free-running execution starts. The Pico never drives the SRAM address bus or masters SRAM writes.

The Z80 is then reset to start at 0000h. Its program disables maskable interrupts with DI and sets SP to 2000h. There is no CP/M, BDOS, UART driver or DCC-generated startup code involved in this diagnostic.

Address range Purpose during the soak 0000h-0FFFh Reserved code region, including the pattern and repeats state bytes 1000h-19FFh 128 reference records, 20 bytes each 1A00h-1FFFh Stack reserve, initially filled with A5h 2000h-FFFFh 56 KiB destructive SRAM work area

The stack grows downward from 2000h. The byte at 1A00h is checked as a lower guard. The code uses only part of its reserved region and only part of the stack reserve.

The work-area sweeps do not overwrite the code, reference table or stack. Those regions receive instruction fetches, table reads and stack accesses, but are not exhaustively swept at 20 MHz. The physical SRAM's inaccessible upper 64 KiB is not tested.

docs.title: Overall execution loop
docs.text:
The Z80 stays resident and repeats this sequence without reloading:

repeat:
    for pattern = 0, 1, 2, 3:
        check nested calls, saved registers, stack pointer and stack guard
        repeat 16 times:
            check all 128 arithmetic/reference records
            check that the reference pointer reached the table end
        check that the outer repetition count was exactly 16
        fill every work-area byte with this pattern
        read every work-area byte and compare with the expected pattern
        report successful completion of this phase through OUT port 06h

One phase includes all of the above checks for one SRAM pattern. Four phases form one cycle. The Pico, not the Z80 program, measures the hour and stops execution at a completed-cycle boundary.

docs.title: Operand corpus and independent expected answers
docs.text:
The first 64 operand pairs are the Cartesian product of these eight values:

0000h  0001h  0FFFh  7FFFh  8000h  8001h  5555h  FFFFh

These exercise zero, carries, the bit-11/bit-12 half-carry boundary, signed limits and alternating data bits. The remaining 64 pairs come from a deterministic 32-bit xorshift generator seeded with 5A801337h.

The Pico calculates expected results with wider C arithmetic before loading the image. The Z80 performs the actual calculations independently and compares against the stored answers. It does not generate its expected answer by repeating the same Z80 operation.

The corpus is fixed and repeatable: the test does not generate fresh random operands on every cycle. Each phase executes 128 pairs 16 times, giving 2048 complete vector checks per phase.

docs.title: Eleven assertions for each operand pair
docs.text:
For each 16-bit pair a, b, the Z80 checks:

Check Z80 operation Assertions Addition ADD HL,DE Result and applicable flags Addition with carry-in 1 SCF; ADC HL,DE Result and flags Subtraction with borrow-in 0 OR A; SBC HL,DE Result and flags Subtraction with borrow-in 1 SCF; SBC HL,DE Result and flags Multiplication 16-step shift/add subroutine Low 16-bit result Unsigned ordering Subtract, then branch on zero/carry Less/equal/greater code Signed ordering Subtract, then branch on zero/sign/overflow Less/equal/greater code

Four result checks plus four flag checks plus multiplication and two ordering checks make 11 logical assertions. A checked 16-bit value counts as one assertion even though its low and high bytes are compared separately.

All arithmetic results wrap modulo 65536. The comparison codes are FFh for less than, 00h for equal and 01h for greater than.

docs.title: Flag checks
docs.text:
For ADD HL,DE, mask 13h checks half-carry, subtract and carry. It does not check preservation of sign, zero or parity/overflow for this instruction.

For ADC HL,DE and SBC HL,DE, mask D7h checks:

  • S: sign, from bit 15.
  • Z: zero across the entire 16-bit result.
  • H: carry/borrow across the bit-11/bit-12 boundary.
  • P/V: signed overflow, not the parity of the result.
  • N: whether the operation is subtraction.
  • C: unsigned carry or borrow.

Undocumented flag bits 3 and 5 are deliberately excluded. The assembly saves AF with PUSH AF, then uses POP HL to recover the saved flag byte in L after checking the arithmetic result.

Examples of cases covered by the corpus:

FFFFh + 0001h       -> 0000h, carry set
7FFFh + 0000h + 1   -> 8000h, signed overflow set
0000h - 0000h - 1   -> FFFFh, borrow set
8000h compared with 7FFFh:
    unsigned: greater
    signed:   less (-32768 versus +32767)

Signed ordering uses sign XOR overflow, not sign alone. The branch paths explicitly handle overflow and equality, so a result with its sign bit set does not automatically mean the original signed operand was smaller.

docs.title: Multiplication and loop invariants
docs.text:
There is no native Z80 multiply instruction in this workload. A subroutine shifts the 16-bit multiplier right using SRL B and RR C. If the shifted-out bit is one, it adds the multiplicand to the accumulator. It doubles the multiplicand with ADD HL,HL, exchanging DE/HL as needed, and repeats 16 times.

Only the low 16 product bits are checked; this is not a full 32-bit product or a multiply-overflow test.

After each 128-record pass, the Z80 checks that IX reached 1A00h, immediately after the reference table. After the 16 repetitions, it checks that IY equals 16. These add 17 loop-bound assertions per phase.

docs.title: Subroutine and stack checks
docs.text:
Each phase loads HL=1357h, DE=2468h, BC=5FAAh, then makes 16 recursive CALL levels. Each level pushes BC, DE and HL and restores them before RET. The recursion stops when the low nibble of B becomes zero.

The subsequent assertions check:

  1. HL was restored to 1357h.
  2. DE was restored to 2468h.
  3. BC was restored to 5FAAh.
  4. SP equals 1FFCh inside the stack-test subroutine: two return addresses are active at that point, one for the phase and one for the stack test.
  5. The lower guard byte at 1A00h remains A5h.

This exercises return-address storage, descending SRAM stack writes, ascending reads, PUSH/POP order and register preservation. It does not scan every byte of the stack reserve or exhaustively prove every possible stack fault.

In addition, pattern_byte is called for every work-byte write and every work-byte verification. Stack traffic therefore continues throughout the SRAM sweeps, not just during the explicit recursive check.

docs.title: SRAM write/read/compare patterns
docs.text:
Every phase fills all 57,344 bytes from 2000h through FFFFh before starting verification. Verification recomputes the expected byte and reads the entire area in ascending address order. Address-pointer wrap to zero ends the sweep, including the last address FFFFh.

Phase Expected byte at address ABCDh Success marker 0: low address byte CDh 40h 1: high address byte ABh 41h 2: complemented low byte 32h 42h 3: complemented high byte 54h 43h

The complementary patterns exercise both states of each data bit. Combining low- and high-address patterns helps expose address aliasing. Filling the whole area first avoids relying only on an immediate write/read to one location. This is not a complete March algorithm, an exhaustive coupling-fault test or a separate long-retention test.

docs.title: Z80 instructions exercised
docs.text:
The table describes the actual resident assembly, including supporting instructions. Being exercised is not the same as having every flag, operand combination or possible failure mode exhaustively checked.

Instruction/forms Role in this program LD r,r, LD r,n Operand movement, expected values, counters and report fields LD BC,nn, LD DE,nn, LD HL,nn, LD SP,nn Register-pair and stack initialization LD IX,nn, LD IY,nn Reference-table pointer and repetition counter LD r,(IX+d) Indexed reads of operands, reference results and flags; displacements 0-19 LD (HL),A, LD A,(HL) Work-area writes and verification reads LD (nn),A, LD A,(nn) SRAM-backed loop state and stack-guard access ADD HL,DE, ADC HL,DE, SBC HL,DE Checked 16-bit arithmetic ADD HL,HL, ADD HL,SP, ADD IX,DE Multiplicand shifting, SP observation and record-pointer advancement ADD A,n, SUB B Progress-marker formation and failure-vector index encoding INC HL, INC IY, INC A, INC C Address progression, repetitions, ordering codes and check stages DEC A, DEC B Multiplication/repetition/vector/recursion loops and ordering codes AND n, OR A, OR L, OR n, XOR A Flag masks, carry clearing, zero tests and marker/phase setup CP D, CP E Byte comparisons for work data and 16-bit expected values SCF, CPL Carry/borrow input setup and complemented SRAM patterns BIT 0,C, BIT 1,C Select low/high address bytes and complement behavior SRL B, RR C Shift the 16-bit multiplier, propagating bits through carry EX DE,HL Swap multiplicand and accumulator during multiplication PUSH AF/BC/DE/HL/IX/IY Save flags, registers, pointers and comparison values POP BC/DE/HL/IX Restore saved values or transfer them through the stack CALL, RET, RET Z Recursion, arithmetic/check helpers and pattern selection JR, JR Z/NZ/C/NC Relative loops and conditional decision paths JP, JP NZ/PE/M Cycle/vector loops, sign/overflow decisions and mismatch exits OUT (n),A Success markers and multi-byte failure packets DI Disable maskable interrupts at program startup HALT Failure path only; Pico reset may stop execution before it reaches HALT

The workload includes ordinary, CB-prefixed, ED-prefixed and DD/FD-prefixed instructions. For example, CB provides bit/shift operations, ED provides 16-bit ADC/SBC, and DD/FD provide IX/IY operations.

It does not exercise IN, DJNZ, LDIR/other block instructions, EXX, alternate-register-bank checking, BCD/DAA, division, every indexed addressing mode, or interrupt-service/acknowledge behavior. DI is executed, but interrupt masking is not verified by injecting interrupts. Failure-packet instructions and HALT are not part of the normal passing loop.

docs.title: How results reach the Pico through OUT port 06h
docs.text: The Z80 performs the checks. The Pico receives compact completion reports; it does not reread every SRAM byte or redo every calculation during the soak.

docs.title: Success reports and the hardware handshake
docs.text:
After a successful phase, the Z80 executes the equivalent of:

ld a,040h       ; Phase 0 complete
out (06h),a

This is an I/O transaction, not a write to SRAM address 0006h.

  1. The Z80 drives the port address and D0-D7 data, asserting IORQ# (I/O request) and WR# (write). # means active LOW.
  2. With Pico IO_RELEASE LOW, HCT32 logic asserts WAIT# using WAIT# = IORQ# OR IO_RELEASE. The I/O transaction is held for the Pico.
  3. Buffered IORQ# interrupts the Pico. Its handler stops PWM, allows settling, samples the port through the LVC244 monitor and validates the controls.
  4. The Pico keeps the upward data driver disabled, enables the downward LVC245 path and reads the byte safely at 3.3 V logic levels.
  5. The receive callback validates the port and marker order. Expected markers are 40h, 41h, 42h, 43h, repeating; each credits one complete phase.
  6. The trap raises IO_RELEASE and completes the transaction using controlled single clock cycles until IORQ# and WR# release. It isolates both data paths, lowers IO_RELEASE and resumes PWM.

Only A0/A1/A2/A4 are decoded (address & 17h). OUT (n),A also presents A on the high address byte, but this circuit ignores those bits. Thus sending 40h to port 06h is still decoded as 06h, not a distinct 4006h service.

The brief I/O reporting pauses are included in execution-phase elapsed time. Memory accesses have no added wait states. During memory cycles IORQ# is HIGH, keeping the HCT32 WAIT# output HIGH.

No IN is needed. An unexpected I/O read or out-of-order/invalid report is a protocol fault, not a valid success.

docs.title: Failure packet and check-stage identifiers
docs.text:
A detected mismatch sends nine bytes, each with a separate OUT (06h),A:

Byte position Meaning 0 E1h, start of failure packet 1 Check-stage identifier 2 Vector index or diagnostic context 3, 4 Relevant address, low byte then high byte 5, 6 Actual 16-bit value, low byte then high byte 7, 8 Expected 16-bit value, low byte then high byte Stage, hexadecimal Failed check 01, 02 ADD result, flags 03, 04 ADC with carry-in 1 result, flags 05, 06 SBC with borrow-in 0 result, flags 07, 08 SBC with borrow-in 1 result, flags 09 Low-16-bit multiplication result 0A, 0B Unsigned, signed ordering code 0C, 0D, 0E Restored HL, DE, BC 0F Stack-pointer recovery 10 Lower stack guard 11 Reference-table end pointer 12 Outer repetition count 80, 81, 82, 83 SRAM pattern 0, 1, 2, 3

Arithmetic records use vector indices 0-127; their address identifies the 20-byte reference record, not a work-area byte. RAM errors use index FFh and report the failing work address; their actual/expected byte occupies the low byte of each value. Structural/stack indices are context only: their address field reflects IX and does not necessarily identify a failing stack location. For example, stack-guard stage 10 identifies the fixed guard at 1A00h even though the reported IX points at the reference table.

The assembly contains HALT after the packet. Once the Pico receives the complete packet, it prints the details, asserts RESET and stops PWM; reset may preempt HALT. A partial packet also fails on the progress timeout.

docs.title: Statistics and what the displayed numbers mean
docs.text:
The Pico generates PROGRESS and STATS over USB serial every ten seconds. The host logger adds the UTC timestamp and SERIAL prefix. The Z80 does not format or transmit those text lines, nor does it send one OUT per assertion.

For p completed phases:

Field Formula completed_math_vectors p * 2048 sram_byte_checks p * 57344 math_assertions p * 2048 * 11 = p * 22528 stack_checks p * 5 loop_checks p * 17 successes Sum of the four check categories: p * 79894 completed_cycles Integer division p / 4 failures 0 until a detected failure; first-failure stop reports 1

Counters credit only completed phases. Successful operations in a partially completed phase are not counted. Counts are logical checks, not CPU instructions, clock edges or unique memory addresses.

For example, this is a progress sample, not a final one-hour PASS:

PROGRESS: actual=20000000Hz pwm_ms=340010 phases=365 completed_math_vectors=747520
STATS: successes=29161310 failures=0 sram_byte_checks=20930560 math_assertions=8222720 stack_checks=1825 loop_checks=6205 completed_cycles=91

It represents 5 minutes 40.010 seconds, 365 phases, 91 full cycles plus one phase, and 29,161,310 completed assertions with no detected failure. Advancing 10 or 11 phases between ten-second reports is normal; reporting and phase boundaries are independent.

actual is nominal selected PWM frequency. pwm_ms is elapsed time since the execution phase began, excluding initial loading/verification but including the brief trapped-I/O pauses. It is not a count of only the intervals when PWM was enabled. A timestamp ending in Z is UTC.

docs.title: Completion, failures and incomplete runs
docs.text:
A valid completed run requires:

  • At least 3600000 milliseconds of execution-phase elapsed time.
  • A complete four-pattern cycle at the stop boundary.
  • No pending failure packet, protocol error, control fault or progress timeout.
  • The final PASS and zero-failure statistics.

The final line has this shape; elapsed milliseconds and totals vary by run:

PASS: one-hour soak complete (functional, not timing qualification); actual=20000000Hz pwm_ms=<at-least-3600000>; RESET# LOW
STATS: successes=<total> failures=0 sram_byte_checks=<total> math_assertions=<total> stack_checks=<total> loop_checks=<total> completed_cycles=<total>

The Pico fails closed on loader/image/clock errors, CPU-reported mismatches, malformed reports and I/O control faults. A five-second lack of phase progress, or an incomplete failure packet that times out, also fails. Some shared trap faults fail closed and reboot; any reboot invalidates the current run rather than automatically resuming it.

x or a console disconnect produces an incomplete STOP, not a PASS. An operator abort/disconnect does not increment the mismatch failure count; therefore failures=0 alone does not prove completion. Reconnecting never automatically starts or resumes the soak.

After completion, failure or abort, the firmware asserts RESET, stops PWM and isolates both Pico data paths. A stopped PWM output must not be assumed to be physically LOW without measurement.

docs.title: Build, flash and run
docs.text: All commands below run from the repository root. Do not flash or reopen the serial port during an existing soak unless intentionally ending it.

docs.title: Fourteen-hour variant
docs.text:
Build in a separate directory to retain the previous one-hour firmware:

cmake -S . -B build/soak14h -G Ninja -DPICO_BOARD=pico2_w
cmake --build build/soak14h --target z80_stage06_math_soak_14h_20mhz

UF2:

build/soak14h/src/stage06_sram_dma/z80_stage06_math_soak_14h_20mhz.uf2

Use this UF2 instead of the one-hour image in the flash procedure below. The banner must say starts 14 hours, and RUN must report minimum=50400s. f starts a fresh 14-hour run; there is no live duration-change command. The final PASS requires at least 50,400,000 ms, zero failures and a complete four-pattern cycle. Success text begins PASS: 14-hour soak complete.

All arithmetic, SRAM coverage, port reporting, error stops and counters are identical. Totals use 64-bit arithmetic; successful checks can exceed 4,294,967,295 during this longer run. Keep external power and USB stable and prevent the host from sleeping for the entire run. On macOS, a logger can use caffeinate -i -w <logger-PID> to prevent idle sleep for its lifetime; keep a laptop's lid open and its power connected. Closing a read-only log viewer does not stop the serial owner, but closing the serial connection invalidates the run.

docs.title: Expected 14-hour completion summary
docs.text:
The following table summarizes the recorded passing run of 19-20 October 2026. It is a human-readable example of the expected completion report, not a table printed by the Pico firmware: the firmware emits PASS and STATS, while the host logger records start/finish times and serial state. Future runs will have different dates, elapsed time and totals. Require at least 14 hours, zero failures, a complete four-phase cycle and a final PASS rather than an exact match to these counts.

Metric Result Overall result PASS Z80 clock 20 MHz, scope-measured on the project prototype Started 19 October 2026, 18:40:12 AEDT Finished 20 October 2026, 08:40:14 AEDT Recorded execution time 14 hours, 1.738 seconds Total successful checks 4,332,172,256 Failures 0 SRAM byte comparisons 3,109,421,056 Arithmetic assertions 1,221,558,272 Completed arithmetic test vectors 111,050,752 Stack checks 271,120 Loop checks 921,808 Complete four-phase cycles 13,556 Completed phases 54,224 Final RESET# LOW - CPU held in reset Final PWM clock Stopped Serial connection Closed

AEDT is UTC+11. The recorded execution time comes from pwm_ms=50401738, not subtraction of the rounded wall-clock timestamps. As described above, it includes brief I/O-trap pauses. This PASS establishes functional endurance for the tested CPU/arithmetic/stack/SRAM workload; it does not establish electrical timing margins or qualify CP/M and disk I/O at 20 MHz.

docs.title: Build the isolated target
docs.text:
Use the project's firmware toolchain setup with CMake, Ninja, Pico SDK, Arm GNU tools and z80asm available:

cmake -S . -B build/pwm17-20 -G Ninja -DPICO_BOARD=pico2_w
cmake --build build/pwm17-20 --target z80_stage06_math_soak_20mhz

Generated firmware:

build/pwm17-20/src/stage06_sram_dma/z80_stage06_math_soak_20mhz.uf2

The build assembles the maintained Z80 source and embeds it in the Pico application. A build-time size check prevents code overlapping the reference table. The normal firmware's clock limit remains unchanged.

docs.title: Flash only with all ICs powered
docs.text:
Close any existing serial console/logger after its run has finished. With external 5 V applied before USB, identify the intended Pico:

picotool info -a

Normal-mode identification can return a nonzero status while listing the USB-connected Pico; that is not a flash-verification result. If exactly one intended Pico is connected, flash, verify and boot:

picotool load -v -x \
  build/pwm17-20/src/stage06_sram_dma/z80_stage06_math_soak_20mhz.uf2 -f

If multiple devices are attached, select the intended device with picotool's --bus and --address options from its current identification output; do not assume USB addresses remain constant. Require verification success. Booting the firmware does not start the destructive test.

docs.title: Start from a serial console
docs.text:
Connect USB serial with DTR asserted. A typical macOS port and command are:

picocom -b 115200 /dev/cu.usbmodem1101

Choose the actual device path on your machine. USB CDC does not use the 115200 setting as a physical Z80 timing reference.

Check the banner:

20MHz math/SRAM soak ready; f + Enter starts one hour; x aborts immediately.
Pico clk_sys=120000000Hz; nominal PWM=20000000Hz, not measured.

That banner reports the firmware's PWM target and does not include a physical measurement. The project prototype's Z80 clock has independently been measured at 20 MHz with an oscilloscope.

Command Action f + Enter Load/verify the image, then start a fresh one-hour run h + Enter Show help s + Enter Show state and current statistics x immediately Abort without waiting for Enter

An abort discards the rest of its input line; press Enter before a subsequent command. Expect LOAD, then RUN, then progress/statistics roughly every ten seconds. Keep external power and USB connected throughout.

docs.title: View live results without disturbing the serial owner
docs.text:
Only one process should own the serial connection. If a logger already owns it, do not open picocom as a second reader: changing DTR or disconnecting can invalidate the run.

Instead, open a foreground terminal that follows the logger's actual file:

tail -n 20 -F /path/to/captured-soak.log

Use the real log path printed by the active logger. Ctrl+C in this read-only viewer stops the viewer only; it does not send x or stop the soak. Commands must go through the process owning the serial connection. Keep the host awake and retain the final PASS/FAIL and statistics, not just an early sample.

For reproducible evidence, record the firmware SHA-256, board/rail conditions, configured clocks and complete timestamped serial output. Do not turn a failed/interrupted attempt into a pass by silently restarting and discarding its earlier evidence.

docs.title: Host validation
docs.text:
The controller tests check DTR/manual-start gating, image loading, clock rejection, abort, disconnect, failure reporting, protocol/control faults and progress timeouts. Simulated time verifies the exact hour boundary, complete-cycle requirement and statistics without waiting a physical hour.

The independent instruction-execution test uses the pinned host-only z80 package. It runs the actual generated resident image through two complete cycles: eight phases, 16,384 vector checks and all four SRAM patterns twice. It independently checks the final work bytes after each phase, reference-table preservation and the stack guard.

Fault injection corrupts each arithmetic-result/flag/comparison expectation, the stack guard, and the first/middle/last work addresses (2000h, 8000h, FFFFh). These cases must produce the correct failure packet without a phase-success marker.

To enable the independent core, use Python 3.10 or newer; substitute an available version for python3.14:

python3.14 -m venv build/math-soak-emulator
build/math-soak-emulator/bin/python -m pip install \
  -r src/common/tests/requirements-soak.txt
cmake -S src/common/tests -B build/host-control -G Ninja \
  -DSOAK_EMULATOR_PYTHON="$PWD/build/math-soak-emulator/bin/python"
cmake --build build/host-control --target math_soak_test math_soak_14h_test
ctest --test-dir build/host-control -R '^math_soak_' --output-on-failure

Without SOAK_EMULATOR_PYTHON, the C controller test can still run when z80asm is present, but independent Z80 execution is explicitly disabled. These checks do not access or interrupt a physical board.

Host success is not a physical one-hour result. Likewise, a physical soak does not replace scope measurements, full instruction-set conformance, interrupt/I/O-read testing, repeated cold starts or testing across voltage and temperature conditions.

docs.title: VS Code tasks
docs.text:
Choose Tasks: Run Task in the Z80ROMlessSBC workspace.

Diagnostic Build task Deployment task Phase 6 one-hour 20 MHz soak Build Pico - Phase 6 one-hour 20 MHz soak Flash Pico - Phase 6 one-hour 20 MHz soak Phase 6 14-hour 20 MHz soak Build Pico - Phase 6 14-hour 20 MHz soak Flash Pico - Phase 6 14-hour 20 MHz soak

Deployment tasks force-update without checking the previous firmware phase. Complete this phase's hardware prerequisites and save work before flashing. See Pico tools.

docs.title: Frequency Qualification (Optional)
docs.text:
The project breadboard has already demonstrated 20 MHz operation. See the 20 MHz oscilloscope measurement for the recorded clock evidence and capture procedure. Phases 9 and 10 use this 20 MHz configuration after SRAM loading and verification.

Additional frequency testing is optional. Complete the normal phase tests; use this check if you change the wiring, components, or clock configuration, or want measurements from your own board.

  1. Run the Phase 6 SRAM screening or 20 MHz soak test appropriate to your setup.
  2. Measure the clock using the oscilloscope guide.
  3. Repeat the applicable Phase 9/10 boot, disk, and terminal checks. Record the measured frequency, firmware revision, and any errors.

A clock capture confirms frequency; functional tests confirm operation under the tested workload. If a check fails, resolve it before continuing.

docs.title: Phase 0 - Empty Sockets and Power Distribution
docs.text: Install: Three boards, empty sockets, all passive defaults and supply wiring. No active devices, including the Pico. Use the inventory and orientation table. This phase has no firmware target.

docs.title: Wiring - Sockets and Rails
docs.text:
Feed three separate +5 V rails from one regulated supply-entry star and bond all grounds with short links. Confirm rail segments are continuous with a meter. Keep a separate Peripheral 3.3 V rail for Pico header 36, U7 and U10; leave any supply-module 3.3 V output disconnected.

Wire supply contacts from the fixed-pin table. External +5 V goes to the 1N5819 anode; its banded cathode goes to VSYS header 39. Leave VBUS header 40 open. Do not bypass the diode.

docs.title: Passive-Component Installation
docs.text:
Keep external power and USB disconnected throughout installation. All IC sockets and the Pico socket strips remain empty. Fit 40 individual 10 kOhm resistors and 11 capacitors using the steps below.

Tick the Done box beside each component as you fit it. With JavaScript enabled, progress is saved in this browser on this device and restored when you return. It does not sync across devices; clearing site data removes it. Use Clear checklist to start again. Ticks record installation only, not electrical verification or a passed test gate.

Clear checklist

docs.title: How to use these connection instructions
docs.text:
• A socket pin means the contact where that IC pin will go when the chip is fitted later. A Pico header pin is its physical header position, not its GP number.
  • Put a component lead into a free hole electrically connected to the named socket contact. Do not force two leads into one hole. If necessary, use a short jumper from that contact to a separate terminal strip.
  • On a BB830, A-E in one numbered row are connected together, and F-J in that row are a separate connected group. Adjacent rows are not connected. Both leads in the same connected group would short out the component.
  • Use the orientation table to identify socket pins. Do not guess universal hole coordinates: chip rotations differ, and the wide Z80/SRAM sockets do not straddle E/F like the narrow logic ICs.
  • Check each endpoint at the actual socket contact with a meter. Signal jumpers to other devices are added in later phases; the passive can be attached to its named socket now.

docs.title: Step 1 - Fit seven local 100 nF ceramic capacitors
docs.text:
A local bypass capacitor supplies short bursts of current at an IC. Fit one beside each DIP socket's supply pin, with short connections to that supply contact and nearby common GND. These ceramic capacitors are not polarized: either lead can face GND. Use capacitors rated at least 10 V.

Done Board Capacitor Socket / device One lead connects to Other lead connects to Core C1, 100 nF U1 Z80 VCC socket pin 11, +5 V Common GND, also connected to socket pin 29 Memory C2, 100 nF U2 SRAM VCC socket pin 32, +5 V Common GND, also connected to socket pin 16 Memory C3, 100 nF U3 HCT32 VCC socket pin 14, +5 V Common GND, also connected to socket pin 7 Core C4, 100 nF U4 AHCT244 VCC socket pin 20, +5 V Common GND, also connected to socket pin 10 Peripheral C5, 100 nF U7 LVC244 VCC socket pin 20, +3.3 V Common GND, also connected to socket pin 10 Peripheral C6, 100 nF U9 AHCT245 VCC socket pin 20, +5 V Common GND, also connected to socket pin 10 Peripheral C7, 100 nF U10 LVC245 VCC socket pin 20, +3.3 V Common GND, also connected to socket pin 10

The GND pin numbers identify the electrical connection; do not stretch the capacitor across the whole package to reach a distant GND pin. Use nearby GND with a short return path. The Pico module already has onboard decoupling; it is not an eighth DIP capacitor in this list.

docs.title: Step 2 - Fit four bulk capacitors
docs.text:
Bulk capacitors support the supply rails. These are polarized: connect the positive lead to +5 V and the negative lead to GND. Identify polarity from the case markings, not just lead length. Use capacitors rated at least 10 V.

Done Capacitor Where to place it Positive lead Negative lead C8, 22 uF Memory board, beside its +5 V supply feed Memory +5 V rail Memory GND rail C9, 22 uF Core board, beside its +5 V supply feed Core +5 V rail Core GND rail C10, 22 uF Peripheral board, beside its +5 V supply feed Peripheral +5 V rail, not +3.3 V Peripheral GND rail C11, 100 uF Common supply entry, before the feed fans out to the three boards External +5 V entry Common GND entry

All four go across their supply and GND, not in series with the supply wire. They supplement the seven local ceramic capacitors, not replace them. The current parts list specifies no separate 3.3 V bulk capacitor; retain the local 100 nF capacitors at both LVC sockets.

docs.title: Step 3 - Fit sixteen SRAM address pull-ups on Memory
docs.text:
For each row below, fit one individual 10 kOhm resistor. Connect one end to the Memory +5 V rail and the other end to the listed U2 SRAM socket pin. The resistor can face either way. Leave SRAM absent.

Done Signal SRAM socket pin Resistor's other end A14 3 +5 V A12 4 +5 V A7 5 +5 V A6 6 +5 V A5 7 +5 V A4 8 +5 V A3 9 +5 V A2 10 +5 V A1 11 +5 V A0 12 +5 V A10 23 +5 V A11 25 +5 V A9 26 +5 V A8 27 +5 V A13 28 +5 V A15 31 +5 V

Do not join the address pins together. A16, socket pin 2, connects to U4 output pin 3. U4 input pin 17 connects to Pico GP8, physical pin 11, with R24 (10 kOhm) from Pico pin 11 to GND. Do not ground A16 or U4 pin 17 directly.

docs.title: Step 4 - Fit eight Z80 control pull-ups on Core
docs.text:
For each row below, fit one individual 10 kOhm resistor from the Core +5 V rail to the listed U1 Z80 socket contact. These define controls while the CPU is absent or its bus outputs are floating.

Done Signal Z80 socket pin Resistor's other end INT# 16 +5 V NMI# 17 +5 V MREQ# 19 +5 V IORQ# 20 +5 V RD# 21 +5 V WR# 22 +5 V BUSACK# 23 +5 V BUSREQ# 25 +5 V

docs.title: Step 5 - Fit twelve Pico pull-downs on Peripheral
docs.text:
For each row below, fit one individual 10 kOhm resistor from the listed empty Pico header contact to Peripheral GND. This group contains four startup pull-downs and eight data pull-downs. Each pin has its own resistor. All twelve connect to GND, not to either positive supply rail.

Done Signal / GPIO (reference) Physical Pico header pin Resistor's other end Default CLK output, GP2 (R21) 4 GND LOW RESET# output, GP3 (R22) 5 GND LOW, reset asserted IO_RELEASE, GP9 (R23) 12 GND LOW SRAM bank select, GP8 (R24) 11 GND LOW, bank 0 D0, GP10 14 GND LOW D1, GP11 15 GND LOW D2, GP12 16 GND LOW D3, GP13 17 GND LOW D4, GP14 19 GND LOW D5, GP15 20 GND LOW D6, GP16 21 GND LOW D7, GP17 22 GND LOW

The GP10-GP17 pulls keep the Pico-side data inputs defined before firmware drives them. They are not pulls on the 5 V Z80 data bus. Keep these eight resistors near the Pico/data-translator region. Later data jumpers join these contacts to U9/U10 A pins; do not add a second set of pull-downs at those devices.

docs.title: Step 6 - Fit four Pico pull-ups on Peripheral
docs.text:
For each row below, fit one individual 10 kOhm resistor from the listed empty Pico header contact to Peripheral +3.3 V, not +5 V or GND. The 3.3 V rail remains unpowered until the Pico is fitted in Phase 1 and supplies it from header pin 36.

Done Signal / GPIO (reference) Physical Pico header pin Resistor's other end Default BUSREQ# output, GP4 (R17) 6 +3.3 V HIGH BOOT_READ_DISABLE, GP5 (R18) 7 +3.3 V HIGH Upward OE# request, GP6 (R19) 9 +3.3 V HIGH, path disabled Downward OE#, GP7 (R20) 10 +3.3 V HIGH, path disabled

docs.title: Step 7 - Connect all IC grounds and grounded fixed pins
docs.text:
These are direct wire links, not additional resistors. Connect every listed empty socket contact to common GND. The checklist includes each IC's power ground, permanently enabled buffer controls, unused inputs, and the downward translator's fixed direction. SRAM A16 and U4 pin 17 are part of the bank-select signal path and are not grounded directly.

The Pico rows use physical header pin numbers, not GPIO numbers. Connect these empty header contacts now while the Pico is absent; Phase 1 checks them again before fitting it. Connect AGND pin 33 to the same common GND.

If already fitted during supply or capacitor wiring, verify continuity at the actual socket contact before ticking it. A capacitor to nearby GND does not replace the IC's direct power-ground connection.

Done Board / socket Pin Function Connect directly to Core / U1 Z80 29 Power GND Common GND Core / U4 AHCT244 1 OE#, permanently enabled Common GND Core / U4 AHCT244 10 Power GND Common GND Core / U4 AHCT244 15 Unused input Common GND Core / U4 AHCT244 19 OE#, permanently enabled Common GND Memory / U2 SRAM 16 Power GND Common GND Memory / U3 HCT32 7 Power GND Common GND Memory / U3 HCT32 12 Unused input Common GND Memory / U3 HCT32 13 Unused input Common GND Peripheral / Pico header 3 GND Common GND Peripheral / Pico header 8 GND Common GND Peripheral / Pico header 13 GND Common GND Peripheral / Pico header 18 GND Common GND Peripheral / Pico header 23 GND Common GND Peripheral / Pico header 28 GND Common GND Peripheral / Pico header 33 AGND (analog ground) Common GND Peripheral / Pico header 38 GND Common GND Peripheral / U7 LVC244 1 OE#, permanently enabled Common GND Peripheral / U7 LVC244 10 Power GND Common GND Peripheral / U7 LVC244 19 OE#, permanently enabled Common GND Peripheral / U9 AHCT245 10 Power GND Common GND Peripheral / U10 LVC245 1 DIR, fixed B to A Common GND Peripheral / U10 LVC245 10 Power GND Common GND

Leave U3 output pin 11 and U4 output pins 3 and 5 open; do not ground them.

No resistor goes in these ground links. They do not change the resistor or capacitor totals below.

docs.title: Step 8 - Connect IC supplies and fixed-HIGH pins
docs.text: Keep external power and USB disconnected, with all devices absent. Fit or continuity-check each connection below at the actual socket contact. These are direct wire connections, not pull resistors. A bypass capacitor does not replace the direct supply connection.

docs.title: Connections to +5 V
docs.text: Done Board / socket Pin Function Connect directly to Core / U1 Z80 11 VCC supply Core +5 V rail Core / U4 AHCT244 20 VCC supply Core +5 V rail Memory / U2 SRAM 30 CE2, fixed HIGH Memory +5 V rail Memory / U2 SRAM 32 VCC supply Memory +5 V rail Memory / U3 HCT32 14 VCC supply Memory +5 V rail Peripheral / U9 AHCT245 1 DIR, fixed A to B Peripheral +5 V rail Peripheral / U9 AHCT245 20 VCC supply Peripheral +5 V rail

docs.title: Connections to Pico-derived +3.3 V
docs.text:
Done Board / socket Pin Function Connect directly to Peripheral / Pico header 36 3V3 OUT, source of this rail Peripheral +3.3 V rail Peripheral / U7 LVC244 20 VCC supply Peripheral +3.3 V rail Peripheral / U10 LVC245 20 VCC supply Peripheral +3.3 V rail

The +3.3 V rail stays unpowered in Phase 0. In Phase 1 the fitted Pico supplies it from header pin 36; do not feed this rail from an external 3.3 V supply or connect either LVC supply pin to +5 V.

docs.title: Pico power input through the isolation diode
docs.text:
Done Connection Required wiring External +5 V to Pico VSYS, header pin 39 External +5 V to 1N5819 anode; banded cathode to header pin 39

Header pin 39 receives the diode-fed supply, not the +3.3 V rail. Leave VBUS header pin 40 externally unconnected and do not bypass the diode. These wire connections do not change the resistor or capacitor totals.

docs.title: Installation count before testing
docs.text:
IC / component group Permanent resistors External capacitors GND pins +5 V pins +3.3 V pins Pico 2 W 16: twelve pull-downs plus four pull-ups None 8 0 1 U1 Z80 Eight CPU control pull-ups C1, 100 nF 1 1 0 U2 SRAM 16 address pull-ups C2, 100 nF 1 2 0 U3 HCT32 None C3, 100 nF 3 1 0 U4 AHCT244 None C4, 100 nF 4 1 0 U7 LVC244 None C5, 100 nF 3 0 1 U9 AHCT245 None C6, 100 nF 1 2 0 U10 LVC245 None C7, 100 nF 2 0 1 Board bulk capacitors None C8-C10, three 22 uF 0 0 0 Common supply entry None C11, 100 uF 0 0 0 Total 40 individual 10 kOhm resistors 11 capacitors 23 7 3

The pin columns count the direct socket/header connections in Steps 7 and 8, including grounded or fixed-HIGH control pins. They do not count resistor or capacitor leads, rail bridges, or supply-entry wiring. The Pico counts include all eight ground contacts and its 3.3 V output pin 36. There is one additional diode-fed Pico VSYS connection at header pin 39; it is not a direct +5 V connection and is not included in the +5 V column. Resistors are counted once at their installation point: Pico pulls at the Pico, CPU control pulls at U1, and address pulls at U2, even though the signal nets also connect to other ICs. The Pico's onboard capacitors are not included in the 11 external capacitors.

Leave all permanent resistors and capacitors installed for subsequent phases. Temporary diagnostic pulls are added only when a later phase requests them.

docs.title: Power Distribution and Isolation
docs.text:
• Apply external +5 V before USB; unplug USB before removing external +5 V. Do not operate a populated board from USB alone: U9 data ports lack Ioff. Program a removed Pico off-board if USB-only programming is needed.
  • All fitted 5 V ICs must be powered together. A fitted unpowered device is not equivalent to an empty socket. Pull resistors do not isolate it.
  • Never connect a 5 V output directly to a Pico GPIO. Both LVC devices run from Pico 3.3 V, not from +5 V. During ramp, asserted RESET and stopped clock prevent execution; RAM is indeterminate until loaded and verified.
  • Arbitrary external-power loss with USB attached is not protected. Add hardware isolation in a separately reviewed redesign if that is required.
  • Power and USB must be disconnected before changing wiring or measuring resistance. Stop on a collapsed rail, excessive current, or warm device.

docs.title: Test Plan
docs.text:
1. With everything disconnected, verify every socket power contact, diode polarity, capacitor polarity, and no +5 V/3.3 V/GND short. Let capacitor resistance readings settle; inspect any near-zero sustained resistance. Check each of the 40 resistor paths from its named socket/header contact to its specified rail: expect approximately 10 kOhm with devices absent. The direct GND links should have continuity, not 10 kOhm. If a resistor reading is unexpected, inspect parallel wiring paths and isolate one resistor lead with power disconnected if needed to verify its value.
  2. With active devices absent, apply +5 V using a 100 mA initial limit. Measure 4.75-5.25 V at every 5 V socket; the unpowered 3.3 V rail must not be driven. Remove power if a rail droops more than 5% or the limit trips.
  3. Record resistance, voltage, and unloaded current. Disconnect power and confirm discharge before fitting the Pico in Phase 1.

docs.title: Pass Gate
docs.text: Correct polarity and supplies at all contacts, no shorts, no unexpected current, and all startup resistors fitted. A blank board's voltage test does not establish loaded-regulator performance; repeat measurements each phase.

docs.title: VS Code tasks
docs.text:
Choose Tasks: Run Task in the Z80ROMlessSBC workspace.

Diagnostic Build task Deployment task Phase 1 supervisor Build Pico - Phase 1 supervisor Flash Pico - Phase 1 supervisor

Deployment tasks force-update without checking the previous firmware phase. Complete this phase's hardware prerequisites and save work before flashing. See Pico tools.

Tick setup items when complete and tests only after recording the measured result. Progress is saved in this browser; ticks are not automatic verification.

Clear checklist

Prerequisite: Phase 0 pass gate. Install: Pico 2 W only; all other active sockets empty.

docs.title: Wiring - Pico 2 W
docs.text: Program Phase 1 off-board, disconnect USB, fit its soldered headers with USB toward row 1, then wire every connection in the Pico table. Continuity-check actual empty socket contacts and adjacent pins, not only wire ends. Keep the clock path short with a nearby GND return; do not add loops to equalize wire lengths.

docs.title: Pico Control Outputs
docs.text:
Done Signal Pico connection Destination socket contact CLK Pico GP2 - header pin 4 U4 AHCT244 input - pin 2 RESET# Pico GP3 - header pin 5 U1 Z80 RESET# - pin 26 BUSREQ# Pico GP4 - header pin 6 U4 AHCT244 input - pin 4 BOOT_READ_DISABLE Pico GP5 - header pin 7 U4 AHCT244 input - pin 6 PICO_DATA_UP_OE# Pico GP6 - header pin 9 U3 HCT32 input - pin 10 DATA_DOWN_OE# Pico GP7 - header pin 10 U10 LVC245 OE# - pin 19 IO_RELEASE Pico GP9 - header pin 12 U3 HCT32 input - pin 5

Wire all Pico connections from the table above with other active devices absent. Continuity-check every destination socket contact and adjacent pins. Tick each row after checking its connection; progress is saved in the Phase 1 checklist.

docs.title: Phase 1 Firmware
docs.text:
Build z80_stage01_supervisor; load build/src/stage01_supervisor/z80_stage01_supervisor.uf2 using the firmware/console procedure. Maintained application.

Done Command Behavior Measurement s Sample input/data levels Monitor inputs may float with U7 absent w Walk seven control outputs, 250 ms each Scope the correct empty socket contact and neighbors r Hold RESET# alternately HIGH/LOW GP3/header 5 and Z80 socket 26: 3.20-3.40 V / near zero d Hold one data GPIO HIGH; advance D0-D7 Probe U9/U10 A pins 2-9 x Restore defaults and data inputs Both OE requests HIGH; RESET LOW

docs.title: Single-Step Data-Pin Test
docs.text: Type d without Enter. One GP10-GP17 output stays HIGH until the next d; all others remain LOW. The ninth step restores input mode. If the initial inputs are not all LOW, firmware refuses the test: check the eight individual 10 kOhm GP10-GP17 pull-down resistors. Use x to stop. USB disconnect restores any held data/reset test.

docs.title: Test Plan
docs.text:
Apply external +5 V before USB. Check Pico 3.3 V and that no GPIO sees +5 V.

At startup GP6/GP7/GP4/GP5 must be HIGH; GP2/GP3/GP9 LOW.

Scope each walking output at its empty destination; software PASS only means the sequence ended. Use held r/d levels for meter checks. Do not run these commands with CPU, SRAM, or any other active device fitted.

docs.title: Pass Gate
docs.text:
• Correct routing and no neighboring pin activity.
  • Isolated defaults.
  • Valid rail voltages.

Floating monitor readings are not a pass or a fault by themselves.

docs.title: Maintained Source
docs.text:
These complete files are included from the repository at documentation build time, not copied into this page.

Phase 1 application - src/stage01_supervisor/main.c 
#include <stdio.h>

#include "pico/stdlib.h"
#include "pico/stdio_usb.h"
#include "z80sbc/pins.h"
#include "z80sbc/supervisor.h"

static const uint TEST_OUTPUT_PINS[] = {
  PIN_CLK,
  PIN_RESET_N,
  PIN_BUSREQ_N,
  PIN_BOOT_READ_DISABLE,
  PIN_DATA_UP_OE_N,
  PIN_DATA_DOWN_OE_N,
  PIN_IO_RELEASE,
};

static const uint DATA_HEADER_PINS[] = {14, 15, 16, 17, 19, 20, 21, 22};
static int data_step = -1;
static bool reset_high = false;

static uint print_data_levels(void) {
  uint high_mask = 0;
  printf("Data GPIO levels:");
  for (uint bit = 0; bit < 8; ++bit) {
    bool level = gpio_get(PIN_DATA_0 + bit);
    high_mask |= (uint)level << bit;
    printf(" D%u/GP%u=%u", bit, PIN_DATA_0 + bit, (unsigned)level);
  }
  printf("\n");
  return high_mask;
}

static void restore_safe_levels(void) {
  z80_safe_startup();
  data_step = -1;
  reset_high = false;
}

static void toggle_reset_output(void) {
  reset_high = !reset_high;
  gpio_put(PIN_RESET_N, reset_high);
  printf("RESET# GP3 commanded %s: Pico header pin 5, Z80 socket pin 26\n",
         reset_high ? "HIGH" : "LOW");
    printf("Expected voltage at both contacts: %s (measure relative to common GND)\n",
      reset_high ? "3.20-3.40 V" : "near 0 V");
    printf("RESET# must never exceed the Pico 3.3 V rail; no 5 V pull-up permitted\n");
  printf("r: toggle RESET#, x: restore safe levels (Phase 1 only); measure the voltage\n");
}

static void step_data_output(void) {
  if (data_step < 0) {
    restore_safe_levels();
    if (print_data_levels() != 0) {
      printf("NOT STARTED: data inputs must all be LOW; check RN3 and wiring\n");
      return;
    }
    for (uint bit = 0; bit < 8; ++bit)
      output_with_initial_level(PIN_DATA_0 + bit, false);
  } else {
    gpio_put(PIN_DATA_0 + (uint)data_step, false);
  }

  ++data_step;
  if (data_step == 8) {
    restore_safe_levels();
    printf("DONE: data steps finished; safe levels restored, GP10-GP17 inputs\n");
    return;
  }

  uint bit = (uint)data_step;
  gpio_put(PIN_DATA_0 + bit, true);
  printf("D%u HIGH: GP%u, Pico header pin %u, AHCT245/LVC245 A%u pin %u\n",
         bit, PIN_DATA_0 + bit, DATA_HEADER_PINS[bit], bit + 1, bit + 2);
  printf("Other data pins LOW; d: next, x: restore safe levels (Phase 1 only)\n");
}

static void print_status(void) {
  printf("BUSACK#=%u IORQ#=%u RD#=%u WR#=%u\n",
         gpio_get(PIN_BUSACK_N), gpio_get(PIN_IORQ_N),
         gpio_get(PIN_RD_N), gpio_get(PIN_WR_N));
  print_data_levels();
}

int main(void) {
  z80_safe_startup();
  stdio_init_all();

  printf("\nZ80 ROMless SBC - Stage 1 supervisor\n");
  printf("r: toggle RESET# HIGH/LOW (Phase 1 hardware only)\n");
  printf("w: walking output test (Phase 1 hardware only)\n");
  printf("d: step D0-D7, hold one HIGH (Phase 1 hardware only)\n");
  printf("x: restore safe levels and return data GPIOs to inputs\n");
  printf("s: sample input status\n");

  while (true) {
    if (!stdio_usb_connected()) {
      if (data_step >= 0 || reset_high)
        restore_safe_levels();
      tight_loop_contents();
      continue;
    }

    int command = getchar_timeout_us(0);
    if (command == 'r') {
      toggle_reset_output();
    } else if (command == 'w') {
      restore_safe_levels();
      printf("walking %u outputs\n",
             (unsigned)(sizeof(TEST_OUTPUT_PINS) / sizeof(TEST_OUTPUT_PINS[0])));
      z80_walking_output_test(TEST_OUTPUT_PINS,
                              sizeof(TEST_OUTPUT_PINS) / sizeof(TEST_OUTPUT_PINS[0]),
                              250);
      printf("PASS: safe levels restored\n");
    } else if (command == 'd') {
      step_data_output();
    } else if (command == 'x') {
      restore_safe_levels();
      printf("DONE: safe levels restored, GP10-GP17 inputs\n");
    } else if (command == 's') {
      print_status();
    }
    tight_loop_contents();
  }
}
Shared startup and isolation - src/common/supervisor.c 
#include "z80sbc/supervisor.h"

#include "pico/stdlib.h"
#include "z80sbc/pins.h"
#include "z80sbc/banked_transfer.h"

static bool banked_memory_available;
static z80_memory_bank_driver_t bank_driver;

void z80_memory_bank_set_driver(z80_memory_bank_driver_t driver) {
  bank_driver = driver;
}

void __not_in_flash_func(z80_memory_bank_select)(unsigned bank) {
  if (bank_driver != NULL)
    bank_driver(bank & 1u);
  else
    gpio_put(PIN_MEMORY_BANK, bank & 1u);
}

void z80_memory_bank_set_available(bool available) {
  banked_memory_available = available;
}

unsigned __not_in_flash_func(z80_memory_bank_status)(void) {
  return banked_memory_available ? BANKED_ABI_STATUS | gpio_get(PIN_MEMORY_BANK) : 0;
}

void output_with_initial_level(uint pin, bool level) {
  gpio_init(pin);
  gpio_put(pin, level);
  gpio_set_dir(pin, GPIO_OUT);
}

void input_with_no_pull(uint pin) {
  gpio_init(pin);
  gpio_set_dir(pin, GPIO_IN);
  gpio_disable_pulls(pin);
}

void z80_isolate_buses(void) {
  gpio_put(PIN_DATA_UP_OE_N, 1);
  gpio_put(PIN_DATA_DOWN_OE_N, 1);
}

void z80_safe_startup(void) {
  output_with_initial_level(PIN_DATA_UP_OE_N, 1);
  output_with_initial_level(PIN_DATA_DOWN_OE_N, 1);
  output_with_initial_level(PIN_RESET_N, 0);
  output_with_initial_level(PIN_MEMORY_BANK, 0);
  bank_driver = NULL;
  banked_memory_available = false;
  output_with_initial_level(PIN_BUSREQ_N, 1);
  output_with_initial_level(PIN_BOOT_READ_DISABLE, 1);
  output_with_initial_level(PIN_IO_RELEASE, 0);
  output_with_initial_level(PIN_CLK, 0);
  for (uint pin = PIN_DATA_0; pin <= PIN_DATA_7; ++pin)
    input_with_no_pull(pin);
  input_with_no_pull(PIN_BUSACK_N);
  input_with_no_pull(PIN_IORQ_N);
  input_with_no_pull(PIN_RD_N);
  input_with_no_pull(PIN_WR_N);
  input_with_no_pull(PIN_PORT_A0);
  input_with_no_pull(PIN_PORT_A1);
  input_with_no_pull(PIN_PORT_A2);
  input_with_no_pull(PIN_PORT_A4);
}

void z80_walking_output_test(const uint *pins, size_t count,
                             uint32_t dwell_ms) {
  for (size_t index = 0; index < count; ++index)
    output_with_initial_level(pins[index], false);

  for (size_t active = 0; active < count; ++active) {
    for (size_t index = 0; index < count; ++index)
      gpio_put(pins[index], index == active);
    sleep_ms(dwell_ms);
  }

  z80_safe_startup();
}

docs.title: Phase 10 - WebSocket Terminal Console
docs.text:
Goal: use CP/M in a web browser over the Pico 2 W's Wi-Fi. USB remains the fallback terminal.

Clear checklist

  • Start here: complete the Phase 9 automatic CP/M loader.
  • Unchanged: 120 MHz Pico clock, 20 MHz scope-measured Z80 clock, BIOS and disk layout.
  • Hardware: onboard Wi-Fi plus the 3.3 V matrix display. PCB changes remain deferred.

docs.title: First connection and USB provisioning
docs.text: See Related projects for building C applications with DCC, importing application disks from Altair 8800 AI Edition, and deploying them with the Z80ROMlessSBC VS Code disk tasks.

docs.title: 1. Deploy from VS Code
docs.text:
Before any update

Save CP/M work. Apply external +5 V before USB and keep it applied. Never power the populated board from USB alone. Disk updates overwrite selected drives without backups.

Open the Command Palette, run Tasks: Run Task, then choose:

Update Exact task name What changes Firmware Build and flash Pico - Phase 10 firmware Preserves disks and ENV settings CP/M system Build and flash Pico - CP/M system and Drive A Rebuilds CP/M; replaces boot package and Drive A; preserves firmware, B-D and ENV All disks Flash Pico - All disks (A-D) Rebuilds and validates matching boot package and A; replaces boot package and A-D; preserves firmware and ENV CP/M system disk Flash Pico - Drive A Replaces A with a regenerated native image; checks boot compatibility BDS C disk Flash Pico - Drive B Replaces B only Escape disk Flash Pico - Drive C Replaces C only Blank disk Flash Pico - Drive D Replaces D only
  • Firmware confirmation: Proceed. Disk confirmation: Replace selected disks. Both default to Cancel.
  • CP/M system confirmation: Replace CP/M and drive A, default Cancel. Use this after changing the CP/M assembly; it updates cold-boot and warm-boot images together. All Drive A files are replaced without backups.
  • Firmware and disk tasks force-update without a previous-firmware handshake; save CP/M work first. All tasks verify written bytes and request reboot.
  • Disk tasks do not rebuild firmware or applications. Install updated applications into the source disk first.
  • Setup/details: firmware build and provisioning and VS Code disk tasks.

Phase 10 firmware deployed.

First checkout or manual build

Initialize the WebSocket submodule before building or running the firmware task:

git submodule update --init --recursive
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DPICO_BOARD=pico2_w
cmake --build build --target z80_stage10_websocket_terminal -j

Output: build/src/stage10_websocket_terminal/z80_stage10_websocket_terminal.uf2. These commands build only; they do not deploy. Flash verification proves written bytes, not a successful CP/M boot.

docs.title: 2. Set Wi-Fi over USB
docs.text:
1. Open the USB terminal. CP/M starts without waiting for Wi-Fi or a browser.
  2. Press Ctrl-] c to open configuration. Missing/invalid Wi-Fi credentials open it automatically.
  3. Select 1 - Wi-Fi, then C. Enter your SSID and password.
  4. Press Q to return to the main menu, then Q again to exit.

Saved changes trigger a safe reboot. No changes means no reboot. A storage error cancels reboot and is reported. Save application work first: flushing disks cannot save unsaved application RAM.

docs.title: 3. Open the browser terminal
docs.text:
1. Press Ctrl-] s on USB to display the Pico's address.
  2. Open http://<pico-ip>:8088/.

  3. Press Enter for a fresh CP/M prompt, then try DIR.

  4. Pico address verified and terminal page opened.

  5. Use a trusted local network only. The terminal has no authentication or TLS; never expose port 8088 to the Internet.
  6. The browser needs Internet access on first use to load xterm.js dependencies.
  7. Reload the terminal page after firmware updates.

docs.title: Unified system configuration
docs.text:
Ctrl-] c opens setup over USB, even while a browser owns the terminal. It saves the same environment variables that you can edit from CP/M with C:ENV.

Menu Use it for 1 - Wi-Fi C sets SSID/password; U clears them 2 - Remote filesystem Stores FS_SERVER only; remote file access is not implemented or required for Wi-Fi 3 - Chat 1 OpenAI, 2 compatible endpoint, 3 Ollama; 4-6 model, token limit and temperature; 7 thinking 4 - OpenWeatherMap C sets API key, location and units 5 - Timezone C sets POSIX TZ; for example, AEST-10 means UTC+10 Key Action Enter Keep the existing value - Clear the value; clearing the Wi-Fi password selects an open network ESC Cancel the current unsaved edit S Show settings, with secrets masked Q Return to the main menu; at the main menu, exit

Settings persist in plaintext onboard flash, not encrypted storage. Passwords and API keys are hidden during entry and masked on display.

Validation, saved changes and service settings
  • Wi-Fi: SSID up to 32 bytes; WPA2 password 8-63 bytes or a 64-digit hexadecimal key.
  • Saving: each key is atomic, but a multi-field edit is not. After a failed save, reopen setup and retry affected fields. Unrelated keys are preserved.
  • Disconnect: unsaved edits are discarded; saved edits still require reboot when exiting setup. Viewing settings does not count as a change.
  • ENV: values are stored literally. Network ENV edits apply on reboot or setup reload; saved Wi-Fi edits can reconnect immediately.
  • Chat: custom/Ollama endpoints need scheme, host and path, for example http://192.168.1.26:11434/v1/chat/completions. Only OpenAI receives CHAT_OPENAI_KEY; custom-provider authentication is unsupported. Model/options are consumed by the CP/M application. See CHAT configuration.
  • Weather: location can be Sydney,AU or lat=-33.8&lon=151.2; units are metric, imperial or standard.
  • Timezone: empty means UTC; AEST-10AEDT,M10.1.0,M4.1.0/3 includes daylight saving. Use TZ, not UTC_OFFSET.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Check or action No Pico address Ctrl-] s shows ip=unavailable; check Wi-Fi settings. Association times out after 30 seconds and retries after 5 seconds. Page opens, but no prompt Press Enter. Old output is not replayed to a new browser. CP/M still does not respond Use Ctrl-] s to inspect boot evidence, disk errors, queue drops and browser ownership. A working web page does not prove Z80 operation. USB ignores normal typing A browser owns CP/M. Close it to return to USB; USB supervisor commands still work. Second browser cannot connect Only one browser may own the terminal. Browser disappears USB ownership returns on disconnect/Wi-Fi loss, or after five missed pongs; pings are sent every five minutes. The Z80 keeps running. Wrong address Use the Pico's address, not FS_SERVER. HTTP/WebSocket use port 8088; ?altair=<pico-ip> changes the host only. Configuration save fails Reopen Ctrl-] c, inspect saved values and retry affected fields.

Confirm boot and network faults separately.

Ctrl-] s also shows uptime, reset causes and matrix status without injecting periodic diagnostics into CP/M output.

docs.title: HT16K33 8x8 matrix
docs.text:
Expected display while the Z80 is running: a horizontal row moves every 500 ms without Wi-Fi; a vertical column moves every 250 ms when Wi-Fi is connected. The display holds its last pattern while the supervisor stops the Z80 or pauses storage work. It is a supervisor diagnostic, not proof that a CP/M application is responsive.

Backpack marking Pico connection J2 pin + / VCC 3V3, physical pin 36 4 - / GND Common GND 5 C / SCL GP26, physical pin 31 3 D / SDA GP22, physical pin 29 2 Vi2c / IO, if fitted 3V3 4
  • Power and both pull-ups must be 3.3 V, never 5 V. Disconnect power safely before rewiring.
  • Follow the printed markings, not an assumed connector order. The external module is schematic A2, with no PCB footprint.
  • Keep other devices off this diagnostic bus. The driver scans 0x70-0x77; the tested board uses 0x72.
  • Check Ctrl-] s for address, state and errors. The module shares the Pico's 3.3 V budget and runs at reduced brightness (wiring guide).
Display implementation and host test

matrix_display.cpp runs on core 1 after network work. Scanning and initialization perform at most one non-blocking FIFO operation per pass. Normal frames use one I2C transaction: RAM pointer 0x00 followed by all 16 display RAM bytes. One DMA channel feeds 20 encoded command words to PIO; a second collects 18 byte ACKs and the final STOP result. No per-byte CPU service or DMA interrupt is needed. Persistent buffers remain unchanged until completion. Each frame uses one connectivity state. USB status reports the last confirmed pattern and its interval.

New transactions require a running CPU and no flash pause. If permission changes, an in-flight transaction finishes through STOP before holding the pattern. DMA results are checked when the next update is due (250 ms online, 500 ms offline), including while new updates are paused. TX completion alone does not confirm STOP; RX must also finish and contain the STOP result. A missing completion, transfer NACK, unavailable DMA channels, or a 5 ms scan/initialization FIFO timeout disables the display, releases resources and records the error. No Z80 bus GPIO or new core-0 handshake is used.

matrix_i2c.pio uses open-drain pins at nominal 100 kHz without clock stretching.

cmake --build build/host-control --target matrix_display_test -j
ctest --test-dir build/host-control --output-on-failure -R '^matrix_pio_HT16K33$'

The original moving row was bench-tested with CP/M and networking. Host tests check row/column RAM writes and connectivity changes between chunks; the new column pattern still needs checking on hardware. Host tests do not qualify physical waveform margins or core-0 latency.

docs.title: Network time and CLOCK services
docs.text:
• Wi-Fi enables automatic time sync with pool.ntp.org; until then, calendar queries return CLOCK_UNSYNCED.
  • Set TZ to AEST-10 for UTC+10 without daylight saving. Use the USB menu or C:ENV literal insert. Direct ENV changes apply on the next request; empty means UTC.
  • Look up time-zone abbreviations and UTC offsets on Wikipedia, or use this city-to-POSIX TZ lookup for complete rules. Enter the POSIX string, not the city name; its offset sign is reversed (-10 means UTC+10).

docs.title: System environment variables
docs.text:
One settings store, two ways to edit it:

  • USB configuration: press Ctrl-] c and choose a menu. It validates and saves the ENV values below.
  • CP/M command line: run C:ENV to list settings, or C:ENV NAME=VALUE to update one.
Used by ENV variables Purpose / values Wi-Fi WIFI_SSID, WIFI_PASSWORD Network name and password; empty password selects an open network Remote filesystem FS_SERVER Server IPv4 address; stored only, remote file access is not implemented Chat connection CHAT_PROVIDER, CHAT_ENDPOINT, CHAT_OPENAI_KEY openai, compatible or ollama; full URL for custom/local providers; API key for OpenAI only Chat options CHAT_MODEL, CHAT_MAX_TOKENS, CHAT_TEMPERATURE Model name, positive token limit and temperature 0-2 Chat thinking CHAT_THINK Chat menu 7: false (off), true (on/medium) or default (server choice); CHAT 1.7-c11 compatible/Ollama requests only Weather OWM_KEY, OWM_LOCATION, OWM_UNITS API key, city/country or coordinates, and metric (default), imperial or standard Local time TZ POSIX timezone string; empty means UTC

docs.title: Update from CP/M
docs.text:
C:ENV -H
C:ENV OWM_UNITS
C:ENV OWM_UNITS=metric

These show help, read one value and update it. ENV listings may reveal passwords and API keys. Both interfaces save to plaintext onboard flash.

Values containing + or -: prefer the USB menu, which saves literal text. The ENV app can interpret ordinary assignments as arithmetic. Use C:ENV -I NAME=VALUE for a literal insert; if the key already exists, delete it first with C:ENV -D NAME. This matters for keys, model names, coordinates and timezone rules.

docs.title: When changes take effect
docs.text:
• USB menu: exiting after saved changes safely reboots; save CP/M work first.
  • C:ENV Wi-Fi settings: reboot or reload the configuration shell.
  • C:ENV timezone/weather: timezone applies on the next request; weather reloads within one second, without reboot.
  • C:ENV chat settings: provider/endpoint/key and CHAT 1.7-c11 thinking settings apply on the next request/turn; restart CHAT after changing model, token limit or temperature.

Weather needs Wi-Fi and synchronized time; missing settings do not stop CP/M. For service-specific setup and errors, see chat, weather and the ENV command reference.

docs.title: Test plan
docs.text:
Tick only after recording hardware results. A successful build or host test is not hardware qualification.

  • Boot: test USB-only, then no USB/no Wi-Fi. Reconnect USB; confirm BIOS/CCP evidence and no fatal error.
  • Ownership: run browser DIR; no duplicate USB output. USB Ctrl-] s still works; a second browser is rejected.
  • Traffic: sustain output and paste over 128 bytes. Check order, zero drops/faults and no duplicate output when ACKs pause.
  • Keys: test Ctrl+C, Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+M/Enter, ESC, arrows, Insert/Delete and Page Up/Down. Ctrl+M is carriage return. On a tablet, test the Keys pad: the arrows send the same WordStar cursor codes (Ctrl-E/S/D/X), held keys repeat, taps do not raise the on-screen keyboard, and the floating pad can be dragged by any non-key part of the panel and keeps its position after rotation.
  • Disks: repeat Phase 9 sentinel, A-D, warm-boot and copy tests through the browser.
  • Recovery: disconnect browser/Wi-Fi during output and writes; verify USB fallback and no stale replay. Suspend the browser computer; verify missed-pong counting and fallback after the fifth missed response. Without a browser, Wi-Fi changes must preserve USB queues.
  • Settings: reboot and verify persistence. Reject invalid/overlong values, hide secrets and report failed saves.
  • Weather: run CLOCK with Wi-Fi/time ready; verify conditions, units and forecast while typing and using disks. Drop Wi-Fi: cached values remain readable with increasing age. Test invalid/missing keys and recovery without reboot.
  • Performance: compare CLOCK redraws and active-play BREAKOUT response. Record bytes/second, key-to-echo latency and maximum network-poll gaps during reads, cached writes and flash commits.
What host tests establish
  • Console tests cover concurrent 256 KiB transfers, handover and queue bounds.
  • Terminal tests cover ordering, duplicate suppression, sequence wrap, backpressure, ACK retries, 1 ms batching and the four-frame window.
  • With PICO_SDK_PATH, WebSocket tests use the actual server with fake lwIP and real Mbed TLS; weather tests also verify the firmware TLS configuration and bundled CA.
  • Weather tests cover all 15 fields, caching, cancellation, malformed responses and failures.
  • These prove software behavior, not wireless throughput or hardware latency. See firmware testing.

docs.title: Pass gate
docs.text:
• Browser remains responsive at the baseline clock.
  • Status matches queued bytes and active transport.
  • Interactive commands, warm boot and A-D copies pass.
  • No HTTP, WebSocket or Wi-Fi work runs on core 0.
  • No unexplained drops, trap faults or storage errors.
  • Complete Phase 9 final acceptance.

docs.title: Core ownership and terminal routing
docs.text:
Developer reference: expand only when changing or diagnosing firmware.

Core responsibilities and terminal ownership
  • Core 0: Z80 GPIO/clock/traps, journal recovery, validated SRAM loading, queued supervisor requests and flash quiescence. No USB endpoint calls.
  • Core 1: USB, runtime storage, ENV, services, Wi-Fi and HTTP/WebSocket. Disk work runs before network work; networking uses pico_cyw43_arch_lwip_poll.
  • Queues: 128-byte console RX, 512-byte TX, four supervisor entries and a 4 KiB diagnostic ring (128-byte drain/pass). Short locks and atomic state publication separate cores.
  • Ownership: one browser replaces ordinary USB I/O; USB supervisor/setup stays available. Switching transports clears queued input/output. Wi-Fi changes alone do not clear USB-owned queues.
  • Disconnected: output is discarded and TX-ready stays set. Intentional discards are distinct from reported queue overflows.
  • Ports: 0x00 data; 0x01 bit 0 RX-ready, bit 1 TX-room/disconnected, bit 7 active transport. Storage/service ports and safe stop/flush are unchanged.

docs.title: Module boundaries
docs.text:
Which module owns what? Module Responsibility network_runtime.cpp Wi-Fi lifecycle, CYW43 polling, IPv4 publication and SNTP; no terminal queues web_terminal.cpp HTTP/WebSocket sessions, heartbeat and flow control; no Wi-Fi configuration network_services.c Schedules network, weather and chat services chat.c, chat_stream.c, chat_network.cpp Bounded chat ABI, HTTP/SSE parsing and asynchronous DNS/TCP/TLS; core boundary is the service mailbox terminal_queue.c Transport-neutral queues and ownership usb_console.c Core-1 USB/alarm initialization and bounded stdout routing

Wi-Fi disables power saving after association; failure drops the link and retries. IPv4 publication refreshes once per second. Chat never touches terminal queues, USB input or Z80 GPIO.

docs.title: Acknowledged terminal protocol, version 4
docs.text:
Protocol and buffer limits

Use the served browser page, not a raw-byte WebSocket client. Version 1/2/3 pages are rejected. Messages start with a one-byte type and four-byte little-endian sequence; data sequences start at 1 and wrap modulo 2^32.

Type Direction Sequence / payload 5 HELLO Pico to browser Version 4 / none 6 READY Browser to Pico Version 4 / none 1 OUTPUT Pico to browser Output sequence / 1-512 bytes 3 OUTPUT_ACK Browser to Pico Last consumed output sequence / none 2 INPUT Browser to Pico Input sequence / 1-64 bytes 4 INPUT_ACK Pico to browser Accepted input sequence / none 7 REBOOT Browser to Pico Zero / none 8 REBOOT_STATUS Pico to browser Status code / none

Reboot Zeta-80: the toolbar button asks for confirmation, then sends a control frame directly to the Pico supervisor, independently of CP/M input and its queue. The supervisor drains outstanding disk/service work, flushes storage, holds RESET and stops the clock, then reboots the Pico after one second. Terminal networking stays active while disk/application workers are paused, so restart and error statuses can still be delivered. Before reboot, the supervisor sends the restarting status and explicitly closes the WebSocket; this starts browser reconnection without waiting for a TCP timeout. Startup reloads and verifies CP/M. Wi-Fi disconnects briefly; the browser automatically reconnects for this operation and clears reboot progress as soon as the terminal handshake completes and controls are re-enabled. The supervisor reports CP/M ready after observing BIOS and CCP boot markers. Unsaved application data is lost; flushing preserves only writes already received by the Pico.

The browser distinguishes Waiting for Pico supervisor (request not yet acknowledged) from Flushing disks (the supervisor has begun the stop). Neither message proves that flash is currently being written.

Storage failure cancels automatic reboot. Core 0 cancels a stop/restart after 30 seconds. Independently, core 1 expires an unfinished request after 35 seconds, including when core 0 stops servicing its loop. That deadline survives browser disconnects; retries cannot extend it. An expired request cannot later start or resume automatic reboot. Any orderly stop already begun remains pending. Timeout is retained until the board restarts; the button stays disabled so reconnecting cannot queue another reboot. Inspect USB supervisor status/logs before manual recovery. No deadline forces reset through unfinished writes.

The browser also reports unconfirmed progress after 40 seconds, including when a newly opened page receives an existing request. It never resends reboot automatically. Ordinary disconnects still require manual connection.

Status codes: 0 idle, 1 requested, 2 flushing, 3 restarting, 4 storage error, 5 timeout, 6 rejected (busy/stopped/storage failure), 7 CP/M ready. Requests during an active reboot are idempotent. Controls require the active connection and completed version-4 handshake. Update firmware and any separately hosted terminal page together.

  • Output: four frames retain at most 2 KiB. ACKs are cumulative, after xterm consumes bytes; duplicates are not rendered twice. Retry after 250 ms; oldest-frame timeout is 5 minutes.
  • Batching: isolated/full frames send immediately. Later partial frames wait up to a fixed 1 ms deadline, then the next service pass. Flash pauses may delay service. Accepted TCP writes are not duplicated after failed flushes.
  • Input: one frame waits for RX space; admission/rejected ACKs retry each pass. ACK means queued, not executed. The browser caps pending input at 64 KiB, rejects an overflowing paste entirely and warns when disconnect discards input.
  • Bounds: 69-byte incoming messages; queued payload at most 1,024 bytes/16 messages; dispatch at most eight per connection/pass. Overflow disconnects.
  • Memory: maximum build buffer 521 bytes; four frames use 2,084 of 5,840 TCP send-buffer bytes. Core-1 stack is 8 KiB in main RAM. These are not total memory-use measurements.
  • Latency: every received segment is ACKed immediately (TF_ACK_NOW) rather than on lwIP's 250 ms delayed-ACK timer, so a browser that coalesces small writes never holds a keystroke behind an unacknowledged OUTPUT_ACK.
