docs.title: 7. Reference Firmware Implementations
docs.text: Build from the repository’s maintained sources. The phase pages include current code directly from the checkout. For native tests, Z80 emulation, and SDK cross-builds, see Building and Testing Pico C Firmware.

docs.title: Breadboard-first, shared Pico firmware
docs.text:
Firmware targets the breadboard circuit. Match firmware to the installed hardware; early walking-output diagnostics require their specified population.

SDK startup uses a 144 MHz system clock and independent 48 MHz USB clock. Phases 9/10 switch to 120 MHz before USB initialization and run the Z80 at 20 MHz after SRAM loading/verification. Other phases retain their own clock limits and defaults. See frequency qualification.

Phase 10 enables PIO clock/bank switching by default after a successful second-bank probe. Without bank hardware or PIO resources, runtime banking is unavailable; other I/O retains PWM/software handling. The diagnostic Phase 9 image starts CP/M on command; its automatic-loader variant and Phase 10 start on reset without waiting for USB.

docs.title: Choose the image for your current phase
docs.text:
Pico firmware supervises the board; Z80 programs execute from SRAM loaded through injected Z80 instructions. Build only the phase matching your installed circuit. Phase 0 is a checklist with no firmware target; the former Phase 7 fixture is now the Phase 6 bus-grant diagnostic.

Phase Source directory CMake target 1 src/stage01_supervisor/ z80_stage01_supervisor 2 src/stage02_buffers_clock/ z80_stage02_buffers_clock 3 src/stage03_mcp23s17/ z80_stage03_control_inputs 4 src/stage04_address_bus/ z80_stage04_address_bus 5 src/stage05_data_bus/ z80_stage05_data_bus 6 src/stage06_sram_dma/ z80_stage06_sram_loader 6 bus grants src/stage06_sram_dma/ z80_stage06_bus_grant 8 src/stage08_virtual_io/ z80_stage08_virtual_io 9 src/stage09_flash_storage/ z80_stage09_flash_storage 9 automatic loader src/stage09_flash_storage/ z80_stage09_cpm_loader 10 src/stage10_websocket_terminal/ z80_stage10_websocket_terminal

Build the target in the table for your phase. Its UF2 is written to build/src/<source-directory-name>/<target>.uf2; for example, Phase 3 uses build/src/stage03_mcp23s17/z80_stage03_control_inputs.uf2.

docs.title: VS Code deployment options
docs.text: Open Tasks: Run Task. Task names below match .vscode/tasks.json.

docs.title: Phase diagnostics
docs.text:
Each entry has both Build Pico - … (build only) and Flash Pico - … (build and flash firmware) tasks. Flashing preserves CP/M storage and ENV.

Task suffix (after either prefix) Description Phase 1 supervisor Check safe control outputs and sampled inputs. Phase 2 buffers and clock Check buffer isolation, clock generation, and reset. Phase 3 control inputs Check control signals and I/O address sampling. Phase 4 address bus Check address-trunk wiring. Phase 4 reset meter Hold reset and static control levels for meter checks. Phase 5 data bus Check data translation and buffer direction/isolation. Phase 6 SRAM loader Load and verify SRAM through injected Z80 instructions. Phase 6 bus grants Check BUSREQ/BUSACK ownership and release. Phase 6 stepped loader Run stepped SRAM diagnostics and full-memory checks. Phase 6 PWM memory Screen SRAM with test patterns under PWM clocking. Phase 6 PWM 20 MHz Screen all 64 KiB with memory patterns at 20 MHz. Phase 6 one-hour 20 MHz soak Run one hour of Z80 arithmetic and SRAM checks. Phase 6 14-hour 20 MHz soak Run the extended 14-hour arithmetic/SRAM soak. Phase 8 virtual I/O Check trapped Z80 I/O and USB terminal handling. Phase 6 20 MHz scope diagnostic Run a no-I/O Z80/SRAM loop for oscilloscope measurements.

docs.title: System and storage deployment
docs.text:
Task Effect Build and flash Pico - Phase 9 firmware Select Diagnostic or Automatic loader; update firmware only Build and flash Pico - Phase 10 firmware Update 20 MHz PIO firmware only Build and flash Pico - Phase 9 firmware and disks Select variant; replace all flash, including disks and ENV Build and flash Pico - Phase 10 firmware and disks Replace all flash, including disks and ENV Build and flash Pico - CP/M system and Drive A Rebuild and replace matching boot package and Drive A; preserve firmware, B–D, journal, and ENV Flash Pico - All disks (A-D) Regenerate/convert all four disks; validate and replace matching boot package and A–D; preserve firmware and ENV Flash Pico - Drive A Regenerate native system disk; check installed boot compatibility; replace A only Flash Pico - Drive B Convert BDS C source disk and replace B only Flash Pico - Drive C Convert Escape source disk and replace C only Flash Pico - Drive D Convert blank source disk and replace D only

Firmware-only tasks preserve the boot package, disks, journal, and ENV. Deployment tasks force entry without a running-firmware stop handshake; finish active work and follow the task requirements. Disk and full-flash replacements create no backups.

docs.title: Host emulator
docs.text: Prepare interactive CP/M emulator builds the host, adapter, and images without accessing the Pico. The Interactive CP/M emulator Run and Debug configuration runs it automatically; see the interactive test.

docs.title: 7.1 Firmware and CP/M Build
docs.text:
Phase 10 combines flash disks, the CP/M loader, and WebSocket terminal. The image target also assembles the optimized CCP/BDOS and board BIOS.

Install and configure the prerequisites using Toolchain. Use the VS Code tasks above to build/deploy; the tasks select the toolchain and configure CMake automatically.

Phase 10 opens USB configuration when Wi-Fi credentials are missing; use Ctrl-] c later. Settings are stored in ENV, including WIFI_SSID, WIFI_PASSWORD, and optional FS_SERVER; keep credentials out of build arguments. USB CP/M remains available without Wi-Fi. The shell also configures chat, weather, and timezone. Quitting after saved changes flushes disks and reboots; save application work first. See Phase 10 setup. Remote-FS I/O remains deferred.

docs.title: Building the full image set
docs.text:
From the configured repository root:

cmake --build build --target z80_cpm_images -j

The z80_cpm_images target builds Phase 10 and writes these files to build/cpm/:

Artifact Purpose z80boot.pkg Header, CRCs, and reset-ready 64 KiB Z80 image drive_a_cpm63k-z80.img Native CP/M system disk with the Z80 SBC BIOS and native AUTORUN AUTORUN.COM Native auto-run configuration utility, also installed on drive A drive_b_bdsc.img through drive_d_blank.img Converted 512 KiB disks z80romless-flash.bin Complete 4 MiB initial-provisioning image manifest.json Geometry, addresses, sizes, and SHA-256 values

AUTORUN supports cold-only, warm-only, both, and disabled modes. Fresh Drive A images disable it; settings occupy the final reserved system record. See native auto-run.

For USB-only Phase 9, choose one of these targets:

Target Output directory Startup z80_stage09_cpm_images build/cpm-stage09/ Ctrl+] l loads/verifies SRAM; Ctrl+] g starts CP/M z80_stage09_cpm_loader_images build/cpm-stage09-loader/ Automatically loads/verifies SRAM and starts CP/M on reset

Both produce the same artifact names with their respective Phase 9 firmware. For firmware alone, use Build and flash Pico - Phase 9 firmware and select Automatic loader. The manual variant’s Ctrl+] t disk test requires a reboot and fresh load before CP/M. See the Phase 9 workflows.

Run the host regression checks with:

python3 -m unittest discover -s src/cpm -p 'test_*.py' -v

docs.title: macOS console with picocom
docs.text:
Install a serial terminal using Toolchain. With the phase firmware running (not BOOTSEL), list its serial ports:

ls /dev/cu.usbmodem*

Identify the port belonging to the Pico, then start the terminal, replacing the example device name with the one listed on your computer:

picocom --baud 115200 --databits 8 --parity n --stopbits 1 --flow n /dev/cu.usbmodemXXXX

Follow the power requirements before connecting USB. Keep picocom open during console-driven tests. For Phase 1, type s to sample the inputs and w to run the control-output walking-one test; neither command needs Enter. Run w only with the required Phase 1 hardware population. To exit picocom, press Ctrl+A, then Ctrl+X. Close it before programming the Pico again or opening another terminal on the same port.

docs.title: 7.2 Flash Provisioning
docs.text:
Finish any running hardware test before provisioning

Building does not deploy. Do not replace firmware, open a second serial owner, or reset the Pico during an active soak. Disk/full-image replacement is destructive. This non-production development workflow creates no backups.

docs.title: Update tools
docs.text:
VS Code tasks use scripts/pico_build.py for firmware builds and scripts/pico_flash.py for firmware, disk, and CP/M updates. The flashing script uses pico_supervisor.py for serial discovery/control. Full-flash provisioning tasks call picotool directly. See Toolchain for setup and device selection and diagnostics below.

Change Procedure / VS Code task Replaced data Firmware only Build and flash Pico - Phase 9/10 firmware Firmware; preserves CP/M, disks, journal, and ENV Selected disks VS Code disk tasks Selected drives only CP/M assembly Build and flash Pico - CP/M system and Drive A Matching boot package and Drive A, including its files Initial provisioning / old 320 KiB layout Build and flash Pico - Phase 10 firmware and disks Entire flash, including disks and ENV

Selective storage updates require matching z80sbc-storage: firmware metadata and compatible BIOS geometry. For an existing 512 KiB installation without metadata, update firmware first. A 320 KiB installation requires full provisioning. Stop/flush and recover any pending journal before replacing disks. Updating the boot package alone leaves stale system records on Drive A.

docs.title: Full provisioning
docs.text:
Save required disks/settings first; full provisioning replaces all 4 MiB without backups. Use Build and flash Pico - Phase 10 firmware and disks, or its Phase 9 equivalent (select Diagnostic or Automatic loader). Follow the task’s device-selection and power prompts.

For routine updates, use the firmware-only, CP/M-system, or selected-disk tasks above. These preserve unselected regions.

Flash offsets (picotool addresses include the 0x10000000 XIP base):

Region Flash offset Boot package 0x1E0000 ENV (preserve during boot updates) 0x1FE000–0x1FFFFF Drive A / B / C / D 0x200000 / 0x280000 / 0x300000 / 0x380000

After Phase 10 joins Wi-Fi, open http://<pico-dhcp-address>:8088/. Use Ctrl-] s for supervisor status. Disk writes persist across reboots; full provisioning replaces them.

docs.title: Phase 10 PIO banking
docs.text:
Build and flash Pico - Phase 10 firmware now includes the board-validated PIO banking path at 20 MHz. It writes firmware only and preserves the matching CP/M boot package, disks and ENV. To build without flashing:

.venv-flash/bin/python scripts/pico_build.py --build-dir build \
  --target z80_stage10_websocket_terminal

Phases 9 and 10 always link the PIO1 20 MHz run-time library (z80_runtime_20mhz); there is no PWM or software-trap build option for them.

See the board verification notes.

docs.title: Deployment task requirements
docs.text:
• Save application work and finish active tests before deployment. Tasks force BOOTSEL entry without a running-firmware stop/flush handshake.
  • Apply external +5 V before USB, keep it applied during programming, and disconnect USB before removing +5 V. Program Phase 1 off-board initially.
  • If USB BOOTSEL entry fails, hold BOOTSEL while connecting the Pico as directed by the phase guide. Build tasks do not access hardware.
  • Flash tasks verify bytes and reboot; verification does not prove CP/M boots. Disk/full-flash replacement creates no backups.

docs.title: Storage update checks
docs.text:
Disk tasks regenerate native Drive A and convert B–D from src/disks/source-altair/. They do not compile applications; update source disks first. The CP/M system task assembles current .asm files without regenerating them through disassemble_cpm64.py; outputs go to build/cpm-system-update/.

Selective updates check installed layout metadata, boot/Drive A compatibility, and journal state before writing. A pending journal must be recovered first. Failed writes leave BOOTSEL without automatic retry/reboot. Multi-drive writes are not atomic: an earlier drive may already be replaced when a later one fails.

docs.title: Device selection and diagnostics
docs.text:
Tools select a unique Pico automatically. With several connected, specify --serial DEVICE_SERIAL. Close the serial terminal before standalone supervisor commands; flashing can close verified picocom owners but rejects unknown owners.

Command after .venv-flash/bin/python scripts/pico_supervisor.py Purpose ports List devices without opening them status / help Read status or the running firmware’s command menu stop Stop/flush CP/M and confirm clean storage wait-boot Await a fresh prompt and check status; does not reset

Supervisor commands use the Phase 9/10 USB protocol. Earlier firmware uses its phase-specific controls. See each script’s --help for current options.

For custom deployments, pico_flash.py supports firmware, system, and disks. Without --force, it requests a clean stop/flush. Useful options:

Option/command Purpose --port PORT / --serial SERIAL Restrict device selection --no-disconnect Refuse a busy serial port --stopped Use an operator-confirmed clean stop --bootsel --stopped --serial SERIAL Select a device already in BOOTSEL --no-reboot Remain in BOOTSEL after writes prepare --power-confirmed Stop/flush, enter BOOTSEL, and check journal without writing journal --serial SERIAL Read-check journal headers in BOOTSEL

prepare changes device state. Investigate failed stops or journal checks; do not bypass them. Custom disk inputs use repeated --drive DRIVE=IMAGE: native images are 524,288 bytes; Altair sources are accepted for B–D, while A requires a prepared native image matching the installed boot package.

  • Missing serial: install scripts/requirements-flash.txt in .venv-flash.
  • No unique Pico: list ports and select the intended serial number.
  • Failed stop/write: retain diagnostics and investigate before retrying.

Host-only script checks (no Pico access):

.venv-flash/bin/python -m unittest discover -s scripts -p 'test_pico*.py' -v
.venv-flash/bin/python -m unittest discover -s src/disks -p 'test_*.py' -v

docs.title: Building and Testing Pico C Firmware
docs.text: Run these software checks from the repository root. Native tests compile Pico logic for the host with hardware replacements; the instruction emulator runs Z80 code, not ARM firmware. Cross-builds use the real Pico SDK. Physical board testing remains a separate qualification step.

docs.title: 1. Understand the four validation layers
docs.text: Layer What runs What it establishes Native C/C++ host tests Maintained firmware logic compiled for the Mac or other host, with test SDK headers and functions Software state transitions, bounds, error handling and scripted fault/interleaving cases Independent Z80 execution Assembled Z80 programs, BIOS and CP/M in an instruction emulator, with modeled peripherals Actual Z80 instruction behavior, console/disk protocol use, boot and warm-boot behavior Pico cross-build ARM compiler and linker with the real Pico SDK Firmware compiles/links for Pico 2 W, SDK APIs are valid and artifacts fit the protected flash layout Physical bench qualification Deployed firmware, real Pico, Z80, SRAM, buffers and flash Actual USB behavior, multicore/interrupt operation, bus ownership, timing, electrical margins and sustained reliability

docs.title: 2. Prerequisites
docs.text:
Follow Toolchain for checkout and installation. Native tests need host C/C++ compilers, CMake, Ninja, Python 3.11+, and z80asm; CP/M images also need cpmtools. Set PYTHON to your installed interpreter:

export PYTHON=python3
"$PYTHON" --version

Node.js optionally enables terminal_keyboard; no npm installation is needed for native tests. The Pico SDK and Arm toolchain are needed only for SDK/TLS checks and firmware cross-builds.

docs.title: 3. Configure, build and run the native C tests
docs.text:
Use a separate build directory from the Pico cross-build. Explicitly select the host compilers, not arm-none-eabi-gcc:

cmake -S src/common/tests -B build/host-control -G Ninja \
  -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=cc \
  -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=c++
cmake --build build/host-control
ctest --test-dir build/host-control --output-on-failure --no-tests=error

The offline suite covers control/loader state, flash recovery, terminal queues, services, PIO banking, and HTTP/weather/chat parsing and transport. Warnings are errors and assertions remain enabled. The optional npm run test:control runs the same configure/build/test sequence.

On macOS/Linux, build the optional live runner with the firmware’s real Mbed TLS configuration and trust bundle, configure with PICO_SDK_PATH:

cmake -S src/common/tests -B build/host-control -G Ninja \
  -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=cc -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=c++ \
  -DPICO_SDK_PATH=/absolute/path/to/pico-sdk
cmake --build build/host-control --target http_live_test
python3 src/common/tests/http_transfer_integration.py \
  --runner build/host-control/http_live_test --https

The live runner needs openssl; --https also needs internet access. It tests local HTTP binary/text transfers, empty files, redirects, chunking, 404 errors, untrusted TLS rejection, and a verified GitHub HTTPS download. The production FT/parser/crypto code runs through a native socket adapter; Pico lwIP behavior is covered separately by offline transport tests.

docs.title: What replaces the hardware?
docs.text: Test SDK replacements model flash as a 4 MiB array, SRAM as arrays or injected cycles, GPIO/clock state, controlled time, USB queues, reboot, and scripted core interleavings. They enforce software contracts without reproducing physical IRQs, dual-core scheduling, or electrical timing.

docs.title: Phase 9 coverage and its boundaries
docs.text:
CTest name Maintained code exercised Important boundary flash_backend_recovery Actual flash_backend.c: manifest validation, byte loading/readback controller, cache, journal programming and recovery Flash, SRAM byte access, bus/clock calls and reboot are modeled stage09_usb_cpm Actual Phase 9 application functions and shared terminal_queue.c Boot/storage and SDK calls are substituted; command/stop interleavings are driven by the harness usb_core1_console Actual usb_console.c routing and bounded diagnostic ring Modeled SDK endpoints assert core-1 affinity; checks concurrent producer/drain, CRLF vs raw console bytes, backpressure, wrap, overflow, disconnect and init failure, not physical IRQ delivery stage09_autoboot_cpm The same application compiled with automatic startup, including its actual main initialization path SDK/storage calls are substituted; tests cover boot before USB connection, retained CP/M output, late failure reporting and no automatic retries disk_protocol Actual disk_device.c: Z80-facing commands, single-slot mailbox, BUSY ownership, reads, read-ahead hits/misses, seqlock fallback, write invalidation and fatal error latch The flash backend is stubbed; this is not the journal test assisted_loader, control_faults Shared injected-loader and control code Cycle/pin models do not establish physical setup/hold timing

Fault cases include invalid packages, cancelled loads, SRAM mismatches, interrupted journal writes, queue overflow, disconnects, and initialization failures. Harnesses check core ownership, disk-first scheduling, safe stops, and automatic boot before USB connection. A requested 20 MHz clock is checked as a software value, not measured as a signal.

For a focused native Phase 9 run:

cmake --build build/host-control \
  --target flash_backend_test stage09_test stage09_autoboot_test disk_test
ctest --test-dir build/host-control \
  -R '^(flash_backend_recovery|stage09_usb_cpm|stage09_autoboot_cpm|disk_protocol)$' \
  --output-on-failure --no-tests=error

The authoritative target/test list is src/common/tests/CMakeLists.txt.

docs.title: 4. Add the independent Z80 instruction emulator
docs.text:
This is an optional host-only dependency, separate from the Pico SDK. The environment name is shared with the existing arithmetic/SRAM soak tests. Create it once; reuse it if already configured:

"$PYTHON" -m venv build/math-soak-emulator
build/math-soak-emulator/bin/python -m pip install \
  -r src/common/tests/requirements-soak.txt

The requirements pin z80==1.0.0. Register that interpreter with the native test project and rebuild:

cmake -S src/common/tests -B build/host-control -G Ninja \
  -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=cc \
  -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=c++ \
  -DSOAK_EMULATOR_PYTHON="$PWD/build/math-soak-emulator/bin/python"
cmake --build build/host-control
ctest --test-dir build/host-control -N \
  -R '^(math_soak_z80_execution|scope_z80_execution|banked_memory_z80_execution|cpm_bios_z80_execution)$'

The listing must contain all four named execution tests. Without SOAK_EMULATOR_PYTHON, those tests are not registered; passing the remaining native suite does not imply they ran. --no-tests=error rejects an empty selection, but does not detect a partly missing selection: inspect the names.

Run the execution tests:

ctest --test-dir build/host-control \
  -R '^(math_soak_z80_execution|scope_z80_execution|banked_memory_z80_execution|cpm_bios_z80_execution)$' \
  --output-on-failure --no-tests=error

The math/scope and bank-transfer programs execute in the independent core. CP/M tests cover cold/warm boot, directories A–D, transients, AUTORUN, expanded disk writes, and the read-only disk diagnostic. Modeled peripherals establish instruction/protocol behavior, not Pico latency or hardware timing.

docs.title: 5. Validate CP/M image construction
docs.text:
With Python 3.11+, z80asm, and cpmtools available:

"$PYTHON" -m unittest discover -s src/cpm -p 'test_*.py' -v

These image tests check packaging, CRCs, exact memory/disk geometry, BIOS jump-table compatibility and CP/M translation. They are not the independent instruction-execution tests above.

The separate project-owned CP/M host also tests multi-extent programs and cross-drive writes; see the end-to-end CP/M procedure for its build and run commands. Neither host model replaces the Pico/physical-board gate.

docs.title: 6. Cross-compile the real Pico firmware
docs.text:
Install the SDK and complete Arm toolchain using Toolchain. Keep the firmware build separate from host tests.

Then configure the separate firmware build:

cmake -S . -B build/pico -G Ninja \
  -DPICO_BOARD=pico2_w \
  -DPICO_SDK_PATH="$HOME/GitHub/pico/pico-sdk" \
  -DPython3_EXECUTABLE="$(command -v "$PYTHON")"
cmake --build build/pico \
  --target z80_stage09_cpm_images z80_stage09_cpm_loader_images z80_cpm_images

This builds both Phase 9 variants and Phase 10 against the real SDK, without flashing. Phase 10 Wi-Fi credentials are configured through USB/ENV at runtime; they are not build arguments.

Output under build/pico/ Purpose src/stage09_flash_storage/z80_stage09_flash_storage.uf2 Deployable Phase 9 Pico firmware src/stage09_flash_storage/z80_stage09_cpm_loader.uf2 Automatic Phase 9 loader, independent of USB connection src/stage10_websocket_terminal/z80_stage10_websocket_terminal.uf2 Deployable Phase 10 Pico firmware cpm-stage09/ Matching Phase 9 boot package, disks, manifest and complete flash image cpm-stage09-loader/ Matching automatic-loader provisioning set cpm/ Matching Phase 10 provisioning set

Both phases run the Z80 at 20 MHz after SRAM loading/verification. Phase 9 starts on command or automatically with its loader variant; Phase 10 starts automatically. The linker reserves flash above 0x1D0000 for storage.

Use VS Code deployment tasks when ready to flash. BIOS changes require matching boot-package and Drive A images; full provisioning replaces disks and ENV.

docs.title: 7. Record software results, then qualify the board
docs.text:
Record the revision/local changes, tool versions, configuration, test names, results, and artifact hashes. Distinguish host tests, Z80 execution, SDK builds, and physical bench results. Software checks do not establish electrical margins, real interrupt/multicore timing, USB behavior, or power-cut recovery. They need no attached Pico; leave active hardware soaks and their serial owners undisturbed.

After software validation, follow the Phase 9 controlled USB workflow and its bench checklist. Observe the CP/M prompt and filesystem behavior, verify safe stop/recovery, and collect the required frequency/timing evidence. The Z80 clock has been scope-measured at 20 MHz on the project breadboard. Integrated CP/M, disk-I/O and receiving-pin timing checks remain separate qualification evidence.

docs.title: I/O Ports and Services
docs.text:
The Pico provides virtual peripherals through Z80 IN and OUT instructions. This page owns the port allocation and the ROMLESS-SVC/1 extended-service protocol, compatible with the ESP32 Altair io_ports.h and dcc DXSVC.H client. Extended services are implemented in both Phase 9 variants and Phase 10. Phase 8 retains its original bring-up diagnostics.

Maintained sources: transport and timers, service worker, clock and utilities, persistent environment store and public constants. See operational boundaries for the terminal, disk and clock-stop trap contracts.

docs.title: Port allocation
docs.text:
The four monitored address bits, A0/A1/A2/A4, provide 16 distinct ports: 0x00-0x07 and 0x10-0x17, using address & 0x17. Other addresses are aliases, not additional ports. For example, 0x08 aliases 0x00 and 0x18 aliases 0x10. No additional wiring is required.

Port (hex) Decimal Function Allocation 0x00 0 Terminal data, IN/OUT Fixed 0x01 1 Terminal status Fixed 0x02 2 Shared service command (OUT) / status (IN) Implemented 0x03 3 Shared service length-prefixed request bytes (OUT) Implemented 0x04 4 Shared service length-prefixed response bytes (IN) Implemented 0x05 5 BIOS cold-entry/CCP-handoff reports; Phase 9 disk-test and Phase 10 qualification results Reserved for diagnostics 0x06 6 Phase 9 disk-test bytes and Phase 10 qualification data; Phase 8 test results Reserved for diagnostics 0x07 7 SRAM bank select (OUT bit 0) / capability and selected bank (IN) PIO-only bank switching at 20 MHz; IN A,(07h) uses the trap to read availability and selected bank 0x10 16 Disk command (OUT) / status (IN) Fixed 0x11 17 Disk drive selection Fixed 0x12 18 Disk sector address, low byte Fixed 0x13 19 Disk sector address, high byte Fixed 0x14 20 Disk data, IN/OUT Fixed 0x15 21 HTTP(S) file-transfer command (OUT) / status (IN) Implemented in Phase 10 0x16 22 File-transfer filename/data bytes Implemented in Phase 10 0x17 23 Independent countdown timers and stopwatches, IN/OUT Implemented

This assigns or reserves all 16 ports. A port supports both IN and OUT, so a command and its status can share one number.

Bank select returns B4h/B5h when the loader verified banked SRAM, or 00h when unavailable (including when PIO is inactive). GP8 drives A16 through a spare AHCT244 channel. Use the banked-memory transfer library and wiring for C programs: a raw bank select also switches the executing code and stack.

The BIOS emits B0h on port 0x05 at cold entry and C0h immediately before handoff to CCP (including warm boot). Phase 9 observes these as execution milestones, not proof of a working CP/M prompt. Its read-only disk test uses port 0x06 for compared bytes and 5Ah/E1h on port 0x05 for completion/ failure. These diagnostic meanings are mode-specific and do not change the fixed terminal or disk ABI.

docs.title: HTTP and HTTPS file transfer
docs.text:
Phase 10 supports the existing FT.COM protocol on ports 21/22. Phase 9 returns ERROR for downloads.

Set HTTP_BASE_URL using interactive ENV to preserve URL case: run ENV, choose A to add or an entry number to edit, then Q to quit. For example:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AzureSphereCloudEnabledAltair8800/RetroGames/refs/heads/main/

Download text with FT -G LOVE.BAS, then run MBASIC LOVE. Use FT -GB PROGRAM.COM for binary files. Text mode normalizes CR LF and appends ^Z; binary mode preserves bytes. Files use uppercase 8.3 basenames and 128-byte record padding. Omit the filename (FT -G or FT -GB) to enter a case-preserving path at the prompt.

Full HTTP/HTTPS URLs need no base setting. Relative paths extend the base; a leading / starts at the server root. For a local server, run python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 0.0.0.0 and set the base to its LAN URL, for example http://192.168.1.10:8000/.

HTTPS requires Wi-Fi, synchronized SNTP time, and a trusted certificate chain and hostname. The CA bundle can be replaced with -DZ80_HTTP_CA_FILE=/absolute/path/to/bundle.pem. Plain HTTP needs no synchronized clock.

The port ABI is independent of shared services on ports 2/3/4:

Operation (decimal ports) Behavior OUT 21, 1 Reset; collect a new filename/URL OUT 22, byte Append filename bytes, terminated by NUL OUT 21, 3 Request the next chunk; status becomes BUSY IN 21 0 IDLE, 1 DATA, 2 EOF, 3 BUSY, 4 missing/empty base URL, 255 ERROR IN 22 Read count (0 = 256), then that many file bytes OUT 21, 4 Cancel/close; return to IDLE

Consume each chunk fully before requesting another. Empty files return EOF; reset after ERROR. Transfers stream on core 1 without loading the whole file into RAM. HTTP/1.0 and 1.1, chunked bodies, and up to five redirects are supported; HTTPS downgrades, compressed or malformed responses fail. Network stalls time out after 30 seconds, excluding consumer backpressure. See http_io.c and http_stream.c for implementation limits.

docs.title: Why A4 is monitored but A3 is not
docs.text:
Only A0/A1/A2/A4 are decoded (address & 0x17). A3, A5–A7, and the high address byte are ignored: 0x09 aliases terminal status 0x01, 0x30 aliases disk command 0x10, and 0xFF aliases timer port 0x17. A4 keeps console and disk registers distinct. This applies only to I/O; A3 still connects Z80 pin 33 to SRAM pin 9, not U7.

Each register has 16 low-byte aliases. A historical Phase 9 SURVEY scan reported 111 active addresses for seven registers (112 aliases, excluding 0x00), not 111 peripherals. Current services change that count. Scanning response ports can cause UNDERFLOW; RESET the shared channel afterward. Service group 0x30 is a command byte written to 0x02, not a port address.

docs.title: Framing and recovery
docs.text:
There is one outstanding shared transaction at a time:

  1. Write RESET (0x01) to port 0x02 to recover an unknown parser state.
  2. Write the service group to 0x02.
  3. Write a 16-bit little-endian payload length to 0x03, then that many payload bytes. Length includes the operation byte and must be 1-2048.
  4. Poll status on 0x02 with a bounded client-side polling limit.
  5. For RESPONSE_READY, read the 16-bit little-endian response length from 0x04, then exactly that many bytes. The last byte returns the channel to READY. An empty response still has its two length bytes.
  6. For COMPLETE, write ACK (0x00) to 0x02.
  7. For ERROR, read the length prefix and one-byte error code from 0x04, then ACK. If an overlapping transaction poisoned the parser, RESET is required instead.
Status Value Meaning READY 0x00 Can accept a new command COMPLETE 0x01 Successful operation with no response; ACK required RESPONSE_READY 0x02 Length-prefixed response can be read COLLECTING 0x03 Awaiting the length prefix or remaining payload BUSY 0x04 Worker executing the request ERROR 0xFF Length-prefixed error can be read

Special commands on 0x02 are ACK (0x00), RESET (0x01) and IDENTIFY (0x02). IDENTIFY needs no request and returns the text ROMLESS-SVC/1 with the usual response length prefix. Text replies have no trailing NUL; binary replies are not strings.

RESET invalidates pending replies through a generation identifier, but does not undo side effects or cancel a worker already writing flash. A new worker request can return BUSY_ERROR until that job finishes. RESET does not reset running timers or stopwatches. There is no automatic server timeout for an incomplete request: the client must use bounded polling, report failure and RESET. Reading status never acknowledges COMPLETE.

docs.title: Worker ownership
docs.text:
Core 0 handles traps and timers; core 1 runs slow services after disk work. The trap never performs flash/network work or waits for a service response. Worker replies are read in place and remain valid until consumed or discarded. Generation tags reject stale replies after RESET. One shared transaction may be outstanding at a time.

Error codes match the ESP32 client:

Code Error 0x01 / 0x02 UNKNOWN_GROUP / UNKNOWN_OPERATION 0x03 / 0x04 INVALID_LENGTH / INVALID_PARAMETER 0x05 / 0x06 UNAVAILABLE / BUSY_ERROR 0x07 / 0x08 / 0x09 TIMEOUT (reserved) / INVALID_STATE / UNDERFLOW 0x10 / 0x11 / 0x12 STORAGE_OPEN / STORAGE_READ / STORAGE_WRITE 0x13 / 0x14 CAPACITY / NOT_FOUND 0x15 / 0x16 CLOCK_UNSYNCED / REBOOT_CONFIRMATION

docs.title: Groups and operations
docs.text:
All integer request fields and binary results are little-endian.

Group Operations and payloads Result Timers 0x10 [0, id, duration_u32] starts/replaces; [1, id] queries COMPLETE or one byte, 1 running / 0 expired Stopwatches 0x11 [0, id] resets; [1, id] reads seconds; [2, id] reads milliseconds COMPLETE or unsigned 32-bit elapsed count Clock 0x20 [0] uptime seconds; [1] UTC ISO 8601; [2] local ISO 8601; [3] long local date; [4] DATE-style local date/time Text Utility 0x21 [0] random; [1, selector] system info; [2, 0xA5] confirmed reboot; [3] version; [4, state] set onboard LED; [5] read LED state Two random bytes, text, COMPLETE, or one LED-state byte Environment 0x30 Operations below Text or COMPLETE Weather 0x40 [0, field_id] reads text; [1] reads status Phase 10 cached weather; Phase 9 UNAVAILABLE Chat 0x50 Reset/append/submit/status/chunk operations below Phase 10 streaming OpenAI/Ollama; Phase 9 UNAVAILABLE Sense HAT 0x60 Recognized group without a Pico driver UNAVAILABLE

There are four countdown timers: IDs 0-2 take 0-65535 milliseconds; ID 3 takes 0-255 whole seconds. The shared duration field is four bytes for client compatibility, but out-of-range values are rejected. Timer 3 uses the ESP32 whole-second boundary rule: (current_ms / 1000 + duration) * 1000. A zero duration expires immediately.

There are three stopwatches, IDs 0-2. Reads do not reset them. A latched 32-bit millisecond count wraps after about 49.7 days; seconds wrap after about 136 years. Internal deadlines and uptime use a 64-bit monotonic clock.

Phase 10 starts SNTP against pool.ntp.org after Wi-Fi association. Calendar operations return CLOCK_UNSYNCED until the first valid synchronization. Phase 9 has no network time source and returns CLOCK_UNSYNCED for calendar queries. Uptime remains available in both. Local formatting uses persistent TZ in POSIX timezone syntax (for example, AEST-10); an absent TZ means UTC.

docs.title: CLOCK application time compatibility
docs.text:
The ESP32 Altair dcc Apps/CLOCK time interface is already provided by these services; no extra physical ports or separate time driver are needed:

CLOCK request Pico interface Result Local time Clock group 0x20, payload [2] on shared ports 2/3/4 YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS (19 bytes) Local date Clock group 0x20, payload [3] Monday, 01 January 2024 Uptime Clock group 0x20, payload [0] Decimal seconds since Pico startup Start refresh timer OUT 23: 0x12, 50, 0 Timer 2, 50 ms, low duration byte first Query refresh timer OUT 23: 0x22, then IN 23 1 while running, 0 when expired

The timer port works while a clock request is BUSY. Phase 10 uses SNTP at pool.ntp.org; calendar calls return CLOCK_UNSYNCED (0x15) until synchronized. Time then advances through Wi-Fi outages. Uptime and timers need no network.

Set local time with POSIX TZ, for example ENV TZ=AEST-10 (UTC+10) or ENV TZ=ACST-9:30 (UTC+09:30). POSIX signs are reversed; daylight-saving rules are supported. Changes apply on the next request. UTC_OFFSET is unused. CLOCK’s weather display requires OWM_KEY and OWM_LOCATION in Phase 10; Phase 9 reports weather UNAVAILABLE.

docs.title: CHAT application: OpenAI and Ollama
docs.text:
Phase 10 implements the framed ABI used by the ESP32 Altair dcc Apps/CHAT/CHATC11.C application. Use the existing CP/M application and its CHAT.SYS system-prompt file; no BIOS, pin or disk-layout change is needed. CHAT 1.7-c11 adds application-side thinking control as described below; earlier versions still work but leave thinking at the server default. Firmware builds do not install the application on a disk. Do not use the legacy physical chat ports 120-124: they alias unrelated peripherals with this board's address decoding.

All requests use group 0x50 through shared ports 2/3/4:

Payload Result [0] Cancel any previous request and clear request assembly; COMPLETE [1, json_bytes...] Append 1-2047 bytes; COMPLETE, or explicit CAPACITY/BUSY/invalid-input error [2] Cancel the connection and clear queued response/error text; COMPLETE; assembled request is retained [3] Submit the assembled request asynchronously; COMPLETE, or BUSY/empty-request error [4] One status byte: 0 EOF, 1 WAITING, 2 DATA_READY [5, maximum_u16] [status, count_u16, text_bytes...], with status after removing the returned bytes

maximum is 1-2045, bounded by the 2048-byte service payload. CHATC11 requests 256 bytes at a time and appends JSON in 2047-byte pieces. The assembled request limit is 8191 bytes, excluding its local NUL terminator. Overflow never silently truncates a request. Appending or resubmitting while active returns BUSY. Operation 0 cancels before reusing the request buffer, so a new turn recovers safely after CHATC11 fills its local response buffer or times out. Operation 2 also cancels immediately. Shared transport RESET only invalidates the mailbox reply; as with ENV, it does not undo service side effects.

docs.title: Provider configuration
docs.text:
For a local Ollama server with its OpenAI-compatible API:

ENV CHAT_PROVIDER=compatible
ENV CHAT_ENDPOINT=http://192.168.1.26:11434/v1/chat/completions
ENV -I CHAT_MODEL=phi4-mini:3.8b
ENV CHAT_MAX_TOKENS=1024
ENV CHAT_TEMPERATURE=0.7

CHAT 1.7-c11 reads CHAT_THINK each turn for compatible/Ollama providers: false sends reasoning_effort=none, true sends medium, and default omits the field. Model/server support determines the effect. Missing/empty values default to false; invalid values fail submission. OpenAI requests omit this setting. Older CHAT binaries retain server defaults.

The USB shell also offers Ctrl-] c → 3 Chat → 7 configure thinking. CHAT_PROVIDER=ollama aliases compatible. Use an installed model name; the example address/model is configuration, not a required endpoint.

For OpenAI:

ENV CHAT_PROVIDER=openai
ENV -I CHAT_OPENAI_KEY=<your-api-key>
ENV -I CHAT_MODEL=gpt-4o-mini
ENV CHAT_MAX_TOKENS=1024
ENV CHAT_TEMPERATURE=0.7

The ENV CLI evaluates +/- inside ordinary assignments as arithmetic. Use literal -I for API keys and model names; it only inserts absent keys. To replace an existing key, first use ENV -D CHAT_MODEL (or ENV -D CHAT_OPENAI_KEY), then its literal insert command. Do not paste real keys into logs or source control. ENV is plaintext onboard flash, not encrypted secret storage.

An absent provider defaults to openai. OpenAI always uses https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions, ignoring CHAT_ENDPOINT. Only OpenAI requests carry CHAT_OPENAI_KEY; a saved OpenAI key is never forwarded to an Ollama/compatible endpoint. Authenticated third-party compatible providers are not supported. URLs require an explicit path and accept HTTP or HTTPS, a DNS name/IPv4 address, and an optional port 1-65535. User-info, fragments, whitespace and control characters are rejected. Limits are 95 host bytes, 103 authority bytes, 159 path bytes, and 255 key bytes.

Core 1 reloads provider/endpoint/key from durable ENV on each submission. CHATC11 owns the JSON model, history, system prompt, token count, temperature and thinking parameter; restart CHAT after changing model/token/temperature settings. Thinking/provider changes are read at the next turn by CHAT 1.7-c11. HTTPS requires synchronized SNTP time and verifies certificate dates, chain and hostname using the bundled GTS Root R4. There is no insecure TLS fallback. Compatible HTTPS endpoints need a chain trusted by that root; arbitrary private/self-signed CAs are not supported. Plain HTTP Ollama works without SNTP but must remain on a trusted LAN.

docs.title: Streaming and limits
docs.text:
Core 1 owns the 4096-byte response ring and async client. Bounded network polls and backpressure keep the trap and other services responsive; generation tokens reject stale callbacks after cancellation.

The decoder requires HTTP 200, uncompressed text/event-stream, and a final [DONE]. It accepts content-length, connection-close, and chunked bodies. Only choices[0].delta.content is displayed; other fields are ignored. JSON/UTF-8 are validated and converted to CP/M-safe 7-bit text. Limits are 4096 header bytes, 4095 bytes per HTTP/SSE line or decoded event, and 16 JSON nesting levels.

The firmware deadline is 120 seconds, including backpressure. Failures publish Chat: ... after queued text, then EOF; requests are not automatically replayed. CHATC11 also has a roughly 30-second no-content timeout and an 8191-byte answer limit, so it may stop first. Diagnostics omit credentials and conversation text.

docs.title: OpenWeatherMap weather
docs.text:
Phase 10 supports the ESP32 Altair weather ABI through shared service group 0x40 on ports 2/3/4. Do not use the old physical ports 46/47/200: these alias other peripherals on this board.

  • Payload [1] returns one status byte: 0 NONE, 1 FETCHING, 2 READY, or 3 ERROR. Status reads never wait for an HTTP request.
  • Payload [0, field_id] returns length-prefixed text, without a trailing NUL. Units and error text are available before the first successful fetch; other fields return UNAVAILABLE until data exists.
  • Unknown operations, incorrect lengths and unknown fields return the usual explicit service errors. An HTTP failure is exposed by status ERROR and field 12, not by inventing weather data or failing every status query.
Field Text 0 City 1 / 2 Current condition / description 3 / 13 Current temperature / feels-like temperature 4 / 5 Humidity percent / wind speed 6 / 7 Forecast condition / description 8 / 14 Forecast temperature / feels-like temperature 9 First forecast block time, as supplied by OWM in UTC 10 Seconds since the last successful current-data refresh 11 Temperature units: C, F, or K 12 Last error or forecast warning; empty after a fully successful refresh

Temperatures and wind speed are rounded to integer strings as in the reference driver; wind is m/s for metric/standard and mph for imperial. Only the first forecast block is requested (cnt=1).

Configure the existing durable ENV store:

ENV OWM_KEY=<your-api-key>
ENV OWM_LOCATION=Sydney,AU
ENV OWM_UNITS=metric

OWM_KEY is limited to 40 bytes, location to 64 bytes. Location accepts a city/country query or a validated lat=-33.8&lon=151.2 coordinate pair. The ENV CLI treats + and - inside assignments as arithmetic; use its literal insert mode for coordinates or names containing these characters: ENV -D OWM_LOCATION, then ENV -I OWM_LOCATION=lat=-33.8&lon=151.2. Units are metric (default), imperial, or standard. Missing keys or invalid settings produce an explanatory error; no request is sent. Settings are reloaded at most once per second. Changing them cancels an in-flight request, clears data belonging to the old configuration, and starts a new fetch without rebooting. ENV remains plaintext onboard flash; do not publish its contents. Firmware diagnostics never print the key, request URL or provider response body.

Core 1 waits for Wi-Fi/SNTP, then 5 seconds before fetching. Refreshes repeat every 20 minutes; initial failures retry every 2 minutes for five retries. Reconnection triggers a fresh fetch. Cached data survives fetch failures with an increasing age and ERROR status. A forecast-only failure keeps current conditions READY and reports a warning in field 12.

HTTPS requires certificate-chain, hostname, and SNTP-based date verification, using weather_ca.pem. There is no insecure fallback. Requests have a 15-second deadline, 16 KiB wire/8 KiB decoded limits, and at most 2 KiB of headers. Content-length, connection-close, and chunked responses are supported; malformed, oversized, or compressed bodies fail. TLS/parsing run on core 1, outside Z80 traps.

docs.title: System information and reboot
docs.text: System-info selectors are 0 = hostname zeta-80-xxxxxx (the final six hexadecimal characters of the board ID, in lowercase), 1 = current Wi-Fi IPv4 address, and 2 = Pico unique board ID. The IPv4 selector returns UNAVAILABLE without a connection, including Phase 9. Reboot requires the exact confirmation byte 0xA5; it flushes queued/cached disk writes, then core 0 disables traps, holds reset, isolates the data paths and stops the clock before watchdog reboot. New disk commands are gated before the reboot job is published, with BUSY+ERROR reported on disk status, so writes cannot race the final flush. Failed flushes reopen the gate and report STORAGE_WRITE instead.

docs.title: Onboard LED device
docs.text:
Utility group 0x21 controls the Pico 2 W LED in Phases 9/10:

  • [4, 0] turns it off; [4, 1] turns it on. Success returns COMPLETE; ACK it.
  • [5] returns the last successfully commanded state (0/1), initially off.
  • Invalid state/length returns INVALID_PARAMETER/INVALID_LENGTH; driver failure returns UNAVAILABLE without changing the reported state.

The worker initializes the wireless-chip driver lazily on core 1. Phase 9 uses its LED-only backend; no Wi-Fi connection is required. State is not persisted, and transport RESET leaves it unchanged. This is asynchronous LED control.

For example, write 21h to port 02h, then 02h,00h,04h,01h to port 03h (group, length prefix, set operation, on). Poll for COMPLETE/ERROR, then ACK success or drain and acknowledge the error.

docs.title: Persistent environment API
docs.text:
Keys are case-insensitive, stored uppercase, and contain 1-16 non-NUL bytes. Values contain 0-255 non-NUL bytes. Empty and absent values are distinct: GET of an empty value returns a zero-length response; an absent key returns NOT_FOUND.

Operation Payload Result 0 reset / 1 initialize [operation] COMPLETE 2 get [2, key_length_u8, key_bytes] Value text 3 set [3, key_length_u8, key_bytes, value_length_u16, value_bytes] COMPLETE, durable before success 4 delete [4, key_length_u8, key_bytes] COMPLETE or NOT_FOUND 5 list [5] KEY=VALUE lines with CRLF 6 count [6] Decimal count text 7 clear [7] COMPLETE, durable before success 8 exists [8, key_length_u8, key_bytes] COMPLETE or NOT_FOUND 9 execute ENV command [9, command_text], at most 511 command bytes Text

The ENV command parser is shared with the maintained host driver. It supports listing, NAME, NAME=VALUE, copying another variable, numeric addition/ subtraction, NAME+N, NAME-N, -I NAME=VALUE, -D NAME, -N, NOW (uptime seconds), and -H/HELP/?. Numeric overflow is an explicit error. No additional physical ports expose the host's private legacy selectors.

The store supports at most 128 entries, subject to a 3,840-byte serialized snapshot limit. Each entry consumes key length + value length + 2 bytes. There is room for at least 14 maximum-length key/value pairs. Requests that exceed storage or the 2,048-byte reply capacity fail explicitly; LIST never silently truncates. After a failed write, the in-memory state is reloaded from the newest valid durable snapshot; an error does not undo a commit that already reached flash.

Two 4 KiB sectors at 0x1FE000 and 0x1FF000 occupy unused space in the boot partition, beyond the boot payload ending at 0x1F1000 (exclusive). Firmware, the disk journal, boot package and all four disk offsets remain unchanged. Each snapshot has a version, sequence number, payload CRC32 and header CRC32. Updates erase/program the inactive sector, verify the payload, and commit the header last. The previous committed snapshot remains recoverable after an interrupted replacement. A durable empty baseline is established before the first mutation. Repeated unchanged writes do not erase flash.

Flash erase/program uses the disk backend's BUSREQ/BUSACK and flash-safe multicore handshake. A non-success flash-safe result fails closed through watchdog reboot. Both sectors erased means a new empty store; neither erased nor CRC-valid means STORAGE_READ, not a fabricated empty environment. Flash has finite endurance: use countdown timers and stopwatches, not repeated persistent writes, for high-frequency counters.

Preserving environment variables during updates

Firmware-only and exact boot-package-only updates preserve variables. Complete 4 MiB provisioning, mass erase and flash_nuke.uf2 destroy them. Do not write a padded 128 KiB boot-partition image: it would overwrite ENV. Full generated images deliberately contain erased environment sectors.

docs.title: Worked request bytes
docs.text:
These examples show the actual wire framing; prefer the existing dcc svc_operation_send(), svc_get_text() and timer helpers in DXSVC.H. Use bounded client polling, drain error frames, and RESET after failure.

Read uptime:
  OUT 02,20
  OUT 03,01  OUT 03,00       ; payload length = 1
  OUT 03,00                 ; operation = uptime seconds
  IN 02 until 02 or FF       ; RESPONSE_READY or ERROR
  IN 04 twice, then length bytes

Set TZ=UTC0:
  OUT 02,30
  OUT 03,0A  OUT 03,00       ; payload length = 10
  OUT 03,03  OUT 03,02       ; SET, key length
  OUT 03,54  OUT 03,5A       ; "TZ"
  OUT 03,04  OUT 03,00       ; value length = 4
  OUT 03,55  OUT 03,54  OUT 03,43  OUT 03,30  ; "UTC0"
  IN 02 until 01 or FF       ; COMPLETE or ERROR
  OUT 02,00                 ; ACK only after success

docs.title: Independent timer port
docs.text:
Port 0x17 uses no shared-service framing and remains usable while the service worker is BUSY. Its timers/stopwatches are the same instances as groups 0x10/0x11.

OUT command Subsequent transfers 0x00 Reset only this parser; running timers remain unchanged 0x10-0x12 Two OUT bytes, low then high: start millisecond timer 0-2 0x13 One OUT byte: start whole-second timer 3 0x20-0x23 IN returns selected timer's running flag 0x30 IN returns running bitmask, bits 0-3 0x40-0x42 Reset stopwatch 0-2 0x50-0x52 Four IN bytes: latched stopwatch seconds, little-endian 0x60-0x62 Four IN bytes: latched stopwatch milliseconds, little-endian

The parser initially selects the timer bitmask. An invalid command, an IN during parameter collection, or stopwatch over-read returns 0xFF and requires recovery. To recover an unknown state, perform IN 0x17, then OUT 0x17, 0x00. Multi-byte port-23 operations must not be interleaved with other users of that port.

docs.title: Availability and validation
docs.text:
Phase 10 implements file transfer, weather, and chat. Phase 9 reports download errors and weather/chat UNAVAILABLE. Sense HAT is unavailable in both. The ESP32 interrupt-timer ABI is unsupported: 0x07 selects SRAM banks, and this board has no Pico-to-INT# driver or interrupt-vector path.

Host tests cover framing, aliases, recovery, timers, ENV persistence/capacity, calendar formatting, HTTP/SSE parsing, cancellation, TLS configuration, and phase routing. They do not establish physical timing, live provider behavior, or power-cut recovery.

  • Phase 3 owns address wiring.
  • Phase 8 owns initial trap checks.
  • Phase 9 owns flash bring-up.
  • DCC documentation covers port access and CP/M BDOS/BIOS APIs.

docs.title: The three operating states
docs.text:
State Who controls the buses? What you should expect Injected loading Z80 alone drives SRAM addresses and writes RESET# is released after slow reset clocks; Pico supplies instructions with SRAM reads inhibited and verifies CPU-written RAM. Normal execution Z80 addresses SRAM directly Both Pico data paths are isolated; ordinary memory access needs no Pico software. Trapped I/O Z80 holds its address while the Pico services one byte HCT32 WAIT and clock stopping hold the cycle; four buffered address bits select the port.

Runtime flash writes temporarily request the Z80 bus using BUSREQ#/BUSACK#. This is different from cold boot: a running CPU must acknowledge the request before flash programming. The Pico never drives memory addresses or writes, even during a bus grant. The detailed rules below protect that boundary.

docs.title: 6.1 Hardware-WAIT-Assisted Clock-Stop Trap Protocol
docs.text:
IORQ# LOW reaches HCT32 pin 4 and makes WAIT# pin 6 LOW while Pico GP9 IO_RELEASE is LOW. In Phases 6-8 the buffered IORQ# GPIO edge interrupts core 0, which stops the PWM clock (Phases 9-10 complete every cycle in PIO; see PIO I/O service). The fully static CMOS Z80 tolerates the stopped clock. After settling, firmware first checks that IORQ# remains LOW, then requires exactly one of RD#/WR# active and samples A0/A1/A2/A4 before servicing data. If IORQ# is already HIGH, it counts an inactive interrupt and resumes the clock without touching the data paths or IO_RELEASE. These events remain included in control_errors so they cannot silently pass timing qualification.

For OUT, U10 receives the CPU byte; for IN, U9 supplies a preloaded reply. Only after the path is configured does GP9 rise. Firmware completes the I/O cycle with slow single clocks, observes IORQ/strobe release, disables both paths, waits at least 1 us for isolation, lowers GP9, then restores the clock. Every slow step includes a fixed 1 us LOW settling interval before the control sample, preventing an extra clock caused by propagation or input-synchronizer delay. This prevents a later memory read from re-enabling the Pico output. RD#-qualified U9 OE provides additional strobe gating, not software-independent ownership arbitration.

WAIT assertion is fixed logic, not IRQ/PIO dependent. HCT32 propagation, WAIT setup/hold, run-clock-to-SIO transitions, and data setup still require captures. The 500 ms release timeout fails closed through RESET and watchdog recovery.

docs.title: 6.2 Terminal I/O over Pico WebSocket
docs.text:
See I/O ports and services for the overall allocation of fixed terminal/disk ports, reserved diagnostics and proposed extensions.

The final terminal is a virtual I/O peripheral implemented by the Pico, not a Z80-side UART. Z80 software performs ordinary IN and OUT instructions against a small terminal port pair; the Pico intercepts those cycles through the Section 6.1 clock-stop trap, then resumes the CPU after sampling or supplying the data byte. A browser connects to the Pico over Wi-Fi and receives the terminal stream through a WebSocket server running on the Pico 2 W.

Wi-Fi/WebSocket is the intended final and day-one operating terminal. Before networking is introduced, Phase 8 and Phase 9 use USB CDC over the Pico's existing USB connector as an intermediate terminal transport. USB CDC consumes no GPIO and appears as /dev/cu.usbmodem... on macOS. It lets the same 0x00/0x01 virtual-port contract and bounded queues be tested without lwIP timing in the loop. Keep diagnostics framed or on a separate CDC interface so debug text cannot become CP/M input. Those applications uses ordinary bytes as terminal input and reserves Ctrl-] followed by one command byte for framed diagnostics. Phase 10 selects Wi-Fi/WebSocket exclusively while a browser is connected. USB remains the CP/M fallback before connection and after disconnect; framed Ctrl-] diagnostics remain available even while the browser owns CP/M. Network setup uses Ctrl-] n and the existing persistent ENV store.

The WebSocket server must run on the Pico's other core so Wi-Fi, lwIP, HTTP serving, and WebSocket polling cannot interfere with the timing of the Z80-facing supervisor path. Core 0 owns GPIO, clock stop/resume, assisted loading, and the I/O trap. Core 1 owns USB initialization and interrupts, USB console/supervisor parsing, Wi-Fi association, the embedded terminal page, WebSocket accept/send/receive, and network polling. The cores share terminal byte queues, one immutable disk-write queue, a small request/result pair for Z80 bus ownership, and atomic terminal/disk status words; they share no raw bus GPIO ownership. Phase 10 uses the CYW43 polling architecture so network callbacks execute only on core 1. USB commands use a bounded queue to request Z80 actions on core 0; USB never directly changes bus pins. Core 0 publishes CPU state and receives published cancellation/connectivity flags instead of reading USB. All stdout uses a bounded diagnostic ring drained only by core 1. Its default alarm pool is explicitly initialized there, keeping USB background work off core 0. Core 1 starts before journal recovery and participates in flash lockout; runtime workers start only after SRAM verification. Only core 1 reads or writes the runtime ENV backend.

Use the pico-altair-8800 WebSocket console as the software pattern: one embedded HTML terminal page, one WebSocket server, and byte queues between the CPU-facing side and the network-facing side. The trap hook must never call lwIP, print, sleep, wait for a browser, or block on a queue. It may only enqueue Z80 output bytes, dequeue already-buffered browser input bytes, and report terminal status. Core 1 may drop, drain, or back-pressure network data; it must not hold terminal critical sections across network or flash work or touch any Z80 bus GPIO. The trap path uses no SDK queues. Terminal status is read lock-free from atomically stored ring counts; because core 0 is the only receive consumer and transmit producer, a racing core-1 update can only make one poll conservative. A short SDK critical section serializes terminal data dequeue/enqueue and disconnect cleanup so output cannot race with a disconnect on the other core. Include that bounded spinlock contention in measured trap-latency qualification.

The initial terminal decode is intentionally small:

Port Direction Function 0x00 Z80 OUT Terminal transmit byte from Z80 to host terminal 0x00 Z80 IN Terminal receive byte from host to Z80; returns 0x00 if empty 0x01 Z80 IN Terminal status: bit 0 = receive byte available, bit 1 = transmit-ready (queue has room or transport disconnected), bit 7 = transport connected (USB in Phase 9; browser or fallback USB in Phase 10)

Connected terminals retain the 512-byte output buffer. If it is full, a new Z80 output write is discarded and the TX-drop counter increments; older queued characters remain unchanged and in order. The trap never waits for space. Transmit-ready remains clear until space is available, so software that polls it can still wait voluntarily before writing. This policy applies to USB and browser output alike. Without a connected terminal, output writes are discarded immediately and transmit-ready remains set, preventing CP/M console output from waiting for a client. Disconnecting clears queued output; reconnecting does not replay it. These intentional discards do not increment the terminal overflow counter. Phase 10 also clears queued input/output on browser/USB handover and rejects additional browser sessions without changing the active owner. Wi-Fi-only events leave USB-owned queues intact. The Phase 10 browser and firmware use a sequenced, acknowledged binary protocol: up to four 512-byte output frames are retained in flight and cumulatively acknowledged after xterm consumes them. Output survives temporary send failures without duplication. One pending browser input frame waits for RX-queue space and is admitted on the next service pass rather than waiting for retransmission or evicting older bytes. The terminal sends a ping every five minutes. A missing pong is counted at the next five-minute heartbeat; a fifth miss releases the browser to USB. A stalled output ACK still times out after 15 seconds.

This is enough for ROM monitors, BASIC, CP/M console glue, and small diagnostics. If later software needs modem-control style signals, add more virtual status bits before adding hardware.

docs.title: 6.3 Onboard Flash CP/M Disk Storage
docs.text:
The Pico's 4 MiB onboard flash stores its firmware, the Z80 boot package, and four persistent read/write CP/M disks. No external storage, SPI bus, or extra GPIO is required. The linker limits Pico firmware to the first 1.8125 MiB and reserves the remainder as follows:

Region Flash offset Size Contents Journal 0x1D0000 64 KiB Eight rotating metadata/data sector pairs Boot partition 0x1E0000 128 KiB Header/image through 0x1F0FFF; ENV in final 8 KiB Environment (inside boot partition) 0x1FE000 8 KiB Two alternating CRC-checked 4 KiB snapshots Drive A 0x200000 512 KiB CP/M system disk Drive B 0x280000 512 KiB CP/M data disk Drive C 0x300000 512 KiB CP/M data disk Drive D 0x380000 512 KiB CP/M data disk

Disk format. Each disk is exactly 524,288 bytes: 128 tracks of 32 sequential 128-byte records. This project-specific format is not IBM 3740 SSSD. CMake automatically converts the current src/disks/source-altair/ images into build/cpm-converted/ before packaging CP/M. It tracks source-disk changes, so rebuilding cannot silently reuse stale checked-in images. src/disks/convert_altair_disks.py removes Altair framing and skew, extracts the CP/M records, and pads the images from 77 to 128 tracks. Its default output remains src/disks/generated/ for refreshing the checked-in reference images.

Build and provisioning. The z80_cpm_images target automatically creates the boot package, four disk images, and combined build/cpm/z80romless-flash.bin. The build does not flash the Pico. For initial setup, put it in BOOTSEL mode and run:

cmake --build build --target z80_cpm_images -j
picotool load -v build/cpm/z80romless-flash.bin -t bin -o 0x10000000
picotool reboot

Use separate artifacts only for selective updates. The firmware build and provisioning page gives their commands and addresses. Full provisioning, flash_nuke.uf2, and mass erase destroy existing disk contents and environment variables, so keep backups.

Phases 9 and 10 implement the ROMLESS-SVC/1 extended I/O protocol, including persistent environment variables. ENV uses the unused boot-partition tail, not the disk journal. Exact firmware-only and boot-package-only updates preserve it; never provision a padded whole-boot-partition image over the ENV sectors.

Runtime behavior. On boot-image initialization, the Pico recovers any interrupted disk update, validates z80boot.pkg, copies its image to Z80 SRAM, and verifies the copy, then resets to PC zero before execution. The BIOS transfers one 128-byte disk record at a time. Core 0 serves reads from memory-mapped flash and queues writes to core 1, which maintains one 4 KiB cache in RP2350 internal SRAM, separate from the Z80's external SRAM. Directory writes flush immediately. Other writes flush on cache eviction, an explicit BIOS request, warm boot, or 250 ms of inactivity.

Phase 9 waits for USB commands rather than automatically executing CP/M: Ctrl+] l loads/verifies with slow injected clocks and holds reset afterward; Ctrl+] g starts at the scope-measured 20 MHz Z80 clock using a 120 MHz supervisor clock. The manifest must describe a complete 65,536-byte image beginning with JP FC00h. BIOS reports on reserved port 0x05 distinguish cold entry (B0h) and CCP handoff (C0h) from the act of releasing reset. A real prompt and filesystem tests remain necessary. The separate Phase 9 automatic-loader target and Phase 10 use automatic verified startup at 20 MHz.

A 64 KiB journal makes 4 KiB sector replacement recoverable after power loss. At startup, firmware replays complete, CRC-valid committed entries and rejects invalid or out-of-range entries. Before erasing a target, it verifies the staged journal data sector and header page by readback; afterward it verifies the complete new target and clears the header. The Phase 9 implementation guide defines the journal sequence, multicore lockout, failure handling, and tests.

Flash has finite erase endurance. The cache coalesces writes and skips clean blocks, but sustained write-heavy workloads should use replaceable or wear-levelled storage.

docs.title: 6.4 System Performance Envelope & Constraints
docs.text:
• I/O Decode Width: Four buffered lines A0/A1/A2/A4, mask 0x17. A3/A5-A7 and the high byte alias; terminal 00/01 and disk 10-14 remain distinct.

  • Trap Latency Profile: HCT32-generated WAIT# covers the interval from IORQ# falling until IO_RELEASE reports a configured data path. The Pico stops the static CPU clock while servicing the cycle. Measure IORQ#-to-WAIT#, WAIT# setup/hold, the final run-clock edge, and IO_RELEASE-to-WAIT# release and completion (stepped in Phases 6-8; PIO in Phases 9-10) at every claimed rate. The design remains suitable for low-rate virtual peripherals, not high-speed line tracing.

  • Clock Validation Targets:

  • Bring-Up Target: 1 MHz, qualified only after a logic-analyzer capture proves every I/O cycle stops before the Z80 samples or releases its data.

  • Qualification Range: 2 MHz – 6 MHz, tested in the increments in the frequency-qualification plan. No rate in this range is guaranteed in advance.

  • Experimental Range: Requests 6.5 MHz – 8 MHz may be attempted in requested 500 kHz steps only after 6 MHz passes. At 144 MHz clk_sys, the 6.5 MHz request still produces 6 MHz; subsequent requests produce approximately 6.545455, 7.2, and exactly 8 MHz nominally. These rates are exploratory, not design claims, because the 55 ns SRAM and breadboard margin dominate despite the faster buffer.

  • Failure Boundary: Any WAIT setup/hold failure, SRAM setup failure, malformed clock edge, or repeatable memory/I/O error ends qualification at the preceding passing step.

  • 20 MHz CPU Rating: The Z84C0020PEC rating applies to the CPU, not this breadboard system with no memory wait states. At 20 MHz a clock period is 50 ns, shorter than the SRAM's 55 ns rated access time even before AHCT244/HCT32 propagation, Z80 setup, and breadboard delay. Reaching 20 MHz requires a redesigned control path, hardware-generated memory and I/O wait states (or deterministic clock gating), and a PCB-level signal- integrity review; changing the Pico PWM frequency is insufficient.

  • PCB Deferred: The existing layout implements the previous circuit. It provides no qualification evidence or manufacturing package for this assisted-loader revision.

docs.title: PIO I/O service
docs.text: Phases 9 and 10 use the PIO clock and I/O engine as their only 20 MHz run clock and I/O entry: every IN and OUT completes in PIO, and the stepped software sequence above is used only by the Phase 6-8 GPIO trap. OUT 07h drives A16 in PIO; other OUTs are queued for core 0, and an IN waits, with WAIT and CLK held, for core 0's reply byte. Core 0 services them in bus order, so an IN always observes every earlier OUT. The supervisor stop parks the Z80 with BUSREQ#, applies queued OUTs and only then checks disk quiescence; its flush is a separate core-1 request, never a command injected into the Z80 disk port. If the PIO resources cannot be allocated, CP/M start fails closed with RESET held LOW. Without a verified second SRAM bank, the engine still runs the clock and I/O but leaves GP8/A16 on SIO, so runtime banking reports unavailable and OUT 07h cannot switch banks. No extra wiring is required beyond the A16 modification.
